title: The Fathers on Isaiah
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The prophets sometimes saw coming events as eyewitnesses, and the kings' times are named so that God may be seen to speak what suited the ways of each.
comments.comment:
I do not think anyone would be speaking falsely if he said this about the holy prophets: they received not only the knowledge of things to come, as the Holy Spirit made the matter shine clear to them and sounded it into their minds, but at times they also became eyewitnesses of the events themselves. So the blessed prophet Isaiah seems to have seen with the eyes of the mind the sufferings that would come upon Judah in due time: here the ranks of the enemy ravaging the land, there the cities laid waste, houses set on fire, and all that enemies do by the laws of war. That is why this stands written at the head of the prophecy: “The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw against Judah and against Jerusalem” (Isaiah 1:1).

He usefully marks the times of the kings, so that God may be seen to speak through the prophet what suited the ways of each.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the opening verse means by a vision and why the reigns are named.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Heaven and earth are called as witnesses so that the angels and the whole earth may know the ways of Israel's impiety and see that God did not cast off His own people without cause.
comments.comment:
He has very good reason, then, to call heaven and earth to witness. He was about to bring charges against Israel, and he wants the angels in heaven, and the whole earth itself, to know the ways of that people's impiety, so that no one would think that God had been moved without cause, or had rushed, over small and quite trivial faults, to cast off the beloved, the people set apart as His own portion, whom long ago He had rescued with very great strength from the greed of the Egyptians.

For He had mercy on them as a people wronged beyond all reason, weighed down by an unwilling servitude, contrary to the nobility that befitted their fathers and was native to them. And when their oppressors resisted, they were bitterly punished, as God hurled every kind of torment upon them. So, just as Israel's being taken up as His own was most conspicuous, He wants the manner of their casting off not to go unknown either.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain reason why heaven and earth are summoned.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If the elements themselves are meant, it is because heaven and earth had been turned against Pharaoh in the plagues for the sake of redeemed Israel.
comments.comment: If some would rather take it that the elements themselves are being called by the prophet's voice, the force of the thought would not miss the fitting sense, for those who have considered the following. Israel, as I said, was being redeemed through Moses from the ungodliness of the Egyptians. But when Pharaoh, impiously rising up against the commands of God, said, “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5:2), creation armed itself with its own Master against those who were hostile. From above, from heaven, came a great many striking signs, and likewise a great many wonders on the earth itself. Heaven sent down hail (Exodus 9:23), and the earth threw up frogs, as it is written (Exodus 8:6); the water was changed into blood (Exodus 7:20); and when furnace soot was scattered and clouded the air, sores and blisters broke out on the bodies of everyone (Exodus 9:8–10). So, since the very elements had all but laboured in vain over those who had been redeemed, he says: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah 1:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In another sense, Israel dishonoured the Law, forsook the one true God and worshipped demons and the works of their own hands, so that God was rightly angered.
comments.comment: But let us approach the sense of the passage in another way as well. Those of Israel dishonoured the training given through the Law and neglected the saving teachings; they forsook the one God, who is God by nature, and brought their worship to unclean demons on mountains and hills, and in the most thickly wooded ravines they burned incense to the works of their own hands and bowed down to them. The God of all was angered at this, and with very good reason…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the Law was given heaven was near and was told to be instructed, but now that the people have departed from upright living heaven is far and is told to hear, while the earth is near through its attachments.
comments.comment: And in Isaiah, 'Hear, O heaven, and be instructed, O earth, for the Lord has spoken' (Isaiah 1:2), is not said in parallel, which is also 'Be instructed, O heaven, and I will speak' (Deuteronomy 32:1)—for instead of 'Pay attention,' other interpreters say 'Be instructed'—'and let the earth hear the words from my mouth' (Isaiah 1:2). And they say such an observation exists: when the law was being given by God, since it happened to be near the heavenly works, for this reason the heaven is commanded to be instructed; but when they departed from the upright citizenship, as to become far from the earth, then it is said, 'Hear, O heaven'—for they happened to be far—'and be instructed, O earth,' for this earth was near through its attachments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By calling heaven and earth to witness and saying that the Lord has spoken, the prophet assures his hearers the words will come to pass and answers in advance their anger against him.
comments.comment:
“Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: Sons I have begotten and raised up, but they have rejected Me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger; but Israel does not know Me, and My people have not understood Me” (Isaiah 1:2–3).

What the matter is, what the reasoning is, and what it means to show, we must look into closely. The blessed prophet solemnly calls, as it were, both heaven and earth to witness, and in doing so he does not act without God; rather, he says that the words are not his own but God's. By this he signifies that they will come to pass in every way and without fail, and he dismays his hearers with dread of suffering, for it is impossible for God to speak falsely.

At the same time, as I think, he is also securing something else. He was about to make his predictions against Judah and Jerusalem, and to announce beforehand sufferings beyond all words and incurable calamities, and he knew well that those to whom the message was addressed would in every way be sharpened to anger. So he says that the Lord spoke these things to them, and so most skilfully turns aside the fury of the ungodly and, as it were, shames their unjust anger into silence. For if he was taken on as a mediator and servant, and was carrying across words from above and from God, how could anyone justly be angry with him? Or rather, how would whatever they did in anger not be aimed against God who had spoken…
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet opens by summoning heaven and earth and says the words are God's.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The rulers of the people were foolish shepherds who ought to have led others to believe in Christ through the Law and the Prophets, so the prophet mixes rebuke into his admonition to reshape them.
comments.comment:
The shepherds truly acted foolishly, and became a cause of ruin for the peoples under their hand.

And yet should they not rather, as men thoroughly instructed in the mystery of Christ through the Law and the Prophets, have become a road for the others toward believing in Him? But, as the Savior says, they received glory from man and did not seek the glory that comes from the only God (John 5:44). “For if they had believed Moses, they would have believed Him, for he wrote about Him” (John 5:46). So they have become blind, and guides of the blind (Matthew 15:14). In this way, too, they have slipped and fallen into the pits of destruction.

What then? The prophet tries to reshape them with good admonitions, so that they would choose to think better things and make trial of the Savior's words. For this purpose he usefully mixes rebuke into his admonitions, healing the wounds of their bad counsel with what is almost a remedy of many ingredients. That is why he says: “Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1:10). You hear how he brings down on peoples and rulers alike the rod that comes from love and from a godly mind, and strikes those gravely sick with disobedience.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Jerusalem was full of sin and had a great scarcity of the righteous, the prophet calls her rulers and people by the names of Sodom and Gomorrah.
comments.comment:
He likens Jerusalem to the most impious cities, as one filled with a very great deal of sin and as having in herself no one at all [The text is damaged here.]. For the God of all was planning to burn the cities of the Sodomites, and He shared the matter with Abraham. Abraham said to Him: “Will You destroy the righteous with the ungodly? And shall the righteous be as the ungodly?” (Genesis 18:23). God promised that if ten righteous men were found in Sodom, He would hold back His wrath against them (Genesis 18:32). But they were not found. Therefore they paid penalties equal in measure to their own impieties. Such was Jerusalem, the slayer of the Lord, with her great scarcity of the righteous.

Indeed, the prophet Jeremiah pleaded earnestly for her, and God said: “Run through the streets of Jerusalem, and see, and know, and search in her squares, if you can find a man, if there is anyone who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to her, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 5:1). Since, then, she is filthy, stained in many ways with the defilements of wickedness, and has a great scarcity of saints, he calls her Sodom and Gomorrah, and lays on peoples and leaders alike the reproach of the Sodomites' uncleanness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jerusalem's rulers are addressed as Sodom and Gomorrah.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's call to remove wickedness from the soul before His eyes means refraining not only from the deed but also from the thought of evil.
comments.comment: To this end, God used to call those repenting: 'Remove the wickedness from your souls before my eyes' (Isaiah 1:16), which implies that we must not only refrain from deed, but also from the thought of evil, as seeing God. The Savior also says in the Gospel: 'But when you give alms, do not blow a trumpet as the hypocrites do' (Matt 6:2). And also: 'He who sees in secret will repay you' (Matt 6:4). Just as he who gives alms in this way does not hear the praise of the many, so he who does not sin against the Lord is free from all evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what removing wickedness from the soul involves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A person settled in evil cannot learn to do good, so he must turn from evil first and then do the good by choice, not merely out of fear of punishment.
comments.comment:
Turn away from evil and do good (Psalm 37:27). This says: if you are already in evil, having settled in it and acting according to it, since I call you to the doing of the good, turn away from the evil. It is impossible to be outside both.

…I call you to do the good. You cannot do it otherwise and act according to it, unless you turn away from the evil. Thus also it is said in Isaiah: 'Stop from your evils, learn to do good' (Isa 1:16); for as long as anyone is in his evils, that is, his wickedness, he is acting in them, and this one is unable to learn to do good. Again the law-giving apostle writes: 'Test all things, hold fast to the good, abstain from every form of evil' (1 Thess 5:21-22). Therefore also, 'turn away from evil and do good.' It is not sufficient to turn away from evil unless one also does the good; for it is possible to turn away from evil being prevented by fear of punishment from going toward this, but this one does not do the good by choice; for if you bypass the good by will, it is no longer at all good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God supplies the persuasive words, but being persuaded takes the hearer's own choice and assent, as the condition 'if you are willing and listen' shows.
comments.comment: And that, even if the speaking of persuasive words comes from God, being persuaded at any rate does not come from God, Paul teaches clearly when he says: “This persuasion does not come from Him who calls you” (Galatians 5:8). Of the same kind too is the saying: “If you are willing and listen to Me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are not willing and do not listen to Me, the sword shall devour you” (Isaiah 1:19–20). For if someone is to will what the one who admonishes says, and, having listened to it, is to become worthy of God’s promises, there must be the hearer’s choice and his assent to what is said.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'if you are willing' wording of the promise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zion was once splendid and righteous under the Law, with prophets, priests and just leaders, but she changed for the worse and went after idols and false guides like a promiscuous woman.
comments.comment:
“How has Zion, the faithful city full of justice, become a harlot? Righteousness once lodged in her, but now murderers” (Isaiah 1:21).

He is in a way astonished at the change in the synagogue of the Jews, so unsound and so without excuse: a change to the worse, I mean, and a passing from better things to more shameful ones. For by the Law given through Moses she was taught the knowledge of what is profitable, and since she had the word of God to guide her in each thing she was to do, she was splendid and highly esteemed and admirable, renowned for a great many men in whom the fruit of righteousness richly flowered, and she was worthy to be accepted by God. There were in her prophets and priests, and guardians of the works of righteousness, and leaders of the peoples who kept judgment, who had the Law on their tongue and were adorned with every good and excellent way of life.

Then she was bereft of all such men; or rather, she chose to take no account of that ancient goodness of hers and set at naught her reverence and love toward God. Before the coming of our Savior she bowed down to those who are not gods by nature, monstrously outraging the one and true Master by harlotries of this kind. Like some promiscuous and frenzied woman, she was impious in many ways, attaching herself now to some guides and now to others, men who knew how to lead her into anything at all that God hates.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse laments: the change from a faithful city to a harlot.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The worthless silver of Israel's false teachers means their deceitful word, not a coin.
comments.comment: And since not all silver mentioned allegorically is praised, but some is also reproached, thus God says to the false teachers of Israel: 'Your silver is worthless' (Isaiah 1:22); He does not mean a physical coin, but a deceitful word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words 'concerning Judah and concerning Jerusalem' speak both of the laying waste of the visible Judah and of the appearing in Christ of the spiritual Judah, the Church, circumcised in heart.
comments.comment:
He is trying to speak of the laying waste of the visible Judah and Jerusalem, but also of the showing forth of the spiritual one in Christ and of her appearing in this world. For this reason he says that he saw the vision not on behalf of Judah, nor yet against Jerusalem, but concerning Judah and concerning Jerusalem.

By the visible Judah, and Jerusalem too, we mean the land itself in which Israel dwelt, and the very body of the synagogue of the Jews. The spiritual Jerusalem, or Judah, we hold to be the Church, that is, the circumcision in the Spirit: those who have the circumcision made without hands in Christ (Colossians 2:11) in mind and heart. So one of the holy prophets cried out to the Jews: “Be circumcised to God, and circumcise your hardness of heart, men of Judah and you who dwell in Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 4:4). And the divine Paul knows another Jew, not the one according to the flesh but the one in the spirit, for he writes: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; his praise is not from men but from God” (Romans 2:28–29).

So we must watch soberly for when the prophet speaks against Jerusalem, that is, Judah, and when he speaks concerning the spiritual one in Christ, which is truly perfect and blameless.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the vision is worded as 'concerning' Judah and Jerusalem.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet marks the time when the devil's power and idol worship fall from the whole world, which has come about in the last days when the Word was born of a woman and presented the Church to Himself as a pure virgin.
comments.comment:
But since mention has been made of the prophecy concerning them, the prophet, beginning the second vision that follows close upon it, marks out the time in which the power of the devil will fall, not in some one part of the earth, nor in a single country and city, while the worship of idols and its profane apparatus are torn down altogether; rather, such a disease will be taken away from the whole world under heaven, and with it the tyranny of the unclean demons.

This too has been accomplished for those on earth “in the last days,” that is, in the final times of the present age, in which the only-begotten Word of God shone forth, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4). It was then that He presented to Himself the spiritual Judea, or Jerusalem, that is, the Church, a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2), “having no spot or wrinkle or any such thing,” as it is written, but rather “holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'in the last days' refers to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The mountain of the Lord is the Church understood spiritually: she is high and seen from every side, and she stands above earthly things while the wisdom of the Greeks stays low.
comments.comment:
Of her he says that “in the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest, and the house of the God of Jacob on the tops of the mountains” (Isaiah 2:2). The Zion in Judea, we are told, lies on a mountain and is built there. But in these words the Church would be understood not in a bodily sense but rather spiritually; and she is likened to a mountain. For she is truly high and seen from every side, and very well known to people everywhere.

She is high in another way too. For she minds nothing earthly, but stands above earthly things; as far as she can, she gazes on the glory of God with the eyes of the mind, and she glories in the very lofty doctrines about Him. The chosen men of the Greeks, though they raise their brows high over their wisdom, make gods of the creation and fasten their reverence on the elements of the world. For their mind is low, their speculations are cast to the ground, and their heart is darkened (Romans 1:21): “claiming to be wise, they became fools,” as it is written (Romans 1:22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the 'mountain of the Lord' is understood.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The spiritual Zion, the Church, rises above all creation and ascribes power over all to the Maker alone.
comments.comment: But the spiritual Zion, that is, the Church, soars above all creation, visible and invisible, and reaches the very nature that is beyond all things. For she is filled with the divine light; and recognising that nature as the Maker and Craftsman of all things, she ascribes to it, and to it alone, the power over all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christians have come in the last days to the Lord's manifest mountain, the Word and His Church built on the prophetic words, and have turned their swords of speech into ploughshares, no longer making war.
comments.comment:
We, then, have come, each of us, “in the last days,” when our Jesus has come to visit us, to “the manifest mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah 2:2), that is, to the Word who is “above” every word, and to the house “of God,” which “is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). And we see in what way this house is built “on the tops of the mountains,” that is, on all the prophetic words, which are its foundation. And this “house” is raised “above the hills” (Isaiah 2:2), that is, above those who appear to profess something exceptional among men in wisdom and truth.

And we, “all the nations,” come to it, and we, the many nations, go, and say to one another, as we urge each other on toward the worship of God that shone out “in the last days” through Jesus Christ: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it” (Isaiah 2:2–3). For the “law” went out from those in “Zion” and passed over to us as a spiritual law (Isaiah 2:3). And “the word of the Lord” also went out from that “Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3), so that it might spread everywhere and judge “between the nations,” choosing those whom he sees are ready to obey, and reproving the “many people” who will not obey (Isaiah 2:4).

… we have come, following the counsels of Jesus, to beat our warlike and insolent “swords” of speech “into ploughshares,” and we are refashioning “the spears” of our former fighting “into sickles” (Isaiah 2:4). For we no longer take up “sword against nation,” nor do we learn “to make war any more” (Isaiah 2:4), since because of Jesus we have become sons of peace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mountain, the nations' going up and the swords made into ploughshares.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God censures them as men never sated in gain and caught in vainglory, and a land filled with horses shows that the sickness had seized them all, against the Law's command not to multiply horses, silver and gold.
comments.comment:
… and very fittingly our God, who loves virtue, censures them as men whose mind is never sated in its love of gain, as men who ride on horses, and as men caught in the snares of vainglory. He says that their land was filled with horses (Isaiah 2:7), because not one or two had fallen sick with arrogance; rather, their whole land, as it were, had been seized by the passion, and the evil was spreading over them all.

Yet by this too He convicts them of having offended against the Law and of having chosen to disobey God, who had said plainly: “If you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance, and you inherit it and dwell in it, and you say, ‘I will set a ruler over myself, like the other nations around me,’ you shall surely set over yourself a ruler whom the Lord your God chooses” (Deuteronomy 17:14-15). Then He says of the one appointed: “For he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor turn the people back to Egypt, so that he may not multiply horses for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:16). And besides this: “Nor shall he greatly multiply silver and gold for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:17).

So He blames them for heaping up wealth, and doing so insatiably, and for multiplying horses for themselves as well. The blame for this, it seems, falls most of all on those whose lot it was to lead, as men who transgressed the commandment; for it was fitting that they, before all others, should be seen to honour what had been decreed and to rebuke those who transgressed it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the charge in the verse about a land full of horses and wealth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's worship of what their fingers had made was complete apostasy, and God, who honoured man by making him with His own hand, grieves that man in honour did not understand.
comments.comment:
“And the land was filled with the abominations, the works of their hands, and they worshipped what their fingers had made. And man bowed down, and a man was brought low, and I will not forgive them” (Isaiah 2:8-9).

Again He charges them with spiritual fornication, and with having chosen to worship many of the falsely named gods. He shows that they had come to such a measure of impiety as to drive every evil to its limit, and to practise the most complete apostasy from God, who knows all things, upholds them by His nod, and brought them into being.

He seems in some way also to grieve deeply for human nature, so utterly dishonoured. For the God of all honoured man by making him with His own hand. Man was not simply produced by a word along with the other creatures, as was, for example, “Let there be a firmament; and it was so” (Genesis 1:6). Rather, “He took dust from the earth and made man” (Genesis 2:7), according to the words of the all-wise Moses. He was made after the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), and was appointed a kind of ruler over the things on earth. Besides this, he was honoured with the spirit of life as well; for “He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7).

So “man, being in honour, did not understand,” as it is written (Psalm 49:12); for he served carved images, and, as the prophetic word said, “they worshipped what their fingers had made” (Isaiah 2:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the charge of idolatry means for human dignity.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The high cedars of Lebanon and balsam trees of Bashan stand for pride and idolatry, which will be crushed and consumed with those who gather sophistically about them.
comments.comment: Since these are wild plants and do not bear edible fruit, in Isaiah it is written concerning others thus: 'The day of the Lord of hosts upon every arrogant and proud and high and lofty thing,' and after a few words: 'and upon every high cedar of Lebanon and upon every balsam tree of Bashan' (Isaiah 2:12). These such wild woods are grown up for idolatry and pride, being crushed and consumed by fire along with those who assemble sophistically about them, according to what is said in the same Isaiah: 'And the Lebanon shall fall with the lofty ones' (Isaiah 2:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'strength' of bread and water is the spiritual power of Scripture, which the Jews no longer have because they read the Law without understanding and hold only the bare letter.
comments.comment:
For he did not say simply that bread and water would be taken from the Jews, but “strength of bread and strength of water” (Isaiah 3:1). We should take it that he means to teach something like this. When we come upon the sacred words and read the divine Scriptures, and then understand them, we receive the strength of spiritual bread. “For man shall not live,” He says, “by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4; compare Deuteronomy 8:3). You will understand spiritual waters in the same way.

The Jews, for their part, still have the bread and the water; for they busy themselves with the writings of Moses and read the Law. But since they understand nothing, they have neither the strength of the bread nor the strength of the water. For only the bare letter has been given them, which looks like bread and water but in no way nourishes them to spiritual health. Paul will bear witness to this when he writes: “For to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart, not lifted, because it is done away in Christ” (2 Corinthians 3:14-15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'strength of bread and strength of water'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: For believers the bread is Christ, whose body is life-giving, and the water is baptism with its putting away of sins and rebirth, and the Jews have been deprived of these.
comments.comment:
In another way too we say that the strength of bread and the strength of water have been taken from the synagogue of the Jews; and this account is a mystical one. For we who have been called through faith to sanctification have the bread from heaven, that is, Christ, or His body (John 6:32-33). And if anyone should ask what kind of strength it has, we say that it is life-giving; for it gives life to the world (John 6:33).

In the same way we also come to the grace given through holy baptism, which sanctifies us; and we say that the strength of the water is the putting away of sins and spiritual rebirth into conformity with Christ Himself, and besides these, an entrance with boldness into the kingdom of heaven. “For unless one,” He says, “is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

So the Jews have been deprived of such good things. They do not have the strength of bread, that is, the life given in Christ. They do not have the strength of the water; for their sin has remained with them unwashed. They will not enter the kingdom of heaven, since they dishonoured Christ, who leads the way in; for they did not believe Him when He said: “I am the way” (John 14:6), and “I am the door” (John 10:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The giant is one who has reached the height of spiritual strength and the strong man one who stands a little below him, since each of us has been given a measure of grace.
comments.comment: Likewise He will take away “the giant and the strong man” (Isaiah 3:2). Who, then, is the giant, and who is the other? For my part, I think he calls “giant” the one who has reached the height of spiritual strength, and “strong man” the one who stands a little below him and falls short of the pre-eminence seen in the first. For to each of us a measure of grace has been given by God (compare Ephesians 4:7). The most wise Paul makes this clear to us when he says: “I wish that all men were even as I myself am; but each …” (1 Corinthians 7:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the giant and the strong man are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Disciples should not simply follow their teachers but test what they are led to, as sheep avoid a pit; and the leaders of the Jews, the scribes and Pharisees, were clever at collecting gains from the people.
comments.comment:
Having declared beforehand, very plainly and quite clearly, that the land of the Jews would suffer the loss of every good thing, and having set out what will happen to those who behaved outrageously toward Christ, he again tries to persuade them in advance to keep away from their offences. With gentle words he all but charms them, to their profit, moving them toward what is better and teaching them to reject those who had become the cause of all their evils.

For I do not think one ought to be fond of submitting to those whose lot is to lead, if they attempt to teach nothing of what serves for profit … For the excellence of a teacher lies in being able to bring those in his charge to an exact knowledge of what is profitable, to expose as counterfeit whatever by nature does harm, and to bid them refuse what usually does wrong.

And those who are counted among disciples would deserve every praise if they looked not simply at the reputations of their teachers but at the nature of the matters themselves; if they admired their teachers, provided these are upright and knowledgeable and guides to what is best, and found fault with those whose aim is not of this kind.

Some men pasture flocks of sheep on mountains and in glens. But if a pit lies beside the flock, or a mountain precipice, the sheep walk around it and do not throw themselves down to their death; for they are taught, as by an inborn law, that they must spare their own life. Is it not absurd, then, that this should plainly prevail among irrational animals, while in us, though we are rational, there is no knowledge of what is useful and necessary for life?

So even if some of those appointed as our teachers and guides should choose to lead us toward what is not fitting, we must not simply be content to bear with it, nor follow without examination wherever they please; rather, we must test each thing that is to be done … to go toward whatever most often does good.

Now the leaders of the Jews, that is, the scribes and the Pharisees, were clever at collecting gains of money and gathering in the people’s offerings: first fruits, tithes, and all that the Law, as a portion for those whose lot was to serve as priests …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The exactors who glean the people were scribes and Pharisees greedy for gain, who ruled like harsh masters instead of teaching gently, as Peter forbids those who lead flocks to do.
comments.comment:
Their aim, pursued with all their zeal, was to persuade people that the law had to be kept in these matters [first fruits and tithes] above all; of the other commandments they took little account. That is why the Savior himself said to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe dill and mint and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith” (Matthew 23:23).

So they were greedy for gain and lovers of money. At times they brought harsh penalties on those who slipped, so that by terrifying anyone accused of anything at all they might induce them to bring offerings, sometimes even beyond their means. That is why he says to those they wronged: “My people, your exactors glean you, and those who demand payment rule over you” (Isaiah 3:12).

By saying “people” he still gives Israel to understand that if they chose to turn to what pleases him, they would meet with his gentleness and love for humankind, and would not fall away altogether from their close bond with him.

By saying that the exactors glean, he shows how great their insatiable greed for gain was. In the cornfields some cut the ears with iron, while others gather the stalks that fall from the reaper’s hand and leave nothing in the fields. Those who harvest vines usually do the same. “So your exactors glean you,” he says. It is as if he said: They have harvested your wealth, and their greed does not stop there. They are already gleaning as well, that is, laying their hands even on what is still left.

Very well and fittingly he does not call them guides or teachers or anything of the kind; he names them exactors and collectors. He teaches that they lord it over the people, not dealing gently with them as teachers with disciples, but like harsh and savage masters, forcing them to think as they see fit and driving them to anything at all, at times even against their own judgment.

But the aim of those in Christ was not of this kind. The inspired Peter writes to those called to oversight, whose lot it is to lead the rational flocks: “not as lording it over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the gleaners are and what the wording shows about them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: After the war there will be so few men that seven women will take hold of one man, asking only to be rid of the reproach of childlessness, which the Law made one of the worst among the Jews.
comments.comment:
“And seven women will take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach” (Isaiah 4:1).

Having fully completed his account of the Jewish women who would go from luxury and wealth into captivity, he tries to show that the cities of Judea will be left empty of men, and will have a great scarcity of those who were once the finest fighters. For he had said, “All your strong men will fall by the sword” (Isaiah 3:25).

What, then, is the proof of what I have said? It is framed with great skill and elegance. The law given through Moses says to the sons of Israel, “There shall be no one childless or barren among you” (Deuteronomy 7:14). So among the Jews it was counted one of the worst reproaches for a woman not to bear children, or for any man to be childless; for at once the stigma of the childless and the barren was fastened on them.

The law was indeed spiritual (Romans 7:14). For the God of all was promising that the spiritual Israel, that is, the mind that sees God, would not be fruitless or made barren, but fruitful instead, like a good and choice land. But the Jews understood it in a fleshly way, for they were natural men, not having the Spirit (Jude 19).

So, he says, there will be such a scarcity of males in the land, once the war has consumed the race, that seven women, that is, many, will take hold of one man and say: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing; only let your name be called over us; take away our reproach.” Do you see how they dread the reproach of childlessness, and how strongly they refuse the name of childless and barren? For they come not seeking the usual things, what wives are accustomed to receive from their husbands; they say they will provide for themselves in this, and ask only, as I said, that their reproach be taken away.

Note the depth of the passage. If the man they appealed to had been rich, the women would not have said, “We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothing.” But since they know that those who were saved from the war and barely escaped have fallen into utter poverty and great misery, they ask nothing at all of them, and seek only to become mothers of children.

That is the sense of the history.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the strange picture of seven women and one man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In the washing of the filth and blood, filth stands for unintentional faults and blood for what is done by intention.
comments.comment: For filth, in relation to pure life, is not the earthly place itself, but as it is said: 'All our righteousness is as a filthy garment before you, Lord' (Isa 64:6). Which the Lord washes according to what is said in Isaiah: 'The Lord will wash the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isaiah 4:4). Filth, then, might be the unintentional things, but blood is that which is done by intention.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Blood stands for sin that cannot be washed away lightly, while the filth is the unintentional acts which the Savior cleansed.
comments.comment: You have concerning filth and sin in Isaiah thus: 'The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isaiah 4:4), the blood signifying sin there, the unclean thing, and the filth the unintentional acts, which the Savior, having come, cleansed by himself. For because blood often signifies sin, it is said toward the ancient evil devil: 'In whatever way a garment stained with blood is not to be clean, in the same way you will not be clean.' For he did not happen to be stained with blood, but it is clear that the blood signifies to him the 'sin unto death.' Therefore, the one having a fault capable of being washed has filth, but the one is as if unrepentant, like the one 'having blasphemed against the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 12:31) and the like, is not under filth, but sin, and the one transgressing the commandments with the intent of knowing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God washes away the filth and blood by a spirit of judgment and of burning, like a refiner's fire and fullers' herb, so that those cleansed willingly hate the reprobate mind.
comments.comment: 'God shall wash,' then, 'the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and cleanse the blood from their midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.' (Isaiah 4:4) For 'he comes as a refiner's fire and as fullers' herb,' washing and cleansing those in need of such drugs, because they would not approvedly 'hold God in knowledge.' Handed to these, they shall willingly hate the 'reprobate mind.' For God wills the good to come to no one as by necessity, but willingly — though some, from longer commerce with evil, hardly perceive its shame, and turn from it as falsely supposed good.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'horn' means the kingship and the 'place of drinking' the instruction through law and prophets.
comments.comment: Israel, being part of the Lord and a son of God, transgressed his commands, even though God was doing all things for him. For what does he say in Isaiah? 'A horn was raised up for the beloved in a horn in a place of drinking' (Isaiah 5:1), where 'horn' refers to the kingship, and 'place of drinking' signifies the instruction through law and prophets. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The vineyard stands for human souls, which God hedges around with the security of the commandments and the guard of the angels.
comments.comment: And he does not cease everywhere to compare the souls of men to vines. For a vineyard was made for the beloved, he says, on a horn, in a rich place (Isaiah 5:1). And, I planted a vineyard, and put a hedge around it (Isaiah 5:2). He clearly means the human souls as the vineyard, around which he put a hedge—the security from the commandments and the guard of the angels. For the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him (Psalm 33:8 (34:7)).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the vineyard and its hedge represent.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Israel was styled a vineyard, its temple the tower and its altar the fore-vat, and the many altars of Christ's churches are the many winepresses.
comments.comment: Of old, then, when the people called Israel was one, this people was styled a vineyard. And the temple among them was a tower, and the altar before the temple was a fore-vat, according to the prophecy of Isaiah (Isaiah 5:1-2). But now the word mentions not one winepress but more winepresses, because of the many altars throughout the whole earth constituted through Christ in his churches.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God planted his people, gave them teaching and the safety that comes from angels, and still they stayed fruitless, so that he asks what more he could do for his vine.
comments.comment: He planted a vine, which is the chosen one; for he planted the people to be a kingdom and a chosen priesthood. He built a tower to provide refuge for the approaching enemies (Isa 5:2); the tower is a teaching tool, guarding and at the same time mocking the enemy's onset. … He also made a hedge and placed a fence around it, which signifies the safety from the angels. And despite all these things having happened, he remained in the same fruitlessness; therefore he says: 'What more shall I do to my vine when I have done nothing for it?' (Isa 5:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God will take away the help the people had from the angels so that they may desire to turn back, and the clouds he forbids to rain signify the prophets and messengers of spiritual rain.
comments.comment: I have done all things without fail; therefore, since they themselves do not have the power to say what must happen, I will say, 'I will announce to you what I shall do to my vine' (Isa 5:5-6); I will take away what I gave it, 'I will pull down its wall and it shall be a pavement, and I will take away the fence and it shall be a plunder' (Isa 5:5-6). For it is useful to provide this help, which they received from the angels, to those who are useless, so that seeing what evils they are, they may desire to turn back; therefore he also rebukes, saying: 'And I will command the clouds not to rain upon it' (Isa 5:6), which signify the prophets and the messengers of the spiritual rain, concerning which it was said: 'The clouds rained down righteousness' (Isaiah 45:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because they raged against Christ, Israel has lost its hedge and the word of the prophets, the rain held back in a famine of hearing the word of the Lord.
comments.comment:
But since they raged against Christ, they have remained without a hedge, and all their security has fallen. This, I think, is what is meant by saying that its wall is pulled down (Isaiah 5:5). Every word of the holy prophets to them has ceased, held back in a way like rain (Isaiah 5:6), and the voices of the saints have failed.

And this, I think, is what God said to them through one of the prophets: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And from the east to the west they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it” (Amos 8:11–12).

These things, as I said, have befallen those of Israel, and with good reason. For they thrust away the Lord of hosts, who waters souls and hearts in a spiritual way and enriches them with spiritual dews …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the wall pulled down and the withheld rain mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In place of the old vineyard a new one has been raised up of those called through faith, and Christ the true vine will himself set a hedge around them.
comments.comment:
In its place a new vineyard has been raised up, made up of those called through faith to holiness. Of them the Bridegroom from heaven, that is, Christ, says: “The vines are in blossom; they have given their fragrance” (Song of Songs 2:13). He himself is the first, all-holy, and true vine, and we hang from him like branches, filled with the life-giving richness that comes from him.

…

So I say that we must hold fast, through faith and love and readiness to obey in everything, to the true vine, that is, Christ. For he will make us fruitful; he himself will set a hedge around us, raise up the wall …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does not leave anyone without cause or judgment: when the vineyard bears thorns after he sends rain, he commands the clouds not to rain on it.
comments.comment: See then how great an evil it is to sin, so that people are handed over to Satan, who takes captive the souls of those left by God. God does not leave without cause, and not without judgment, those he has left. For when he sends the rain on the vineyard, and the vineyard bears thorns instead of grapes, what will God do but 'command the clouds not to rain' (Isaiah 5:6) on the vineyard?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who join house to house do it by inventing pretexts to drive their neighbors out, as Ahab's desire for the vineyard killed Naboth, and the greedy person respects no boundary.
comments.comment:
Woe to those who join house to house and bring field near field, so that they may take something from their neighbor (Isaiah 5:8). And what do you do? Do you not make countless pretexts to take your neighbor’s property? “My neighbor’s house blocks my light,” he says, “it causes disturbances,” or “it shelters runaways,” or whatever charge he happens to make, driving out, pushing out, always dragging and tearing, he does not stop until he brings upon them the necessity of moving away. What killed Naboth the Jezreelite? Was it not Ahab’s desire for the vineyard? A wicked fellow citizen in the city, wicked in the fields, is the greedy person.

The sea knows its boundaries; the night does not overstep its ancient limits. But the greedy person does not respect time, does not recognize a boundary, does not allow the order of succession, but imitates the force of fire: it seizes everything, it devours everything.
comments.selected_reason: Shows concretely what joining house to house and field to field looks like.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Isaiah laments those who give the whole day to strong drink, because they leave no time to look at the works of the Lord and so perceive the Creator.
comments.comment: Isaiah laments over such people: "Woe to those who rise early in the morning and chase after strong drink, who linger late into the evening, for wine inflames them. They drink wine with lyres and flutes, but they do not regard the works of the Lord, nor consider the work of His hands" (Isaiah 5:11-12). The Hebrews customarily call every drink that can produce drunkenness "strong drink." So those who at daybreak look around for where drinking parties are happening, who peer about at wine shops and taverns, who invite one another to drink, and who spend all the soul's concern on attending to such things—these are the ones the prophet laments, because they leave themselves no time to contemplate the wonders of God. Their eyes have no leisure to look up to heaven and learn its beauties, or to examine the whole order of creation, so that from its arrangement they might perceive the Creator.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the verse means and why their drinking is faulted.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Because God long held back punishment, the people mocked his prophets, and Isaiah calls wretched those who drag their sins on a long rope, meaning the penalties still far off.
comments.comment:
The Maker and Lord of all, overcoming the weakness of human nature by his gentleness, spoke to the people of old through the holy prophets the things by which they might be expected to leave the worse and turn to the better, to cease from wickedness and sin, to live in virtue instead, and to choose to do what is good. For this reason he sometimes set before them the rewards prepared for the saints, and at other times described the kinds of punishment that fit those who love sin, so as to drive them from every side toward what would profit them.

But no means could drive out the degeneracy of the Jews. For they had turned aside to the love of gain and to luxuries, and, already sick with the utmost madness against God, they set upon the holy prophets fiercely. Some, wholly disbelieving what was spoken through them, said: “Speak other things to us, and announce to us another deception” (Isaiah 30:10). Others, all but blaming the forbearance of the divine nature, and no doubt laughing at one another, said: “The days are far off; every vision has perished” (Ezekiel 12:22).

…

Others again, as though they had all but despaired of their own salvation and life, grew insolent toward his wrath and even said: “Let the time of war come quickly; those who wish to ravage us will not find us cowardly or timid. We too are skilled in war and know tactics well.”

Those who thought this way he rightly calls wretched, saying: “Woe to those who drag their sins as with a long rope, and their lawless deeds as with the strap of a heifer’s yoke.” By “sins” and “lawless deeds” here he means the penalties or punishments for sins, which were still far off and not yet near, because God still wished to bear with them …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the woe addresses and what the dragged sins are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: These men drag punishment on themselves as one drags a heifer under the yoke, so when we learn that God is grieved we must repent and soothe him with prayers.
comments.comment:
… and yet in a way those punishments were being dragged on by them, because they wished to fall even into the outbursts of divine wrath. I think that we can say to each such person, most fittingly and truly: “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5).

For, as I said, they drag the time of punishment upon themselves, perhaps fretting that he was slow to punish them and was not laying penalties on them as they sinned without restraint. So they drag their sins as with a long rope, and their lawless deeds as with the strap of a heifer’s yoke. For just as those who bring heifers, that is, oxen, under the yoke sometimes drag them with great force and bind them to their labor, so in the same way, I think, these men too put themselves under what was about to befall them from divine wrath, and said: “Let what he will do come near quickly, so that we may see; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel come, so that we may know” (Isaiah 5:19).

…

So when we learn that God has been grieved, we must repent at once and soothe him instead with unceasing prayers, not provoke him further once he has been moved, nor despise him when he threatens. For he is patient and rich in mercy, taking away lawless deeds and passing over wrongs (compare Numbers 14:18; Micah 7:18), and sometimes, at the few tears of those who have sinned, he turns back to the calm that is dearest to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the long rope and the heifer's yoke.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who drag their sins show themselves without understanding, debasing what is most profitable for their salvation, and so the woe fits them.
comments.comment:
“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter. Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight” (Isaiah 5:20–21).

By these words too he shows that those who drag their sins as with a long rope are utterly without understanding. When they ought to have counted the duty of repentance worthy of all praise, to free themselves by every kind of gentleness from the wrath hanging over them, and to make their defense with fasts before God, the ruler of all, whom they had grieved, they have become untrustworthy money-changers, valuing the baser things and debasing what is incomparably better and most profitable for their salvation.

So the “woe” fits those who think this way. For they have become unholy and senseless judges against themselves. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the woe falls on those who reverse good and evil.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is said to sit where he is known, and a pure mind is called his throne.
comments.comment: … For he [Isaiah] beheld with the prophetic eye the rational nature, exalted through the praktike [the practice of the virtues], having received into itself the knowledge of God. For God is said to sit where He is known, since a pure mind is also called the throne of God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The seraphim cover God's face and feet because the divine nature is beyond sight and its ways cannot be traced.
comments.comment: The prophet Isaiah, too, portrays the Son in the form proper to him, saying, ‘I saw the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and seraphim stood around him’ (Isaiah 6:1–2); and he says that six wings had grown on each, and that with two they covered the feet, with two the faces, and with the others they flew (Isaiah 6:2). If someone thinks that the seraphim were covering the face of God, and his feet too, there is nothing unreasonable in taking it so. For if we put the meaning of the word ‘seraphim’ into Greek, we shall find that it signifies a fullness of knowledge, or an outpouring of wisdom. By their posture, then, these all-wise and highest powers hint very clearly that it is not lawful for God’s face to be seen by anyone. For the nature that is beyond all understanding is wholly beyond sight, and ‘dwells in unapproachable light’ (1 Timothy 6:16), in the words of blessed Paul; and ‘no one shall see the face of God and live’ (Exodus 33:20), as God rightly told the most holy Moses. Nor could anyone know his footsteps and his ways. For it is written, ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!’ (Romans 11:33) Blessed David, too, sings and strikes up a wise song: ‘Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known’ (Psalm 77:19). For just as no one could see a track in water, whether of a man, perhaps, or of a ship, or of the creatures that swim in it, so no one could make out the divine and ineffable ways. The feet would be a type of these ways.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the seraphim cover the face and feet.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The prophets saw and heard by a divine sense, a sight able to see things higher than bodies, such as the seraphim.
comments.comment: But one who examines the matter more deeply will say this. There is, as Scripture has named it, a divine sense, general in kind, which only the blessed man finds even now, according to what is said in Solomon too: “You will find a divine sense” (Proverbs 2:5). This sense has its kinds: a sight naturally able to see things higher than bodies, among which the cherubim or the seraphim are shown (Ezekiel 10:1; Isaiah 6:2); a hearing that receives voices whose being is not in the air; a taste that feeds on living bread, which has come down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33, 51); so too a smell that smells such things as Paul means when he speaks of being “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15); and a touch, by which John says he has handled with his hands “the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). The blessed prophets found this divine sense. They saw in a divine way and heard in a divine way, and tasted and smelled in the same way, by a sense that, if I may so name it, is not of the senses; and they touched the Word with faith, so that an outflow from him came to them to heal them. In this way they saw what they record that they saw …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: According to Jewish tradition the earthquake named at the start of Amos belongs to the vision that appeared to Isaiah in the year King Ozias died.
comments.comment: … The earthquake now being declared lies also at the beginning of the prophet Amos: 'For words,' says Amos, 'which came from Tekoa, two years before the earthquake in the days of Ozias,' the earthquake being said here, according to the circulating Jewish tradition, of the vision appearing to Isaiah, concerning which it has been written thus: 'It happened in the year in which King Ozias died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lifted-up throne, and Seraphim were standing around him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other' (Isa 6:1-2), and after a little: 'And the other cried to the other: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, full is the heaven and the earth of his glory' (Isa 6:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By saying 'Holy' three times and closing with 'Lord of hosts', the seraphim place the holy Trinity in one nature of Godhead.
comments.comment:
… Their mouths too are given to praise. They give glory, and do so in turn, not because they grow weary, I think, but rather yielding the honor to one another and exchanging their praises as gifts. For all things above are in good order.

Saying “Holy” three times, they close the doxology with “Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), placing the holy Trinity in one nature of Godhead. For we say, as all confess, that the Father truly subsists, and so too the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet no reasoning divides each of those named into a difference of nature; one Godhead is understood in three hypostases [the distinct persons].
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the cry is threefold, in terms the verse itself supports.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The seraphim's third 'Holy' glorifies Father, Son and Holy Spirit, because the deity is one God in three persons.
comments.comment: And when the seraphim glorify God, saying for the third time, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts,” they glorify Father and Son and Holy Spirit. And for this reason, just as we are baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son, so also into the name of the Holy Spirit, and we become sons of God, not of gods. For Father and Son and Holy Spirit is Lord of hosts. For the deity is one, and one God in three persons.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: The seraphim's words that the whole earth is full of God's glory foretell that after the Word became man every nation would worship him.
comments.comment:
This is attested to us by the holy Seraphim themselves, who also say that the whole earth is full of his glory (Isaiah 6:3), foretelling what was to come and announcing beforehand the mystery of the saving plan carried out through Christ. Before the Word became flesh, the destroying demon, the dragon, the apostate, held sway over all that is under heaven, and the creation was worshiped in place of the Creator and Maker (Romans 1:25). But since the only-begotten Word of God became man, the whole earth has been filled with his glory.

For every knee will bow to him, and every tribe and tongue will confess him and serve him, as it is written (Isaiah 45:23; Philippians 2:10–11; Daniel 7:14). Blessed David also cried this out beforehand in the Spirit, for he said: “All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord” (Psalm 86:9). This has been fulfilled now that the multitude from the nations has been called, and all worship him who for our sake became as we are, yet in himself remained above all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the whole earth is full of his glory' announces.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah confessed unclean lips, not unclean works, so a seraph touched his lips with the coal from the altar and took away his iniquities.
comments.comment: Watch the difference between Jeremiah and Isaiah. Isaiah says, 'I have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.' (Isaiah 6:5) And since he confessed that he did not have unclean works, but only small words (for to that point he was a sinner), the Lord did not stretch out his hand. One of the seraphim touched his lips with his hand, and said, 'Behold, I have taken away your iniquities.' (Isaiah 6:6–7) But because this one [Jeremiah] was sanctified 'from the womb,' no tongs are sent to him, and no coal 'from the altar' (he had nothing worthy of the fire). The Lord's own hand touched him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a seraph touches Isaiah's lips and what it accomplishes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The weighing down of the ears is a matter of choice: they chose to remain in malice and impiety, so they did not hear the words about virtue and turn back.
comments.comment: … That the weighing down of the ears of the inner man is a matter of choice, as has been closely stated, is testified to by the prophecy of Isaiah, being proclaimed in such a way to those who attend to these things with a heavy heart: “For the heart of this people has become thick, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and their eyes they have dimmed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart and turn, and I should heal them” (Isaiah 6:10). For, desiring to remain as they had chosen to have through malice and impiety, they weighed down the ears and their eyes were dimmed, the heart of them having become thick, so that, not having heard the words concerning virtue and the knowledge of the truth, they might not be improved and turn back to Him from whom they had turned away through their sunset and blindness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the heavy ears and dull heart come about.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The captives lie like acorns fallen from their husk, as a bird fallen from its nest, and nothing is more pitiable than people in their conquerors' hands.
comments.comment: … they will lie like acorns, as if they had fallen from the very husk that bore them (Isaiah 6:13). Solomon too says something of the kind: “As a bird when it falls from its own nest, so is a man when he is torn away from his own places” (Proverbs 27:8). For what could be more pitiable than those in captivity? What is so wretched and downtrodden as for people to fall into the hands of their conquerors?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the acorns and the fate of the captives.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who dismiss the history in Scripture as stale miss how to read it, for we should hunt above all for what is useful in the history.
comments.comment:
“And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel went up against Jerusalem to wage war on it, and they could not take it by siege” (Isaiah 7:1).

Those who reject the history in the divinely inspired Scriptures as stale are, it seems, running away from being able to understand what is written in them in the proper way. Spiritual contemplation is good and profitable, and by greatly brightening the eye of the mind it makes people most discerning. But whenever some event of history is set before us through the sacred Writings, then above all we should hunt for what is useful in the history, so that the divinely inspired Scripture may be seen to save and benefit us from every side.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah marks the times of each of the four kings, and the impieties of Ahaz, who followed the king of Israel and served idols, provoked God to bring Pekah's war upon Judah.
comments.comment:
Here, then, the prophetic word recounts for us what befell those of Judah and Benjamin in the times of Uzziah’s reign, and the ten tribes in Samaria, which were called Ephraim and also Israel. Since the whole word of the prophecy came in the times of four kings (Isaiah 1:1), the prophet sets down what happened in the times of each, and he necessarily marks them, giving the best order to his visions, that is, to his own words.

When Azariah, also called Uzziah, had died, Jotham succeeded to the kingdom and followed the aim and practices of his own father. He too is said to have done what was right in the eyes of the Lord, as Uzziah had, except that he did not remove the high places, but the people still burned incense on the high places (2 Kings 15:34–35). Uzziah had sought, against what was lawful, to serve God as a priest and to offer incense, and for this reason he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Jotham, however, did not do so (2 Chronicles 27:2).

When he too died, Ahaz succeeded to the kingdom, while Pekah son of Remaliah was reigning over Israel, that is, over the twelve tribes. He waged war against Ahaz and Judah, and killed a hundred and twenty thousand in one day (2 Chronicles 28:6). For the God of all was provoked by the impieties of Ahaz, of whom it is written in the Second Book of Kings that he walked in the way of the king of Israel (2 Kings 16:3). For he was an impious man; he served idols and made his children pass through fire, burning incense to the unclean demons.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: An ember has lost the strength of wood, and such were the enemies God said not to fear.
comments.comment: An ember is half-wood, having reached the point of turning into charcoal, no longer possessing the strength and hardness of wood. Such were also the enemies of the King of the Hebrews, concerning whom God said to him: "Do not fear, nor let your soul faint because of these two smoking embers" (Isaiah 7:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the two smoking embers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Faith is the first approach that leads on to understanding.
comments.comment: ‘For if you do not believe, neither will you understand,’ (Isaiah 7:9) he says. For faith is the first approach that leads on to understanding, and it opens the mind, as it were, to receive the divine light.
comments.selected_reason: States plainly how believing leads to understanding.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: No child of Ahaz's time fits 'God with us', so the words went to the house of David, and the sign 'in the depth or in the height' fits him who descended and ascended.
comments.comment: And if he [the Jew] quibbles in this way too, saying that the words “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God” were spoken to Ahaz, we shall answer: who was born in the time of Ahaz at whose birth it is said, “Emmanuel, which is, God with us”? For if no one is to be found, then clearly what was said to Ahaz was said to the house of David (Isaiah 7:13), because the Saviour is recorded to have come “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). Moreover, this sign is said to be “in the depth or in the height,” since “he who descended is the very one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Ephesians 4:10). I say this as to a Jew who accepts the prophecy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the words are addressed to and what 'in the depth or in the height' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Ahaz, alarmed by the two kings, refused to ask for a sign, so God himself gave the house of David the sign of the virgin who bears Emmanuel.
comments.comment: Ahaz was greatly alarmed at the alliance of the two kings, Rezin and Pekah, and the God of all promised him help. Since he wished to establish him further in faith, he told him to ask for a sign, “in the depth or in the height” (Isaiah 7:11). But Ahaz refused, and said most perversely, “I will not ask, nor will I put the Lord to the test” (Isaiah 7:12), for he was looking instead for the trickery of false prophets. So God in a way came forward of his own accord and himself gave a sign to the house of David. For he said: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The salvation through Christ is announced to David's house, but the dreaded things to come are announced to those who chose disobedience and weary the Lord by worshiping others.
comments.comment: When the word about these things had been fully completed, he turns the prediction of what was to come back to the person of Ahaz himself. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that the announcement of the salvation through Christ be made to those of the house of David, that is, to those of the tribe of Judah, from which Christ himself arose according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14). But the announcement of the terrible and dreaded things that would happen in due time he makes to those who had chosen to disobey, so that they might know that it is truly bitter, and not without cost, for those who dishonor the divine glory to weary the Lord (Isaiah 7:13), and to choose to worship, in place of him, others who are not gods.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sign would be no sign if a young woman who was not a virgin gave birth, so it fits a pure virgin to bear Emmanuel, 'God with us'.
comments.comment: The Lord is recorded as having said to Ahaz: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height” (Isaiah 7:11), and next comes the sign that is given: “Behold, the virgin shall be with child and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14). What sort of sign, then, would it be for a young woman who was not a virgin to give birth? And to whom is it more fitting to bear “Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23)? To a woman who has had intercourse and conceived through a woman’s passion, or to one still pure and chaste and a virgin? For it is fitting for her to bring forth the offspring at whose birth it is said, “God with us.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sign must be a virgin birth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Emmanuel, 'God with us', is Jesus, born of a virgin without a man, and the angel gave him that name because he will save his people from their sins.
comments.comment: For who is so saving and a savior of the world as 'God with us, Emmanuel,' born from the experience of a woman not having a man, fulfilling the prophecy that says: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son' (Isa 7:14). The angel named the child Jesus, marking this mode of the virgin bearing without a man, and giving the reason for this designation thus. For this, he says, he shall be called Jesus, 'for he will save his people from their sins' (Matt 1:21).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah's words that before the child knows good or evil he refuses evil are said of the Savior, who as a child advanced in stature, wisdom and grace.
comments.comment: … Bring the Old Covenant as a witness: 'Before the child knows good or evil, he refuses evil to choose the good.' (Isaiah 7:15–16) And these things are said outright about the Savior in Isaiah: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.' (Isaiah 7:14) And there it is added: 'before the child knows.' (Isaiah 7:16) And if an example must also be taken from the gospel: Jesus, not yet become a man but still a child, since 'he emptied himself,' was advancing. For no one who is already perfected advances; he advances who still needs advance. So he 'advanced in stature, advanced in wisdom, advanced in grace with God and men.' If he emptied himself coming down here, and emptying himself was taking again from what he had emptied himself of, having emptied himself willingly, what is strange if he also advanced 'in wisdom and stature and grace with God and men,' (Luke 2:52) and if what I set down from Isaiah is true of him: before he knows good or evil he will choose the good and refuse evil?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The obscure words foretell the worst miseries for Jerusalem, and 'from the day that Ephraim took away' means the ten tribes tearing away from Judah under Rehoboam.
comments.comment:
So he subtly signals in advance that in time Jerusalem itself, and the whole land of the Jews, would fall into the worst miseries and come under the hand of their enemies. Since the arrangement of the words is rather obscure, I will try, as far as I am able, to make it clear before anything else.

“God will bring,” he says, “upon you, and upon your people, and upon the house of your father, days that have not yet come, from the day that Ephraim took away from Judah.” The sense of the lines is this: in the times of the reign of Rehoboam son of Solomon, Ephraim “took away,” that is, tore itself away (Ephraim meaning, again, the ten tribes) from the tribe of Judah. For they were separated: the ten tribes, parted from the tribe of Judah, settled in Samaria, while the tribe of Judah and the half-tribe of Manasseh remained in Jerusalem. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the obscure wording of the verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The days not yet seen are the coming of the king of the Assyrians, Nebuchadnezzar, who sacked Jerusalem and burned the temple.
comments.comment: … For Samaria has been sacked, and the neighboring nations, the Edomites, the Moabites, and the people of Philistia, have overrun Judea as well. So both these and those have suffered many terrible things and have known hard days. Therefore God, he says, will bring days whose like have not yet been, that is, have not yet come upon you, since the time when Ephraim “took away,” that is, tore himself away, from Judah (Isaiah 7:17). And what is this time for us, or what are these days? “The king of the Assyrians,” he says (Isaiah 7:17), that is, Nebuchadnezzar, who sacked Jerusalem, took all Judea by force, and burned the divine temple as well; and of all the savagery fit for a wild beast he left out nothing at all that he is not found to have done against the whole nation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'days not yet come' are and who 'the king of Assyria' is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet describes the onset of the war, with enemies overrunning all the land, as the later history of Josiah, Pharaoh Neco and Nebuchadnezzar shows.
comments.comment:
“And it shall be in that day that the Lord will whistle for the flies, which rule over a part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee, which is in the land of the Assyrians; and they will all come and settle in the ravines of the land, and in the holes of the rocks, and in the caves, and in every cleft, and on every tree” (Isaiah 7:18-19).

He widens the account and describes in detail the onset of the war, and how those who would come against them from time to time would overrun all their land, villages and cities alike. I think it necessary here to tell again what is written in the Second Book of Kings, to make clear exactly what was to come.

Ahaz, to whom the word is now addressed, had a son, Hezekiah; Hezekiah's son was Manasseh, and Manasseh's was Amon. His son was Josiah, a godly man, but he died in this way. Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, left his native land, marched out with his whole army, and pressed on against the land of the Assyrians. Josiah was afraid that he might come against Judea too, bring it under his own hand, and rule over it, and so he wanted to march out against him, although Pharaoh was trying to avoid a battle with him. But in resisting him Josiah died in the war, and the Egyptian took control of the land of the Jews. He grew so strong that he removed Jehoahaz, Josiah's son, from the throne after he had become king, carried him in chains into his own country, appointed Eliakim king, laid tribute on the nation, and demanded a great sum of money.

Then, after Eliakim had reigned over Judea for eleven full years, his son Jeconiah succeeded to the throne, and after him Zedekiah. While Zedekiah held the kingdom, Nebuchadnezzar made war on Judea.
