He burned all the cities, adding Jerusalem itself to the rest, and took Israel captive, together with the vessels…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ was not set in Israel to make them fall; God foretold the stumbling so that, knowing it beforehand, they might rise above the evil.
comments.comment: “A stone of stumbling” (Romans 9:33). Surely we do not say that Christ was set in Israel for this purpose; but since this was foreknown to God, he of necessity foretold what was to be: that a cause of slipping would lie in the foundations of Zion, and that some of the foolish would fall upon it and suffer this from their disobedience (Isaiah 8:14; Isaiah 28:16). He made the prediction for their benefit, not that they should stumble, but that, knowing it beforehand, they might rise above the evil. So Christ has been laid as a precious stone (Isaiah 28:16); but for those who stumble out of unbelief the loss was ruin, while for those who have believed the gain is life and justification.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the prophet speaks of a stone of stumbling.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who trust in Emmanuel are told to refuse the necromancers and ventriloquists, because it is senseless to ask the dead about the living, and the Law was given as a help.
comments.comment:
“…who talk emptily, who speak from the belly. Should not a nation go to its God? Why do they seek the dead on behalf of the living? For He gave the Law as a help, so that they might say: Not like this word, for which there are no gifts to give” (Isaiah 8:19-20).

Emmanuel Himself weaves a discourse of instruction for those who have set their hope on Him, who were reckoned among the children and have been given to Him by God the Father (Isaiah 8:18), as to the Savior, Redeemer, and Life-giver, who is able to enlighten them and to free them from every evil. And He draws them wholly away from their ancient habits and their former madness. For it is the custom of idol worshipers to love the oracles of demons and to cling to certain empty-talking necromancers, who say nothing true but simply belch out whatever comes into their heads.

But you, He says, even if someone comes to you and says, “Seek those who speak from the earth,” that is, those who pretend to bring up the dead and to give divinations as if from Hades, or the ventriloquists, who pretend to have certain gods in their belly and so to tell those who come to them what those gods say, do not accept the advice. For they speak only from their own belly, and they are not an understanding nation, such as would seek God and learn something from Him. And say to those who give that advice, “Why do they seek the dead on behalf of the living?”

Do you see how He makes them most sensible? For He not only commands them to turn away from the perversity and madness of those people, but also directs them to become good counselors to those who have gone astray. For say, He tells them, “Why do they seek the dead on behalf of the living?” The reasoning is common sense and human. For what reason could there be in wanting to question those who lie in the earth, or souls that have perhaps come to be in Hades, about people who are still alive?

And in another way too it is utterly ignorant to give heed to necromancy and to the lies of sorcerers, who have a dead mind and, as it were, a heart grown cold. For they do not know the Creator of all; they do not have within them the life-giving Word of God. Besides this, they also busy themselves with dead works. How then can the living, that is, those who have within themselves the life-giving power from above and are rich in the living Word of God, ask the dead about themselves?

So say these things, He says, adding that “He gave the Law as a help,” that is, the Law of the Gospel, so that those who heed it may say: “Not like this word, for which there are no gifts to give.” …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses mean and why they are worded as they are, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ and the gospel are the great light, while the law was only a lamp whose gleam reached no further than the Jewish boundaries.
comments.comment: … Christ our Lord is a great light, and so is the brightness of the gospel proclamation — not the law, which had been compared to a lamp. That is why a lamp always burned in the tent: the law’s gleam was short, able to send its own light only as far as the Jewish boundaries. So the gentiles were in darkness, as those who did not even have lamp-light (Matthew 4:12–16) (Isaiah 9:1–2).
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what the great light is and why the nations were in darkness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who sit in darkness are those who gaze at made things and will not rise in mind to the Maker, and the Word leads them to the light, who is Jesus.
comments.comment: To this too we shall reply that all those sit in darkness and are settled in it who gaze at the wicked crafts of painters, modellers and makers of statues, and who refuse to look up and to rise in mind from things visible and from everything perceived by the senses to the Maker of the universe, who is light (1 John 1:5). But everyone who has followed the rays of the Word is in light. For the Word has shown from how great an ignorance and impiety, and from how great a want of learning about the divine, these things were worshipped instead of God, and has taken the mind of anyone who wishes to be saved and led it by the hand to the uncreated God who is over all. For “the people who sat in darkness”, the people of the nations, “saw a great light, and for those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light dawned” (Matthew 4:16; Isaiah 9:2), namely Jesus, who is God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus is more than an angel: he is the Angel of great counsel, who announced to men God's great counsel about them.
comments.comment: Next, since he [Celsus] is thought to be speaking by way of concession when he says of the Saviour, “Let this man be taken to be truly an angel,” we say that we do not take this as something Celsus concedes; we take it from looking at the work of him who has visited the whole human race with his own word and teaching, as far as each of those who received him had room for it. That was the work of one who was not simply an angel but, as the prophecy about him named him, the Angel “of great counsel” (Isaiah 9:6). For he announced to men the great counsel of God, the Father of all things, concerning them: that those who yield to it by living in pure godliness are going up to God through great deeds, while those who do not receive him are putting themselves far from God (Psalm 73:27) and travelling toward destruction through their unbelief concerning God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the title in the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'whose rule is upon his shoulder' point to the cross, which became his rule and through which he reigns over what is under heaven.
comments.comment: The Savior is led to the saving suffering. They laid his cross on Simon of Cyrene. Another of the holy evangelists also said that Jesus himself “bore” (John 19:17) the wood. Both are wholly true: the Savior bore the cross, and somewhere in the middle of the road they met the Cyrenean, seized him, and transferred the cross onto him. For it was said about him through Isaiah’s voice: “A child was born to us, a son also was given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder.” (Isaiah 9:6) For his rule became the cross, through which he has reigned over what is under heaven — if it is true that he “became obedient unto death, even death of a cross; therefore God also highly exalted him.” (Philippians 2:8–9)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the rule on the shoulder means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Now that the shadow of the Law has given way to the truth, God has no joy in those who still live by the Law, and the lawlessness of Israel shows in what they did to Christ.
comments.comment:
… So before the coming of Christ, the Savior of us all, some who were well esteemed for the glories of the Law were strong and in the vigor of youth. But after His appearing and the preaching of the Gospel, the things of the Law have ceased, the shadow has passed over into the truth, and the worship that is in spirit and in truth has been brought in (John 4:23). God therefore does not rejoice over the young men of the Jews (Isaiah 9:17), that is, over those who still show their strength by choosing to live according to the Law. The sacrifices offered through blood are not accepted, nor circumcision of the flesh, nor teachings about washings, nor the idleness of the Sabbaths. But we have been taught, as I said, the way of the life that pleases God.

So, quite rightly, once the shadow came to an end, the young men who live by it are cast off, and the orphans and widows are far from being pitied (Isaiah 9:17). By orphans he means those who, as it were, lack spiritual upbringing and the guidance that comes from teachers. Likewise we say that the widows are souls that have come to lack the power to bear fruit, because they do not have the one who sows and supplies for them all good teachings.

No one would praise the state in which we shall find the people of Israel: without any share in true instruction because of their drunken outrage against Christ. For “their eyes were darkened so that they could not see,” as the psalmist says, and “their backs were bent” (Psalm 69:23), and this “continually,” so that they cannot look at the things above but, as if stooped over, are fixed on earthly things.

They will suffer this, he says, not without cause, but because “all have become lawless and wicked, and every mouth speaks lawless things” (Isaiah 9:17). For how are they not lawless and full of every wickedness, who strove to bring death upon the One who calls them to life, the One who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), although the Law says plainly, “You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous” (Exodus 23:7)? How has not every tongue of the Jews spoken unjust things? For they cried out against Christ to Pilate, saying, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” (John 19:15). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Assyrian's great boast to seize the whole world proved empty, for he barely escaped and went home a fugitive.
comments.comment: … But the bold and arrogant one, who shouted that great and empty boast, “I will seize the whole world in my hand like a nest, and like eggs left behind I will take it up, and there is no one who will escape me or speak against me” (compare Isaiah 10:14), was shown to have thought great things of himself in vain. For he barely escaped, and leaving Judea he withdrew home a fugitive.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fire consumes 'from soul even to flesh', that is, from the mind's intent to evil deeds.
comments.comment: … in Isaiah: 'And the light of Israel shall be as fire, and it shall consume like grass the wood, and it shall be consumed from soul even to flesh' (Isaiah 10:18), that is, from the mind's intent to evil deeds; for through the soul he touched the intention, and through the flesh the deeds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though Israel be as many as the sand, only the remnant justified through faith in Christ is saved, and the gospel is a concise word compared with the long circuit of the Law and prophets.
comments.comment: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea” (Romans 9:27). So even if Israel were as many as the sand, “the remnant will be saved” (Romans 9:27; Isaiah 10:22), that is, those who have been justified through faith in Christ; and this has come about because God had mercy on them. “For he is completing and cutting short the word” (Romans 9:28). He saved, he says, by “completing and cutting short the word”; that is, he declared to us the preaching of the gospel as an apt and concise and, so to speak, cut-short saying. For the law and the prophets, by a long circuit of words, scarcely set before us through the letter the meaning of what they say; but the preaching of the gospel is simple and a word cut short.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the saved remnant is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel was saved from the Assyrians by God's power and not by arms, so God told his people in Zion not to fear them.
comments.comment: In the book just completed, our discussion concerned the Assyrians and the one who ruled the realms of the Persians, who marched against Judea and Jerusalem but unexpectedly suffered what came from divine wrath. For Israel was saved beyond all expectation: not by stretching a bow, not by snatching up a shield, not by leading out horsemen or skillfully setting forces against his phalanxes, not by overpowering the enemy’s hand by the law of war, but by the power and grace of God. For “the angel of the Lord went out,” it says, “and killed in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of the Assyrians” (Isaiah 37:36). … That is why the God of all said: “Do not be afraid of the Assyrians, my people who dwell in Zion” (Isaiah 10:24). The manner of his flight was also described, as he all but shook cities and villages as he passed. And again: “Fear will seize Ramah, the city of Saul” (compare Isaiah 10:29).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil made war on the Church and was cast out of his tyranny through the passion of Christ, and God then announces beforehand the birth of the Only-Begotten.
comments.comment:
… He [the devil] made war on the Church of God, shaking at her the most unholy phalanx of the spirits under his hand. Perhaps he even thought he could overturn her with very little effort, the truly venerable and holy city of God, the spiritual Jerusalem. But he was caught, for none of his plans was possible. He could not besiege and take the holy city, or overpower a right hand so very strong. For who will stand against God, who can do all things?

So he perished together with his own shield-bearers, and was driven away from the flock of the godly, though he sprang on it like a savage beast; and he has been cast out of his tyranny over us. The Savior taught us this when he said: “Now is the judgment of this age; now the ruler of this age will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up on the earth, will draw all to myself” (John 12:31–32). For the passion of Christ became the overthrow of death, the pulling down of the devil, and the destruction of sin: he was lifted up on the cross, and he brought down the devil’s boast and threw it to the ground.

In due time, then, after those events, the God of all now brings in the account of the Only-Begotten’s birth according to the flesh, and reveals the mystery beforehand through the voice of prophets, so that when the events came to fulfillment, it might be believed by all without dispute. What, then, does he say? “Behold, the Master, the Lord of Hosts, will throw the glorious into confusion with strength” (Isaiah 10:33).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ came to proclaim that the law in letters had reached its end and all things are new, yet the leaders of the synagogue, who boasted of the priesthood, opposed him.
comments.comment:
The mystery of Christ refashions those on earth into the newness of gospel life (compare Romans 6:4), since the older customs are plainly overturned, and what was in shadows and types no longer has power to prevail. This was the purpose of his coming into this world. He came to proclaim, to the people of Israel before all others, that what was imposed until the time of reformation (compare Hebrews 9:10), that is, the law in letters, now at last comes to its end, as the mind of believers is remolded, as I said, into what is better and into a spiritual way of life. For all things in Christ are new (compare 2 Corinthians 5:17).

Yet though they ought to have been persuaded by him, the leaders of the synagogue of the Jews above all, who boasted not a little of the glories of the priesthood, opposed him headlong, worked against him impiously, and, though always talking of the law given through the most wise Moses, wanted to make of no effect, as far as it lay with them, the mystery of the Only-Begotten’s economy in the flesh …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The seven spirits resting on the rod from Jesse are the seven eyes of the Savior, who has each of them as his own and is filled with the spirit of fear, called reverence, as a man.
comments.comment: Who is this, if not the Savior who sojourned, having the seven-powered discerning nature? For it has been said in Isaiah concerning him: 'A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and he shall fill him with the spirit of the fear of God' (Isaiah 11:1-3). And see the seven eyes of the Lord upon one stone, of which one is the spirit of wisdom, another of understanding. For what eye is so luminous, beholding all good and great things, as the spirit of wisdom, and likewise the spirit of understanding? The spiritual stone thus eyed, being itself counsel and strength, beholds all things with counsel and strongly, having been filled knowingly and piously with the Spirit of God especially when he took the form of a servant. For at once he does not receive from without the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety resting upon him; for it was said to rest upon him. For each of the things said is his own and fitting to him, only the spirit of fear coming upon him so as to fill him. This spirit of fear is called reverence by another name, belonging to the man from Mary; the Apostle writes concerning this verbatim thus: 'Who in the days of his flesh, having offered prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, to the one able to save him from death, and having been heard from his reverence' (Hebrews 5:7). And he has reverence not as God, but as he is man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As love covers a multitude of sins, so the knowledge of God, like living water, covers the seas and makes them sweet and drinkable.
comments.comment: This indeed the vision has attained clarity, as we were explaining recently the one in Isaiah having it thus: 'The whole earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea' (Isa 11:9). For just as the divine love, that which is from God toward those experiencing good, and that of the benefactors toward the magnanimous, 'covers a multitude of sins' (1 Pet 4:8), vanishing the sins, but not guarding them, and covering what was done crudely, so the knowledge of God, existing as living water, covers the seas, changing them into sweetness and something drinkable.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Afflictions are a help for the improvement of those who ask for it, and God, who wishes all to be saved, heals again after the painful discipline.
comments.comment: The afflictions are like a help for the improvement of those asking for it, for the purpose of ceasing sin and the diseases and wounds from it. It is his to hear 'the one desiring to save all and to come to the knowledge of truth' (1 Timothy 2:4); 'When the wrath of my spirit arises, I will heal again', as he says graciously, having been tested for healing through painful discipline: 'I will bless you, Lord, because you were angry with me; you turned away your wrath and had mercy on me' (Isaiah 12:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The springs of salvation are the prophets, evangelists and apostles, who pour out the saving word with the Holy Spirit's help and so gladden all under heaven.
comments.comment: “And draw water with gladness from the springs of salvation.” (Isaiah 12:3) And we say that the springs of salvation are the holy prophets, evangelists, and apostles, who pour forth the word from above and from heaven and saving for the world, the Holy Spirit supplying them, and thus gladden all under heaven. Come then, letting the mind down into the depths of the thoughts beside them, let us draw the finding of the truth from there.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the springs of salvation are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: After the blows that fell on them, God promises Israel a return from captivity, and the prophecy turns first on the Chaldeans of Babylon, whom Cyrus conquered because God put them under him.
comments.comment:
… So the God of all, in His wise ordering, after the blow and the scourges and the things that had befallen them at the hands of their enemies from time to time, foretells also things most pleasant and able to gladden them. He promises that He will bring back home even those already taken captive, will release them from the bonds of their misery, and will hand over to their enemies those very people who had once conquered them. … Many had sacked the land of the Jews at various times, but the harshest and fiercest of all were above all the Chaldeans and those who reigned over Babylon in their turn. So the word of prophecy leaps on them first, as it were, and says: “Raise a signal on a mountain of the plain” (Isaiah 13:2).

Since we have chosen to give an exact account in interpreting the passage before us, I think we must first relate some of the most necessary facts. Cyrus, then, son of Cambyses by his father and of Mandane by his mother, who reigned over the Persians and the Medes, marched against Babylon and against the whole land of the Chaldeans, which was wide and very large, and he conquered it.

He did not take it by his own forces, nor because he could use a stronger hand, for the Chaldean nation was unbeatable and without rival because of its numbers and its thorough training in warfare. Rather, God put his opponents under him and shook down the ungodly power of the Babylonians. He did this because sorcery abounded among them beyond measure and the swarm of their idols was past counting. Indeed, it has been called “the land of carved images” (Jeremiah 50:38), either because of the multitude of idols or because each of those who lived there was found to differ in no way from an idol, I mean in turning aside to error without check or restraint.

Besides this, He did it because they laid waste the holy land allotted to God, that is, Judaea, burned Jerusalem and the divine temple itself, carried off the sacred vessels to their own land, and in unrestrained fury killed Israel, though it was called a holy people, the portion and lot of God. That God handed Israel over into the hands of enemies when it worshipped idols is not unclear to those who know the sacred writings; but they punished him beyond measure …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wild beasts, echoes and demons will fill the ruined houses of Babylon, and the word that it comes quickly promises Israel a swift release.
comments.comment:
… “And wild beasts will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo. And sirens will rest there, and demons will dance there. And donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs will make their nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay” (Isaiah 13:21-22).

Wild animals somehow always like to make deserted places their home, and a city falling into ruin gives them a great many hiding places, wide ones too, roofed over by themselves and makeshift, found, as it were, by chance and of their own accord. In deserts and silent places a faint echo, I do not know how, rises as if out of the very depth of the silence and steals into the ears of those who keep still.

So wild beasts, he says, will rest there, and the houses will be filled with echo; that is, having no one at all living in them, they will come to hold the echo that belongs to desolate places. And demons too, he says, will dance there. For they say that these also especially like to linger in quiet places and to make them a kind of leisurely lodging.

By “sirens” he means, I think, the birds that know how to sing sweetly, or, according to the Hebrew edition, the owl. The wild donkeys he has called “donkey-centaurs”; and by “hedgehogs” he means those mice that bristle, as it were, with sharp spines. All these would fittingly suit cities or houses that are wholly deserted.

To these he adds that “it comes quickly and will not delay” (Isaiah 13:22). He does this either to put a sharper anxiety into the Assyrians, or else to make it no small comfort to those of Israel's blood. For since they were in captivity and were expecting to be set free when Cyrus marched against the land of the Babylonians with the Persians and the Medes, he promises them a swift release from their troubles: what they prayed for would not be put off for long, but would follow, as it were, close on the heels of the word. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the desolation of Babylon looks like and why the verse adds that it comes quickly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hades was embittered when it met Christ because it was abolished, mocked and bound, having swallowed life and been swallowed by life.
comments.comment: Hades was embittered when it tasted the precious and holy flesh of the Master, as Isaiah foretold when he said, "Hades was embittered when it met you below" (Isaiah 14:9 LXX). It was embittered because it was abolished. It was embittered because it was mocked. It was embittered, for it was also bound. It received a body and encountered God. It received what it could see, and it fell by what it could not see. Death swallowed without knowing, but after swallowing it recognized whom it had swallowed. It swallowed life, and it was swallowed by life. It swallowed the one along with all, but through the one it lost all. It seized like a lion, but its teeth were crushed.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
comments.work: Oration on the Resurrection of the Lord

comments.capsule: The words 'how did he fall' show he was in heaven, and 'I will ascend' shows he desired another heaven.
comments.comment: He says: 'I will ascend into the heaven' (Isaiah 14:13), which implies he fell from the heaven he possessed; for how 'did the morning star, rising early, fall from heaven?' (Isa 14:12) by saying 'how did he fall?' He showed that he was in heaven, but by saying 'I will ascend into the heaven and I will be,' he showed that he desired to become in another heaven. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the devil was already in heaven, his words 'I will ascend into heaven' mean a desire to become God, whom he called 'heaven' in thinking to be like the Most High.
comments.comment: For certainly the devil was found in heaven; for there he fell along with those who blasphemed and were puffed up. For it is said toward him: 'You said: I will ascend into heaven' (Isaiah 14:13). Being in heaven, how does he ascend into heaven? He was in heaven, in which also other divine and blessed essences are. But he took a fantasy and a desire to be God. Thinking he would become 'like the Most High' (Isaiah 14:14), he named the likeness to the Most High 'heaven' while being in heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why one who is already in heaven can say 'I will ascend'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Babylon, though brought against Jerusalem at God's will, is justly punished because it was merciless, like Pharaoh, a vessel of wrath already liable to punishment.
comments.comment:
But someone, I think, who has considered the calamities that befell Judaea and Jerusalem itself might say: “Did the tyrant of the Babylonians come of his own accord, march against the land of the Jews and take the holy city, without God letting him do it, or rather without God giving it to him? Yet the prophet Isaiah himself tells us: ‘The Lord will whistle for the fly that rules part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of the Assyrians, and they will all come and rest in the ravines of the land, and in the holes of the rocks, and in the caves, and in every cleft, and on every tree’ (Isaiah 7:18-19). How then can the Babylonian, who served God's command, bear a charge he cannot escape, and be punished so terribly that nothing can be seen beyond the wrath brought upon him?”

Yes, and with very good reason. For the God of all willed to rebuke Israel when he had turned aside to apostasy, and by measured chastisements to persuade him to run back to the worship he was used to, I mean the worship of the Law. But the Babylonian, though brought in for this purpose, was merciless like a wild beast and gave free rein to his fury. So he is accused, as God says plainly: “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that join in the attack; for I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack for evil” (Zechariah 1:14-15).

God raised up Pharaoh, who was a vessel of anger and wrath (Romans 9:22) and was already liable to punishment for his own offences, so that, as He Himself says, He might show in him His own power and the exactness of His just judgment (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16). In the same way you should understand the case of the Babylonians. They were vessels of wrath who justly deserved punishment, and they were brought against Jerusalem so that, after disciplining Israel, they too might afterward be given up to the punishment that most befitted and best suited them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God can use a nation and still punish it, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The offspring of Nebuchadnezzar, down to Belshazzar, followed their father's perversity and outdid his deeds.
comments.comment:
“Wicked seed, prepare your children to be slaughtered for the sins of your father, so that they may not rise up and fill the earth with wars. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will destroy their name and remnant and seed” (Isaiah 14:20-22).

Nebuchadnezzar did most terrible things against every nation; and those who came after him and were descended from him, down to Belshazzar, followed their father's perversity and outdid his deeds…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The oracle is against the land and kingdom of Moab, a nation hateful to God for idolatry and magic, whose king Balak tried through Balaam and then through the women of Moab to bring Israel down.
comments.comment:
“The oracle against Moab” (Isaiah 15:1).

Having fully finished his discourse on the Babylonians and the Philistines, he now turns his prophecy to Moab, that is, against the capital city of the Moabites, the whole country, and the kingdom itself. They too were a barbarous nation, hateful to God, because they were wholly given over to the worship of idols, trusted above all in the art of magic, exalted themselves against the glory of God, and were among the bitterest enemies of the people of Israel.

Indeed, when the Israelites had been freed from the greed of the Egyptians and were going to the land of promise, they very nearly all perished, as far as the scheme of Balak, then king of the Moabites, could bring it about. It is written thus in Numbers: “And all the sons of Israel encamped on the west of Moab, by the Jordan opposite Jericho. And Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorite; and Moab was greatly afraid of the people, because they were many; and Moab was filled with dread before the sons of Israel” (Numbers 22:1-3).

Then what was his wicked scheme? He hired Balaam from Mesopotamia, a false prophet and an augur, and then appealed to him, saying: “Curse Israel for me. For I know,” he says, “that those whom you bless are blessed, and those whom you curse are cursed” (Numbers 22:6). So Balaam went through his ways of sorcery, with altars set up and sacrifices offered (Numbers 23:1-2). But Balak was cheated of his hope and missed his aim, for the man brought in to curse them unexpectedly blessed Israel (Numbers 24:10).

When his attempt had turned out contrary to his hopes, he pursued his malice against them again by another way. For he caught the Israelites as in a net, carried away by the beauty of the women, so that they forsook their love for God and chose to worship Baal of Peor, an idol of the Moabites. It is written thus again in Numbers: “And Israel lodged at Shittim, and the people were defiled by committing fornication with the daughters of Moab; and they invited them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices and bowed down to their idols. And Israel was initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor, and the Lord was angry with Israel in His wrath” (Numbers 25:1-3).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the background a reader needs to understand why Moab is the target of the oracle.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moab, which jeered at Israel's misfortunes, was given over to desolation, and its wall fell by night in an earthquake before the enemy attacked.
comments.comment:
They kept this attitude to the very end. Whenever Israel had offended God and happened to fall into misfortune, they boasted over him and jeered, charging God with being utterly powerless, the God who promises to save those who worship him.

The blessed Jeremiah is witness to this in his vision against them, where he says: “The horn of Moab is broken, and his arm is shattered. Make him drunk, for he magnified himself against the Lord” (Jeremiah 48:25–26). And again: “For thus says the Lord: Arioth is taken, and the strongholds are seized. And Moab will perish as a people, for he magnified himself against the Lord” (Jeremiah 48:40–42).

For in time the tyrant of the Assyrians and Babylonians came to lay Judea waste, and he took the cities of Samaria. The Moabites, for their part, smiled at those who had perished, mocked them beyond measure, and went on heaping insult on the glory of God.

For this reason they too have been given over to desolation and have utterly perished, cities, people, and every household together, so that now it seems almost as if they had never existed.

The vision before us, then, recalls what befell them, plainly by wrath from above, and says: “By night the Moabite will perish; for by night the wall of the land of Moab will perish” (Isaiah 15:1).

Some who have studied these matters closely have handed down that, when the Babylonians were about to make war on them, an earthquake struck and shook the chief city of the Moabites so violently that its whole wall fell of itself in the night and the dark. When this happened, before the enemy attacked, their hope of safety all but perished. That is why he says that the land of Moab will perish by night.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the words 'by night' point to and why Moab was judged.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moab, who gloated over others' misfortunes, is told to grieve over itself, and even its place of divination at Lebedon will perish.
comments.comment:
“But grieve,” he says, “over yourselves” (Isaiah 15:2). It is as if he said: Many times you raised your brows high and gloated over the misfortunes of others; but now the war is running against you yourselves, and the harm that comes of it hangs over your unholy heads. Grieve, then, not over any others, but over yourselves.

“For Lebedon will perish, where your altar is” (Isaiah 15:2). I said that the Moabites had become fierce and arrogant, trusting in the deceits of demons and supposing that by the magician's art they would prevail over the power of all, even of Israel himself, though God should defend him. So in the place called Lebedon they had an altar and a sacred precinct of no ordinary construction. There they performed their divinations and prided themselves greatly, and they held the place more sacred than any other. But, he says, even the workshop of your divination will perish.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the command to grieve and the altar at Lebedon mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet will make Moab's suffering known far and wide, as widely as its wall fell, the wall it renewed to no good purpose.
comments.comment:
…For I proclaim your sufferings and make widely known the calamity brought upon you. Like a well-tuned lyre I will cry out; I will strike the strings so, and make the song heard far and wide, as with the wall which you renewed.

At the beginning of the vision the blessed prophet said: “By night the land of Moab will perish; for by night the wall of the land of Moab will perish” (Isaiah 15:1). In explaining the force of these words, we said that when an earthquake struck, the wall of the land of Moab burst apart, and before the enemy's invasion it was all but levered up from its foundations and came crashing down over the land of the Moabites. They renewed it, but spent their labour on it entirely in vain, for the Assyrians and Babylonians took the whole land without effort.

“My inward parts,” he says, “will sound like a harp” over your misfortunes (Isaiah 16:11), and so I will make your suffering known far and wide, just as your wall came down, the wall you renewed, but to no good purpose. For when the wall fell of itself, what had happened escaped no one in the whole land of the Moabites, nor those living in other cities and countries.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moab will be put to shame, wearing itself out at its altars and praying to handmade idols that cannot rescue it.
comments.comment:
“And it will be, when you are put to shame, that Moab has wearied herself at the altars; and she will go into her handmade things to pray, and she will not be able to deliver him” (Isaiah 16:12).

Something more, he says, will happen to you besides, which will bring you shame and disgrace: you will endure labours in vain, filling your altars with blood, making your sacrifices unceasing, and offering prayers to things made by hands. You will obtain nothing that brings help or safety, for they will not be able to free you from the evils hanging over you.

What strength is there in lifeless idols, which are inventions of human skill and have for their makers the very people who worship them? So, as the blessed David says: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8).

It should be known that the Moabites were extremely superstitious: readers of bird omens, false prophets, and tellers of wonders, who put very great confidence in the evils of sorcery. For they perhaps supposed that they could prevail over the enemy's power, not so much, I think, by skill in tactics as by the help of their own gods.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moab's prayers at its altars bring no help.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: This is the vision God spoke against Moab, though he had spoken many things about her even before.
comments.comment: “This is the word which the Lord spoke against Moab, when he spoke” (Isaiah 16:13). This, he says, is the vision spoken by God against the land of the Moabites; “when he spoke,” that is, even before the words came through me, he had spoken a great many things about her…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The enemy host came on Judea like a rushing flood but, like chaff and wheel-dust before a wind, was driven back, as Sennacherib was.
comments.comment:
They came upon the lands, that is, the cities of Judea, like a great flood of water rushing down with violence and raising a roar, all but sweeping over those who resisted like the waves of the sea.

Here he calls them “the back of many nations” (Isaiah 17:12), because many nations were pursued by them; and pursuers always and everywhere run at the backs of those who flee.

Then what follows? “He will drive him off,” he says, that is, he will send him back, “and pursue him far away, like the fine chaff of winnowers before the wind, and like the dust of a wheel which a storm carries” (Isaiah 17:13). For what is so easily scattered as dust from a wheel and a threshing floor when a fierce wind sweeps down on it?

That Sennacherib went off a fugitive, the God of all will confirm when he says to him through the voice of Isaiah: “I will put a muzzle in your nose and a bridle in your lips, and I will turn you back by the way by which you came” (Isaiah 37:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the images of the flood and the chaff for the Assyrian host.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The mourning at evening ended before morning, since God destroyed the Assyrian ranks before dawn and so punished those who plundered his people.
comments.comment:
“Toward evening there will be mourning; before morning it will be no more. This is the portion of those who plundered you, and the inheritance of those who inherited you” (Isaiah 17:14).

I said earlier that Rabshakeh surrounded Jerusalem with his fighting force and threatened to take it before long, but perished with his whole army before dawn and daylight. So there will be mourning toward evening, he says, since those in Jerusalem no doubt expected the assault of the war to come in the morning; but it ended before dawn.

That is why he says: There will be mourning toward evening, but before morning it will be no more. That is, the weeping will stop and come to an end, and it will vanish together with the fear of suffering, since God comes to their help, destroys the enemy's ranks beyond all expectation, and drives their leader out of the land of the Jews besides.

The blessed David also explains this when he says: “At evening weeping will stay the night, and at morning there will be gladness” (Psalm 30:5).

But this, he says, is the lot, this the portion of those who plundered you and seized you as their own inheritance. By these words he reproaches the people of Israel: they themselves had done the things for which the nation might well have perished utterly, yet he takes pity on them once more and punishes with death those who plunder the people allotted to him.

For, it says, “when the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; and his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:8–9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'toward evening' and 'before morning' refer to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet announces how Egypt, sunk in idolatry, was saved through faith in Christ; some take the light cloud to be the Lord's holy flesh, others the Virgin.
comments.comment:
In these words the prophet sets out to teach how the land of the Egyptians was saved and drawn as in a net into true religion, plainly through faith in Christ, although it worshipped many gods and was sick with error beyond measure.

For they were, as it were, in deep darkness. They knew nothing at all of him who is God by nature and truly the Maker and Lord of all, and they fastened their worship on the creation. What was still more absurd, they made themselves the craftsmen of their own gods and kept a swarm of idols of every shape in their temples, so that they even moulded likenesses of irrational animals, set up altars, and sacrificed to them.

Since sin had multiplied among them, grace had to abound all the more (Romans 5:20); the Physician had to shine upon those so grievously sick, and the divine and heavenly light had to flash upon those darkened in heart.

“Behold, then,” he says, “the Lord is seated on a light cloud, and he will come to Egypt.” But what might it mean that the Lord is seen on a light cloud? Come, let us say what we can.

Some interpreters have said that the light cloud is the holy flesh of the Lord, that is, the temple taken from the Virgin. They liken it to a cloud because it is free, perhaps, of the more earthly impulses and desires, and is, as it were, above and on high. For the holy body of Christ, the Saviour of us all, is truly all-pure and free of every earthly impurity. Others again have taken the holy Virgin to be what is called a light cloud.
comments.selected_reason: Says whom the verse is about and gives early readings of the 'light cloud'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophets saw God's glory in many forms, and the light cloud may likewise hint at a breadth of meanings.
comments.comment:
For my part, I think that saying he sits on a light cloud may also hint to us at a breadth of other meanings. For the blessed prophets, when they beheld the glory of God, wrote down their visions in many ways. Isaiah says that he saw the Lord of hosts on a throne, high and lifted up, with the highest rational powers standing in a circle around him, singing his praise and saying that heaven and earth are full of his glory (Isaiah 6:1–3).

The all-wise Daniel seats the Ancient of Days on a throne; he insists that a thousand thousands serve him, and says that ten thousand times ten thousand stand around him (Daniel 7:9–10);…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cloud is a type of baptism, and it is called light because baptism takes away the burden of sin and lifts the mind upward; Christ sitting on it means rest and rule.
comments.comment:
In each of these visions he subtly hints to us at an image of the glory that befits God and of the mystery of Christ. Nothing, then, prevents us from understanding that here too the Lord was seen on a light cloud for a most useful and necessary purpose. For the cloud fills out for us a type of spiritual rain and dew, and of saving baptism itself.

Indeed, the blessed Paul says that those of Israel's blood were baptized in the cloud and in the sea (1 Corinthians 10:2). As they crossed that deep desert, the cloud hung over them by day, and by night a pillar of fire went before them (Exodus 13:21). Through both of these Christ was being portrayed, that is, the mystery concerning him: justification and sanctification in faith and holy baptism.

So the Lord, coming to cleanse and transform the Egyptians, in a manner fitting God and spiritually, of course, had to be seen on a light cloud. For there was no other way to scrub from the soul of those in error the stain ingrained in it except through holy baptism; and we hold that the cloud is a type of that baptism.

And the cloud is very fittingly called light. For we are baptized for the putting away of sin; and as we turn away from ungodliness as from a burden truly hard to carry, we become, in a way, winged by this, and learn to set our minds on things above (Colossians 3:2) and to keep our hearts on high.

As for the Lord's sitting upon the cloud, I think it shows this: sitting hints to us at either rest or authority. So Christ rests, not in any way in worship according to the law, but rather in the perfection that comes through holy baptism; and in this way he has come to reign over those on earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'light cloud' as baptism and what it means that the Lord sits on it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: With baptism revealed, the idols of Egypt had to be shaken and the devil's snares broken, for Egypt was among the most superstitious of nations.
comments.comment:
He says that the handmade things of Egypt will be shaken before his face (Isaiah 19:1). For once holy baptism had been revealed and Christ had shone forth, it was wholly necessary that the playthings of the ancient deceit should vanish and the snares of the devil be seen broken to pieces.

For the devil had caught in his net, for ruin and destruction, practically every nation and race, but the Egyptians more than the rest. They were the most superstitious of all, perhaps outdoing even the Persians and Assyrians in error, although the God-inspired Scripture says of those peoples' land that it is a land of carved images (Jeremiah 50:38).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those in these cities speak the Canaanite tongue and swear by the name of the Lord, which only those who have come to know and believe in him do.
comments.comment:
…we say that the first [of the five cities] is what is now the city of the Rhinocorurans. They do indeed speak the Canaanite tongue (Isaiah 19:18), for the people in these cities have taken pains to adopt not so much the speech of the Egyptians as that of the Syrians.

Some say that Josephus clearly records in his own writings that a certain Ionias, who was of the blood of Levi and honoured with the priesthood under the law, left the land of the Jews, either after quarrelling with some of his own people or perhaps after suffering persecution, and occupied these five cities, since they bordered on the Canaanites. This man, he says, gathered a multitude of Jews past easy counting and settled in one of these five cities, which was also named the city of Asedek, that is, of righteousness (Isaiah 19:18). From that time, they say, those living at the borders of Egypt grew accustomed to speaking the language of the Canaanites and came to love it.

And they will learn, he says, to swear by the name of the Lord (Isaiah 19:18). This too is remarkable. For worshippers of vain things are accustomed to swear by whichever element of the world each of them fancies. Some name heaven, others the sun, others even the handmade things in their shrines; but they make no mention at all of the true God, for they have not known him. But to swear by his name belongs to those who have already come to know him and believe.

So too the all-wise Moses, when Israel had come away from the worship of Egypt, led them to the knowledge of the true God, saying: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve”; and he added to this: “And by his name you shall swear” (Deuteronomy 6:13). That these five cities swear by no vain thing, but rather take up the name of the Lord for their oaths, is therefore clear proof that they received the faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's details, the language and the oath by the Lord's name.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Egypt, once full of temples and altars to idols, will accept the worship of the true God when the saving preaching shines among them.
comments.comment:
“On that day there will be an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the Lord at its border; and it will be a sign to the Lord for ever in the land of Egypt” (Isaiah 19:19–20).

For the whole land of the Egyptians was crowded with temples and full of altars, and there were libations and sacrifices everywhere, offered by them partly to the elements of the world and partly, as I said, to the statues set up in shrines, and indeed to the pillars of demons. And why do I say this, when they even set up the shapes of irrational animals and bestowed on them the glory that befits God?

See, then, from what to what the state of the Egyptians has changed. For those who were once more superstitious than all others, and had plunged without bridle into lawless excess, will on that day, he says, that is, at that time when the saving preaching shines among them, accept the worship of him who by nature…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the altar and pillar as the change from idol worship to the worship of God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Egyptians cried out, wronged by Satan and the demons, and the man the Lord sends is Christ, who saved them by judging and casting these out.
comments.comment:
…since they had not come to know the Master of all, would they have cried out to him at all? But just as the blood of Abel is said to have cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), not, surely, as though it had a voice of its own, but because God abhorred the very outrage of the deed, in the same way, I think, one might understand it also of those who used to worship the unclean demons. For even if they do not know the God of all, yet because they have been wronged by Satan, through the deed itself, in a manner, they have cried aloud, surely asking for help for themselves.

In this sense we say that the Egyptians too cried out to God because of those who oppressed them, that is, those who had brought them under their own hand and crushed them as with a most bitter slavery: plainly, the unclean demons. “But the Lord will send them a man who will save them” (Isaiah 19:20). And who is the man, if not, plainly, Christ, that is, the only-begotten Word of God who appeared in human form? He saved not only the Egyptians but the whole earth.

And he saved by judging. What does “by judging” mean? It means that he brought a just judgment in their case. For Satan, who had wronged them, and with him the unclean demons, he subjected to holy verdicts, cast them into Tartarus with chains of gloom, and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment of the great day (compare 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). But those who had endured so unbearable a wrong he saved and rescued, and made them his own worshipers, flashing on them the light of truth and clothing them with the glories of freedom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'man who will save' is and what 'by judging' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's judgment of the world drew all to himself, and those who sacrificed to demons will now offer him worship in spirit and pay their vows.
comments.comment:
So the Savior himself says somewhere: “Now is the judgment of this world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up, will draw all to myself” (John 12:31–32). You see that he has given judgment for the world, cast out Satan, who long ago tyrannized over it, and drawn all to himself. For the Egyptians too have come to know him. And indeed, having come to know him, they offer sacrifices, they make vows, and they carry out what they promised (compare Isaiah 19:21). This is what is sung through the voice of David: “Make vows and pay them to the Lord our God” (Psalm 76:11).

See, then, the newness of things. Those who formerly used to sacrifice to demons, who brought their worship to Satan and dedicated thank offerings to him, and who eagerly fulfilled vows, that is, promises, will be enlightened in mind through Christ and made bright by the doctrines of truth. They will run from their ancient error, and having once come to know the Maker and Lord of all, they bring him worship in spirit, fulfilling most pure vows…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sight of the enemy host is enough to strike fear, and the attackers' lawless boldness cannot be checked.
comments.comment:
“As if a storm of winds should pass through the desert” (Isaiah 21:1), raising the dust and all but throwing everything into confusion.

He adds: “For the vision is fearful, and a harsh one was announced to me” (Isaiah 21:1–2). For the mere sight of the enemy alone, and a most valiant host of fighting men equipped for war, is quite enough to strike harsh fear into those who see it. Yet he does not say only that he saw it, but also, “It was announced to me”; for together with the sight he was taught the outcome of events, plainly by God.

“The one who deals faithlessly deals faithlessly, and the lawless one acts lawlessly” (Isaiah 21:2). The boldness of the attackers, he says, cannot be checked. For no human reasoning kindles them to gentleness; no one among them gives thought to what is right, but each acts lawlessly without restraint and deals faithlessly as he pleases, with no mercy in him. For they do not look to mercy; rather, he says, their whole eager work will be to act lawlessly and faithlessly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the storm image and the fear of the vision.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words are a speech put in the mouth of the Assyrian, who groans and laments, broken to weakness before the battle has begun.
comments.comment:
“The Elamites are upon me, and the envoys of the Persians are coming against me. Now I will groan and comfort myself. Therefore my loins are filled with faintness, and pangs have seized me like a woman in labour. I did wrong so as not to hear; I hastened so as not to see. My heart wanders, and lawlessness plunges me under; my soul is set in fear” (Isaiah 21:2–4).

The words here have the force of a speech put in a character's mouth. For the Assyrian is brought on stage, fearing the assault, well aware of the enemy's ranks and of whom their war is aimed at. “Not against any others,” he says, “but against me the Elamites and the very best of the Persians have set out. So I will groan and comfort myself.”

For those who have fallen into the worst misfortune seem to find some kind of comfort in lamenting and wailing, since pain squeezes out tears. Yet it is a strange thing if the Assyrians lament, since they had always been harsh and arrogant, carried their brows very high against all the nations, and thought themselves hard to stand against.

But those who were so bold, swollen with thoughts beyond what is human, give way to womanish tears and compose a lament over themselves, broken down to weakness before they have even tasted battle.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the speaker is the Assyrian brought on stage, afraid of the attack.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel, given to idolatry, did not even in disaster seek God with repentance, but went up to useless housetops.
comments.comment:
Since Israel, then, gave free rein to its advance in sin, and was devoted, as I said just now, to the false worship of idols, God through the prophet foretells the capture of Jerusalem that would come in its time, and says: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up to useless housetops? The city is filled with people shouting. Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead the dead of war” (Isaiah 22:1–2).

It seems to point here to the devastation in the days of Jeconiah, and to accuse those of Israel severely, because even amid these very evils, in misfortunes at their very height, they did not know how to do what leads to their good and what would win them favor from above. For they ought to have gone up to the house of God weeping and lamenting, to promise repentance, to ask pardon for the outrages they had committed, and to seek the helping hand from him, and from him alone.

And he himself taught this, saying through one of the holy prophets: “Gird yourselves and beat your breasts, you priests; wail, you who minister at the altar. Go in, sleep in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and drink offering are withheld from your house. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a solemn service, gather the elders, all who dwell in the land, into the house of your God, and cry out earnestly to the Lord: Alas, alas, for the day” (Joel 1:13–15).

These are the things they ought to have done to appease the one who has power to save, since he had been provoked. But it seems that they did not even let it enter their minds that they ought to do these things. Instead they went up to the highest parts of their houses, and everywhere there were laments, and the wailing of children, wasting away, it may be, from hunger and thirst. For such things must happen to cities under siege.

That is why he says: “What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up to useless housetops?” Why, he says, even amid terrors so unbearable, when your peril had reached its last extremity and everything was at stake, did you not cry out to God, but instead leapt up to the housetops, though that did you no good at all? That is why he calls them useless housetops.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'useless housetops' say about the people's response to the siege.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The city was filled with random shouting instead of tears before God, and was full of dead before the fighting began.
comments.comment: And why was the city filled with people shouting? Not, surely, people crying to God, but people crying out at random, and all but beside themselves at the evils that had come within their doors. The lament ought to have been for repentance; the tears ought to have been shed before God. See, he says: before you joined battle, before you took up the sword, before you planned any resistance, the city became full of dead.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the shouting in the city was useless.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Tyre joined in plundering the Jews and carrying sacred vessels to its false gods, so God returned the payment on its head.
comments.comment: In another way, too, they themselves joined in plundering the nation of the Jews: on the one hand by falling on them when they were worn down and seizing those who were left; on the other by dedicating sacred vessels to their falsely named gods, and by driving those who had come under the yoke of slavery to them away, by force as it were, from the worship the law prescribes. And so God said through one of the holy prophets: “And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back, or do you bear a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your payment on your own heads, because you took my silver and my gold, and carried my choice and fine things into your temples, and you sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks, to drive them out of their own borders” (Joel 3:4–6).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Tyre fell when the Babylonian joined its island to the mainland; many sailed away, and the prophet commands the ships of Carthage to wail over it.
comments.comment:
So Tyre too was captured through the wrath of God, in this way. It was an island, with a strait still running between, which separated it from the mainland by no great distance. When the Babylonian came and sought to take it along with the other cities, he ordered the armies under his command to fill in the sea between, to join it to the mainland, and to let it remain an island no longer. When this had been done, or was expected to be done before long, most of those in Tyre, since trade was their occupation and they were used to sailing, sailed away from the island with their children and wives and went off to other cities and villages.

The Babylonians then marched in, killed those who remained, took many captive, and did what victors usually do. Yet they were grieved not a little to learn that a great many, among them the most prominent in the city, had put their goods on ships and fled.

The prophecy of Ezekiel also records this history. For the God of all spoke to him thus: “Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre; every head was made bald, and every shoulder rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army received any wages for the hard service he served against Tyre. In return for this I have given him the land of Egypt” (Ezekiel 29:18–20). For after the capture of the Tyrians the Babylonian turned the war against the nation of the Egyptians.

This is the history the blessed prophet Isaiah now recalls, when he commands the ships of Carthage to wail. They are to wail, clearly, over Tyre, because it has perished, and they no longer come from the land of the Kittim (Isaiah 23:1).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the history of Tyre's fall that the verse recalls.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The seventy years are to be read not as history but as seventy cycles of the sun of righteousness, completed when one is perfected.
comments.comment: He asks: 'Tell me, when do you think that which is in Isaiah will be fulfilled?' 'And it shall be,' he says, 'after seventy years Tyre shall be restored to its ancient state' (Isaiah 23:15). From when of the seventy years are they counted? Not so that I may take them according to history, but seventy cycles of the sun of righteousness, seventy years. For the sun goes around, illuminating souls and making the doctrines of truth manifest and sending forth its rays. Therefore, when anyone is perfected and has reached the end of his progress, then the seventy years are established for him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is refashioning all things as at the beginning, and Isaiah foretold the equality of life to come, in which people are as the priest and servants as their masters.
comments.comment: …Christ is refashioning all things to what they were in the beginning. For what is in him is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and there is neither slave nor free, but he himself is all and in all (Colossians 3:11). Indeed Isaiah cried out beforehand about the state of the life we await, the life that is to be, and about the equality that is found with God, saying, “And the people shall be as the priest, and the servant as his master, and the maidservant as her mistress” (Isaiah 24:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Prophets always give the cause of God's wrath, and here the earth is cursed because Israel set the law aside for the commandments of men.
comments.comment:
“Because they transgressed the law and changed the ordinances, an everlasting covenant, therefore a curse will devour the earth, because those who dwell in it have sinned” (Isaiah 24:5–6).

The discourse returns again to the exact sense of the prophecy. So that no one may think that the God of all brings punishments on anyone without cause, the prophets join the causes to the stirrings of wrath and plainly announce the charges against those who are punished. The earth will mourn, then; for what cause? “Because they transgressed the law and broke the everlasting covenant.” That is why he says: “And the earth will be accursed, for those who dwell in it have done wrong.”

Since the land of the Jews too, together with the other cities or countries, was made to pay the penalty (for it was laid waste, as I said), the prophet again seems to bring into the open the offenses of those under the law. “For they transgressed the law,” he says. Those of Israel held it of no account, and turned as it were onto another path, giving heed to teachings that are commandments of men (compare Isaiah 29:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the earth is cursed, as the prophet states the charge.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law God engraved on man and wrote on the heart was transgressed, and the earth is cursed because men turned to the flesh and an earthly mind.
comments.comment:
Taking the words in their universal sense and giving their meaning, we say that in the beginning the God of all fashioned man and engraved on him a natural law, training him toward the knowledge of evil and good. And this, I think, is what was said through the voice of John about the only-begotten Son of God: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9). We understand that this also came about in the last times, I mean the times of his coming. For it is written: “In those days, says the Lord, putting my laws into their mind, I will also write them on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10).

This law, then, which steers us from within toward the knowledge of good and evil, those on the earth transgressed, and they changed the ordinances. For though they were created for good works (compare Ephesians 2:10), they turned to love of the flesh and to an earthly mind. That is why the earth has become accursed: those who dwell in it have offended the Creator by a great many wrongs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'law' and 'ordinances' as the natural law within.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because lawlessness filled the earth, those who dwell in it will be weighed down by poverty and few will be left.
comments.comment: “Therefore those who dwell in the earth will be poor, and few people will be left” (Isaiah 24:6). For since, he says, the earth has become accursed because so very much lawlessness arose in it, they will therefore be weighed down by unexpected poverty and will barely be saved; for those left will be few and easily counted.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet, filled with joy, praises God for the ancient and true counsel, which is the mystery of the Only-Begotten becoming man, foreordained before the foundation of the world.
comments.comment:
“O Lord my God, I will glorify you; I will sing hymns to your name, for you have done wonderful things, an ancient and true counsel. So be it, O Lord” (Isaiah 25:1).

In the book just completed, the prophet spoke at length, and through hidden meanings, about the devil’s perversity, the punishment and judgment that will come upon him, and also the overthrow of the wicked and hostile powers. To these he added the proclamation of Christ’s kingdom. For he said that the Lord will reign in Zion and in Jerusalem, and will be glorified before the elders (Isaiah 24:23). For all these reasons, then, the prophet is filled with great joy and honors with praises the one who accomplished things so marvelous. That is why he says: “O Lord my God, I will glorify you and sing hymns to your name, an ancient and true counsel, and you have done marvelous things.”

Since he says “you have done” about things that had not yet happened at that time, he indicates by adding “So be it, O Lord” that, though it has not yet happened, it will surely happen in every way. For with the eyes of the mind they gazed on the time of his coming as though it were present, yet they were by no means unaware that it was not yet present. He calls the mystery of the Only-Begotten’s becoming man an ancient counsel, and calls what it has accomplished for those throughout all the earth marvelous things.

For we have been saved in Christ, who was foreknown before the foundation of the world but made manifest in the last times of the age (compare 1 Peter 1:20). As the most wise Paul says, the mystery of Christ is not new or lately come to light; it was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but has been made manifest in its own times (compare Titus 1:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'ancient and true counsel' and the 'marvelous things' are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wonders are Christ's: he freed souls from the devil and set up God's ancient purpose, and this fits the preaching to all nations, not the return from Babylon.
comments.comment: The prophet Isaiah says that the cause of these wonders is: 'Lord my God, I will glorify you, I will sing praise to your name, for you have done wonderful things, a true ancient purpose' (Isa 25:1). For Christ the Savior has done wonderful things, having freed every soul suffering under the devil, establishing the ancient purpose of God, according to which man existed as being straight, having come to be in the image and likeness of the Creator. And if you wish the things being proclaimed to the people to be wonderful, immense powers, such as Jesus raising the dead and restoring the blind to sight, and if anything else of this kind is written, you do not err. And it is also possible to do so: manifest through theology the most unclouded knowledge concerning God, so that the nations might have right discourse concerning God, being freed from much-godly fear. These things will in no way suit those returning from Babylon in the times of Cyrus or in the times of Darius, who perceptibly built the temple while Zerubbabel and Joshua the priest were presiding over the building in Judah after the captivity. For these things are fulfilled through works after the presence of our Savior, with all his disciples wandering through the whole earth and evangelizing, having announced his salvation to all.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's counsel includes that strong cities, which are the wicked and hostile powers, be shaken down and never built again.
comments.comment:
“For you have made cities a heap, strong cities, so that their foundations might fall; the city of the ungodly will never be built, forever” (Isaiah 25:2). This too belongs to the true counsel and the blameless purposes of God, who is able to do all things: that strong cities should be shaken down and become a heap, be as it were heaved up from their foundations, and be past hope, so that they will never be able to recover. For it will never, he says, be built, forever.

But we say that the cities shaken down are not, surely, in every case the cities of sense, that is, the people in them; rather we think it is each of the wicked and hostile powers…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Satan is called a strong city, which Emmanuel shook from its foundations, so that it has no hope of rising again.
comments.comment: …that Satan has been called a city, and a strong one at that. For it is the custom of the God-inspired Scripture at times to liken the very mightiest to towers and walls, or even to cities. So, as we said earlier, even the blessed prophet Jeremiah was set by God as a fortified city and as a strong bronze wall (Jeremiah 1:18). But when Emmanuel was revealed and shone upon the world, the unholy throng of the opposing powers was destroyed, and Satan was shaken from his very foundations. He has fallen so as to sink into endless weakness, and he has no hope of ever rising again or lifting up his head.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The nations, strangers to God's gifts, were taken from the devil's grasp by Christ and enriched, and so they send up songs of thanksgiving.
comments.comment:
“Therefore the poor people will bless you, and cities of men who are wronged will bless you. For you have become a helper to every lowly city, and a shelter to those who lost heart through want; you will rescue them from wicked men. A shelter for the thirsty, and the breath of men who are wronged. They will bless you as faint-hearted men who thirst in Zion, from ungodly men to whom you handed us over” (Isaiah 25:3–5).

Israel was called to the knowledge of God through the tutoring of the Law, and was made rich in the things that come from God; for it was saved, and inherited the land of the promise. But the countless multitude of the other nations, I mean those throughout the whole earth under heaven, had been utter strangers to the spiritual goods from above. They had no taste of the gifts that come from God. They were, in a way, naked and unclothed, having neither the divine shelter nor the covering from on high, neither the wealth of mind that comes from virtue nor anything else of all that is full of praise and counted worthy of every wonder. But when Christ himself appeared, he took them out of the devil’s grasping and brought them to God the Father. They have been made rich with the light of the truth, with a share in the glory that comes from him, and with the greatness of the gospel way of life; and for these things they send up songs of thanksgiving to God the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the poor and wronged are and why they bless God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Master has carried out the ancient counsel and been helper and shelter to the poor and to those in Zion who thirsted for the Savior's coming.
comments.comment: So then, he says, O Master, since you have carried out an ancient and true counsel (Isaiah 25:1), summing up all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10), enlightening those in darkness and casting down the world-rulers of this age (Ephesians 6:12), strong as cities though they were, the poor people will bless you, and whole cities will glorify you. For you have become a helper to every one of them, and a shelter to those unbearably grieved by their poverty in the goods of their fathers; and you rescued them from wicked men. For in Zion too there were some who had lost heart in this way, just like men who are thirsty. And perhaps by these words the prophet shows us this: there were, yes, there were in Israel too those who thirsted for the Savior’s coming…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The peace the prophet asks for is Christ himself, or friendship with God, which only God gives and which removes sin so that we are joined to him.
comments.comment:
It is the custom of the holy prophets to make supplications on behalf of Israel. For they were lovers of God and richly crowned with the glories of piety. And since they had sprung from the root of Abraham and from the blood of the holy fathers, they are of necessity downcast when they see those of Israel, as their own kin, perishing because of their impiety toward Christ. For this reason the blessed prophet Isaiah now comes forward and says: “Lord our God, give us peace; for you have rendered all things to us” (Isaiah 26:12). For if you grant us peace, he says, we shall be full of every good thing, and we shall have received in full the most perfect share in your gifts.

We must consider what kind of peace they ask for. Either they ask for Christ himself, for he is our peace, according to the Scriptures (Ephesians 2:14), and through him we have been joined to the Father, by kinship, that is, spiritual kinship. Or at least they mean this: those who have not yet believed, and whose stain of sin has not been cast off, stand apart from God and are rightly reckoned in the rank of enemies; they hold their necks high and fight against the laws of the Master. But those who are obedient and easily led, and ready for anything at all that those laws approve, are very dear to him and have peace with him. Yet this thing is truly given by God and comes through the generosity from above. Grant us, then, O Master, to be at peace with you, and, once profane and loathsome sin has been taken out of the way, to be united to you spiritually through Christ the Mediator.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the peace of verse 12 is and why it must come from God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those at peace with God belong to him alone and must name no other god, because he alone is God over us by nature and in truth.
comments.comment: Such is the word rightly spoken through the voice of Paul: “Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). When this has come about, we shall be God’s possession and his inheritance. That is why it is wisely added: “Lord, take possession of us; apart from you we know no other; we name your name” (Isaiah 26:13). For those who are at peace with him must be single-minded and yoked to God alone, so as to know him only and not even to carry on their tongue the name of any other, falsely named god at all.
