For we must name him alone, because he alone is God over us by nature and in truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains verse 13's claim that we know and name no other lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah foretold the resurrection of the dead, and the dew he mentions is God's life-giving working that gives being and well-being.
comments.comment: The prophet Isaiah cried out long beforehand the mystery of the resurrection from the dead, that it will take place in due time, as God grants it and by his unspeakable power refashions into life what death held fast. He said, “The dead shall rise, and those in the tombs shall be raised, and those in the earth shall rejoice; for the dew that comes from you is healing to them” (Isaiah 26:19). By dew, I think, he means figuratively the life-giving working of God, by which he gives being to things that are not, and grants well-being to things already brought into existence. For all things hold together in him (Colossians 1:17), just as they were also brought into being through him (compare John 1:3).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the dead rising and the dew mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The "little while" of hiding is little by God's measure, which may be a whole age to us.
comments.comment:
If you see what is grim after the consummation of the world—what follows as almost the whole race of human beings are punished for what was sinned—you will see that what surrounds then grew dark, and no longer can anyone glorify God, if indeed the word of God also commanded the righteous saying: 'Go, my people, enter into your storeroom, shut your door, hide yourself a little while, until my wrath of anger passes.' (Isaiah 26:20) … But that 'little' is little to God; it is not little to a human being. For one must see that for each there is something little and great. And from an example I will show that for each there is something little or great.

For each living thing food of such-and-such amount is little by comparison with its constitution, and much food of such-and-such amount again by comparison with its makeup. And so what is little for a human being is great for another living thing. What is little, say, for a man is much for a child. So the whole time of human life is a little time, and that of one long-lived, as toward the whole of the present age. So also what is little to God is much toward us, and a whole age is God's little.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'a little while' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jacob's lawlessness is taken away because God's gentleness overcomes human pettiness: he forgives rather than repaying every offense, and so keeps Abraham's blessing.
comments.comment:
Having set in between his reproof of those who had acted impiously toward the holy prophets, the blessed prophet again holds to the sequence of his thoughts, and says, as from the person of God: “Therefore the lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away” (Isaiah 27:9). “Therefore”: for what reason? Because he will not be slain as he himself slew, nor struck as he himself struck (Isaiah 27:7). For the gentleness that is in God always overcomes human pettiness; he does not in every way and in every case bring penalties equal to the offenses committed on earth, but rather tempers his wrath with mildness.

This is why he says: “The lawlessness of Jacob will be taken away”; that is, he will receive loving-kindness, and God will in due time remit his charges and free him even from the accusations themselves. “And this is his blessing.” For God promised Abraham, saying: “Surely I will bless you, and I will greatly multiply your seed” (Genesis 22:17). But the godlike Abraham would not truly have been blessed, nor would his seed have been multiplied, if those of his blood had been required to pay penalties in proportion to their sins. But since they too, though they had done nothing good, and had rather been carried down into the utmost impiety, were enriched with forgiveness, the ground of the blessing has been kept and has passed on to them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jacob's lawlessness is taken away and what the blessing is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's offenses will be remitted when the nations turn from idols and burn their temples, as Paul too declares.
comments.comment:
He also makes plain the time at which Jacob too will be free of his offenses. For when, he says, those called through faith to the knowledge of him who is truly God take the field against the ancient error; when altars and sacred precincts and the swarm of idols are taken out of the way; when they consume with fire the temples built with toil for lifeless idols; when they cut down their trees, and besides these the things made with hands, like a forest: then, then indeed God will remit their stumblings to those of Israel as well. And this, I think, is what the godlike Paul declared: “But when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26).

For to burn the temples down completely, to shear off the groves planted beside them, and to add as well the overthrow of the statues themselves, would signify nothing else, surely, than this: that those who long wandered in error and worshipped the works of their own hands will be changed and come to the knowledge of the truth …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophets had foretold both punishments (evils) and promised honors (message) to Israel, yet Israel gained nothing from them.
comments.comment: In explaining the force of what was said before, we say that the person of the holy prophets was brought in, rebuking in a way those of the blood of Israel, because they had met the prophets’ words to no purpose and had gained no benefit at all, even though both evils and a message had been foretold to them. By “evils” we firmly hold that the punishments prepared for those used to sinning are meant, and by “message” the honors that rest on good hopes. So, since those of the blood of Israel had gained nothing whatever, even though the prophets had announced to them the things that come from God, I mean threats and promises of the good things to come, he says: “To whom have we announced evils? And to whom have we announced a message?”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God calls those weaned from the Law's milk to take the gospel as mature people and to endure affliction a little while so that they may be rich in hope.
comments.comment: But now that the holy prophets have, as it were, fallen silent and brought their own speech to a stop at this point, the God of all himself calls out to the saints, saying: “Those weaned from milk, those drawn away from the breast: expect affliction upon affliction, hope upon hope.” For the undisciplined, he says, who are badly sick with unruliness, have rightly been thrust out; they have no share in the salvation that is in Christ, and they will go on to destruction. But you, from now on, who through faith have been called to the knowledge of the truth; who have been drawn away from the tutoring of the Law as from a breast and from milk; who once received food fit for infants and had a less instructed mind, but have now advanced “to a mature man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13), and have moved on to the food that suits the mature, and have not remained “unskilled in the word of righteousness” (Hebrews 5:13–14): direct your hearts to receive the new proclamation of the gospel way of life, of the decrees given through Christ. Take courage to endure. Even if affliction comes upon you, again and again, one blow after another, as trials rise up and the cruelty of your persecutors grows against you, hold out a little while, and for a little while expect afflictions, so that you may also be rich in hope, I mean the hope that is beyond human understanding.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'weaned from milk' are and what is asked of them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those weaned from milk are mature believers for whom affliction upon affliction is foretold, and whoever expects it like a noble athlete will enjoy hope upon hope after a little.
comments.comment: And you, then — after Isaiah — as no longer carnal nor babes 'in Christ,' advanced 'in' your intelligible 'stature,' most godly Ambrose and most pious Protoctetus, no longer 'having need of milk' but of 'solid food' — hear, as 'weaned from milk' and 'drawn from the breast,' in what way, as for weaned athletes, no simple affliction but an 'affliction upon affliction' is prophesied. He who does not push away the affliction 'upon affliction,' but as a noble athlete 'expects' it, straightway expects 'hope upon hope' too — which, after a little of the affliction 'upon affliction,' he shall enjoy. For such is the 'yet a little, yet a little.' …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The "other tongue" was fulfilled at Pentecost, when the apostles spoke in other tongues and Israel, instead of believing the sign, mocked them as drunk.
comments.comment: This, I think, is the “through contempt of lips, through another tongue.” For they spoke in other tongues, and the God who can do all things had foretold this too: “In other tongues,” he says, “and with the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they believe” (1 Corinthians 14:21). They ought to have accepted the sign as full proof, bearing in mind the prediction God had made about it. This they did not do; instead they mocked the apostles as drunk and remained in disobedience.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the verse's 'another tongue' was fulfilled in Acts.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel, having refused the bread of life, has been given a spiritual famine, a lack of the word that God gives.
comments.comment:
God once said, angered at the madness of the Jews: “Behold, I am bringing a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord. And from the east to the west they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it” (Amos 8:11-12).

So a spiritual famine has been brought upon those of Israel. Since they did not receive through faith the bread of life that came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33), they have quite fittingly come to lack the food that God gives: “For man shall not live by bread alone,” it says, “but by every word that comes out of the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The vain comfort of their covenant with Hades and death will bring them no shelter, for the rushing storm will trample them down.
comments.comment:
Having promised them amnesty for their drunken outrages, and having said very plainly that He will not be too harsh with them, He bids them lay hold of good counsel. But He rebukes them because they thought a vain comfort to be something great and lofty, and so were carried beyond what is reasonable. And what was this comfort which they held to be great, though it brought no profit? Surely that one. For they said: “We have made a covenant with Hades and agreements with death; if a rushing storm passes through, it will not come upon us; we have made a lie our hope, and by the lie we shall be sheltered” (Isaiah 28:15).

But those who pondered these things and held an empty hope, supposing that they would die before the calamities came, heard plainly: … “If a rushing storm comes upon you, you will be trampled down by it. Whenever it passes by, it will take you” (Isaiah 28:18-19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the unshakable foundation laid in Zion, holding up those built on him, as God the Father spoke through the prophet.
comments.comment: Since he called believers the house of God, he fittingly names Christ the foundation. There had been many teachers among the Corinthians, but Paul boasts that he was the first of them all, a kind of firstfruits among those who preached to them the mystery of Christ. Christ is the unshakable foundation. He holds up those who are built upon him and shows them to be temples, fitted together with one another through faith (Ephesians 2:21) and brought together into one mind by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Of this foundation God the Father spoke through the prophet: “Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a costly stone, a precious cornerstone, in her foundations; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 28:16).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Ariel's siege under David is a type of what Jerusalem later did against Christ, since the blind and lame who opposed David foreshadow those who opposed the Savior.
comments.comment:
He takes up something that happened in history in the time of the reign of blessed David, and he does this as if to bring to light what the synagogue of the Jews dared to do against Christ. For the things that befell the people of old as in shadows are types of the true things.

Now the present Jerusalem was once called Jebus. Blessed David besieged it, and for what cause we shall learn from the holy Scriptures themselves. For it runs thus in the Second Book of Samuel: “And David and all his men went to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite who inhabited the land; and it was said to David, David shall not come in here; for the blind and the lame rose up, saying, He shall not come in here. And David took the stronghold of Zion; this is the city of David. And David said on that day: Let everyone who strikes a Jebusite attack with the dagger the blind and the lame, who fight against the life of David” (2 Samuel 5:6-8).

So the blind and the lame from Jerusalem, or Jebus, opposed blessed David, and for doing this they perished miserably; for he took the city. And at the time of His coming, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, lame and blind, opposed Christ, the Savior of all; for they did not know how to walk uprightly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel planned bitter things not through God, as its council against Christ and the parable of the tenants who killed the servants and then the son show, adding sin upon sin.
comments.comment:
Again he laments over those from Israel as lovers of sin who have become apostates, exceedingly wicked and planning bitter things, not through God (Isaiah 30:1).

… He therefore accuses chosen Israel of bringing in, concerning Christ, a mind out of tune with God. For they deliberated, sitting in council, and indeed said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away both your city and your country.” And another, one of those set among the leaders, says: “You know nothing at all; it is better that one man should die, and not that the whole nation should perish” (John 11:47-50).

The Lord teaches this very thing more clearly in the parables of the Gospel: “The master of the house who planted the vineyard sent his own servants to receive the fruits, but the tenants killed them” (Matthew 21:33-35). And the charges of their impiety did not stop there; for when they saw the son, sent by the father after the servants, they said among themselves, it says: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him and have his inheritance for ourselves” (Matthew 21:38).

So the authors of such bitter and unholy schemes are apostates, who add sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to take counsel not through God and how Israel did so.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel ran to Egypt for help when Assyria threatened, when they should have appeased God by turning to better ways.
comments.comment:
And he tries to show that their mind had long been turned toward apostasy from God, saying: “Those who set out to go down into Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and to be sheltered by the Egyptians” (Isaiah 30:2). He threw in the words “but they did not ask Me” in between.

The train of thought runs like this: Woe, he says, to those who go down into Egypt to be helped by Pharaoh and to find shelter from the Egyptians. For when war and battle had been announced to them, and the king of Assyria had taken up arms against the land of the Jews, they ran ahead to the Egyptians and called for their help. Yet they ought to have appeased God and, by turning to better ways, to have wiped away the offences by which they had struck against Him. For had they been rich in His favor, they would not have fallen under the feet of those making war …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The broken potter's vessel in Isaiah has become so useless that nothing, neither water nor fire, can be taken from it.
comments.comment: Furthermore, the prophet, after seeing in the "house of the potter" the shaping of the "vessel", takes a "small shard" and "breaks" it. And he says: "thus I will destroy the pride of Jacob". Therefore they were rejected, therefore "they are cast out". And he says concerning this in Isaiah, of this "broken shard vessel", that thus "it was broken" (Isaiah 30:14) so that "not to be found" is a part of it "in which" anyone is able to take a little "water" or "fire", that is to say, having become completely useless, not even the "water"—the little bit or that still capable of quenching—can be received, nor the "fire" that brings to the "shard" itself hardness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophecy, framed as about the Assyrians and the return from captivity, is directed in its true meaning against Satan, whose tyranny ends when Christ shines on the human race.
comments.comment:
Having said very well that the light of the sun will be sevenfold for those who believe in Christ, at that time when He heals the bruise of His people (Isaiah 30:26), he usefully adds that the divine wrath will also be against Satan, who did the bruising, and against the demons with him. For their tyranny over us was not going to last without end, nor their strength to remain unshaken, above all once Christ, the Savior of all, had shone upon the human race.

The word of the prophecy is not bare and unclothed, as it were, but rather shadowed and deep. For it is framed as though about the Assyrians, who sacked Jerusalem and took all Judea, and, holding beloved Israel captive by the spear, went back to their own land, all but dancing in mockery over the divine glory and supposing that they had overpowered His worshippers even though God did not will it. Indeed Rabshakeh called out to those on the wall, saying: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, saying that God will deliver Israel out of my hand. Have the gods of the nations each delivered his own land out of my hand?” (Isaiah 36:14-18).

So those of whom the word speaks, having boasted greatly and babbled much against the ineffable glory, would be brought to judgment. And when Israel had spent seventy years in captivity and in slavery among them, the God of all rescued and saved him again. For He brought them back to Judea, under the leadership at that time of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who was of the tribe of Judah, and of Joshua the high priest as well.

So the force of the prophecy seems, as far as what lies on the surface, to recall what befell the Chaldeans and Babylon. But the true meanings of what is said are directed against the spiritual Assyrian, that is, Satan …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The name of the Lord comes after a long time: historically when God pitied Israel after seventy years and Cyrus fell on Babylon like fire, and inwardly when the Word appeared after the long tyranny of the inventor of sin.
comments.comment:
So the name of the Lord, he says, will come after a long time (Isaiah 30:27). If someone chooses to understand this historically, God took pity on Israel after seventy years. But if he follows the inner and hidden path of the meanings, he will grasp that the inventor of sin went on for a very long time laying the yoke of his own perversity on all who are on the earth, so as to make them his own worshippers and to bind them fast in the snares of sin. But after a long time the only-begotten Word of God appeared to us, and then came “wrath burning with glory,” and “the oracle of His lips, an oracle full of wrath” (Isaiah 30:27).

For Cyrus son of Cambyses, with God urging him on and rousing him to battle, marched against the land of the Chaldeans and took the land of the Babylonians by force. He became to them like wrath and fire, for he all but devoured them all; and since his assault could not be withstood, he appeared to those there like water rushing in a ravine, and filled all the nations of the Chaldeans with uproar and confusion, for they were justly condemned for vain error.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is said to be wise in bringing evils because, unlike the wicked, he looks to the end of the evils he brings, and his word is not set aside.
comments.comment: But it appears most clearly from Isaiah, the prophet saying thus concerning God: 'And he himself was wise to bring evils upon them' (Isaiah 31:2). Even for a wise man it is not easy to bring the kinds of evils that are the 40 evils, how much less for God. Indeed, even the wicked, when they pretend virtue, do not say: 'we are bringing evil to someone.' But it is said concerning God that as a wise one he brings evils. He speaks of things that are harmful. And he views the end of the bringing of evils: 'and his word shall by no means be set aside.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the Spirit comes from on high upon those who believe, Carmel, that is Jerusalem and its crowded country, will become a wilderness and be counted as wild woodland fit for burning.
comments.comment:
He makes clear also the time at which the disobedient race from Israel will be empty of spiritual fruitfulness. For he turns the discourse, I mean, toward those who have honored our Lord Jesus Christ by their ready obedience, who have been cleansed through faith in Him and have come to share in the Holy Spirit. … So when, he says, the Spirit of God from above and from on high comes upon you who believe, then Chermel too will be a wilderness. Chermel, or Carmel, is a very large mountain in Judea, thickly covered with dense woodland. So he likens to Chermel both Jerusalem itself and all the country around it, since it too had a countless multitude of inhabitants.

But it will be, he says, a wilderness, and will be counted as a forest. By forest he means wild woodland, which is of use for burning.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jews' leaders gave no counsel that would have kept the people from being despised, and the people, lacking understanding, did not test their leaders' words.
comments.comment: So they did not give counsel to the people, he says, nor did the people know Him whose speech is deep. Nor did they give the counsel that would have kept the people from being called a despised people. For if they had given counsel, the people would not have been called despised; they would rather have been called blessed, as those who had recognized the Redeemer. But there was, he says, no understanding in the one who heard (Isaiah 33:19). For the Jews, being without understanding, did not test the voices of their leaders, nor discern whether they were giving good counsel or doing the opposite.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zion, the Church on earth and the city above, is an unshaken tent because the name of Christ is great to those who believe.
comments.comment:
Between these come the words which God addressed to the senseless scribes of the Jews and to those who gave unholy counsel. Now the voice of the lovers of truth is brought in again, of those who have recognized the appearing of Christ and who say “Behold Zion,” meaning either the Church on earth or the fair city above in the heavens, the nurse of the saints. So whether one names the Church on earth or has that other city in mind, the thing shown by both will be one. For those who have been in the Church below will in due time be also in that city above, in the heavens.

Since, then, they all but leap for great joy at having recognized Zion, in which is our salvation, that is, Christ, and point it out to one another, at once the divine word takes up their words and says: “Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich city.” He speaks as if by likeness to the ancient tent in the wilderness. He calls Zion rich and says that the tent will be unshaken; for he declares that it has cords that cannot be broken and pegs fixed for ever. For the Church has been firmly set, and its continuance in well-being cannot be moved: “for the gates of Hades,” he says, “will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

And He gives the reason why it will be such, saying to those who have believed in Christ: “because the name of the Lord is great to you.” For to those who have not accepted the faith the name of Christ is not great and glorified; but with us who have believed it is great and exalted. For we worship Him as God, as truly the Son of the Father, as the Word made man for the salvation of all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Zion and the unshaken tent are and why the name is great.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sword stands for punishment, which becomes drunken among the angels who have fallen.
comments.comment: For God himself says in Isaiah from his own person: 'My sword is drunken in heaven' (Isaiah 34:5). And the sword signifies punishment, as it is said: 'My sword shall eat blood of wounds, and my arrows shall be drunken with blood' (Deuteronomy 32:42). Thus, among the angels who have fallen, he says the sword becomes drunken, bringing punishment called heavens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blind, deaf and lame of the prophecy are healed again in the soul as people come to the Word, and the healed lame leap like a deer, which tramples serpents.
comments.comment: … For my part I would say that, in keeping with Jesus’ promise, the disciples have done even “greater” works (John 14:12) than the visible works that Jesus did. For the eyes of those blind in soul are always being opened, and the ears of those who had been deaf to words of virtue hear eagerly about God and the blessed life with him. Many, too, who were lame in the feet of what Scripture calls the “inner” man (Romans 7:22; Ephesians 3:16), now that the Word has healed them, do not merely leap but leap “like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6), an animal that is the enemy of snakes and stronger than all the venom of vipers. And these lame who have been healed receive from Jesus “authority to tread,” with the very feet in which they were formerly lame, “upon” the “serpents and scorpions” of wickedness, and in a word “over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19); and as they tread they are not harmed, for they too have become stronger than the venom of all wickedness and of the demons.
comments.selected_reason: Shows plainly how the healing of the blind, deaf and lame in this verse is understood as healing of the soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sennacherib came against Jerusalem because Hezekiah, unlike his father Ahaz, refused to pay tribute to Assyria, and Rabshakeh was sent to win the people with threats and promises.
comments.comment:
The account is plain to all who love to learn history; yet I will tell it, as briefly as I can. While Ahaz was reigning in Jerusalem, Pekah son of Remaliah and Rezin king of Syria were besieging Judea and planning to lay their hands on Jerusalem itself. Ahaz, too weak to resist, sent an embassy and called to his aid Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, and with many gifts persuaded him to help him and to check the greed of the kings who had banded together against him, I mean the king of Samaria and the king of Syria (2 Kings 16:5-9).

When this was done, those who were making war on him perished. For the Assyrian took Damascus and Syria; and Ahaz came under his hand, and from then on under tribute and taxes. He was one of the very worst. He was an idolater and hateful to God, and perhaps surpassed all the others in his perversity toward God.

When Ahaz ended his human life, Hezekiah reigned in his place. He was his son, but a man dear to God, who had won the glories of the highest righteousness and piety. He, it says, “rebelled against the king of the Assyrians” (2 Kings 18:7); for he would not let his kingdom be brought under tribute, as Ahaz of course had done.

For this reason Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, as though he had the right to hold all Judea, and its very kingdom, under tribute, was inflamed with anger. He laid waste Samaria and sent his army against the cities of Judea, and when he had taken many of them, he then sent Rabshakeh against Jerusalem itself, not to take up arms for the time being by the law of war, but rather to lure the common people with threats and with promises of gentle treatment.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the history behind the invasion in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rabshakeh mocks Hezekiah's trust, calling Egypt a staff of reed that breaks and wounds whoever leans on it.
comments.comment:
The gates, clearly, had been shut, and the people, no doubt the most warlike of them, stood on the walls; and to carry out the business of the embassy, the king's chosen men and the foremost among the priests went out to Rabshakeh. But he, a man of Persian savagery, with “a mouth speaking great things,” as it is written (Daniel 7:8), grew insolent against the glory of God. He calls Hezekiah by his bare name, without adding “king” or any other of the titles that best befit men in such high stations. But the king of the Assyrians he does not simply call by that title; he calls him great as well.

And he says: “Is a battle line drawn up by counsel, or by words of the lips?” For the Jews, who had the Law given through Moses, were thought wiser than the other nations; indeed, they used to say, “Blessed are we, Israel, because what is pleasing to the Lord is known to us” (Baruch 4:4). So Rabshakeh brings their boast in this to nothing, saying that when war and battle are upon them, all this will be wholly useless to help them: their knowledge of the laws, their shrewdness in counsels alone, and even their practised skill, as it were, in words.

And since some of those who had reigned over Judea had called on the hand of the Egyptians for help, though in doing so they acted most wrongly, the Assyrian supposed that now too Hezekiah was trusting not in God but in others, or rather in those who held the land of the Egyptians. That is why he calls it a staff of reed. For the hope placed in them, he says, is rotten and always easily broken, and it harms those who rely on it rather than being able to help them, just like a staff of reed: if anyone leans his weight on it, he will surely break it, and it will hurt the man who trusted in it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Rabshakeh's taunts mean and why Egypt is called a reed.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Rabshakeh speaks insolently against God by telling Hezekiah to fight his lord, and offers him two thousand horses.
comments.comment: He runs loose at the mouth again, lifts his horn on high, and speaks injustice against God (Psalm 75:5). For if indeed, he says, you have put your trust in Him, engage my lord, that is, arm yourselves and stand ready for battle. And I will add two thousand horses for you, and this will be enough …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God had decreed the Assyrian conquests long before and withdrew the hand that defended the cities, using Assyria as an axe or saw that does nothing without the hand that moves it.
comments.comment:
But you, who lift your brows in vain over nothing, “have you not heard long ago these things which I have done?” (Isaiah 37:26). For if only you were willing, He says, to look closely into the words of My prophets, I said beforehand that these things would come to pass. For “I arranged them from ancient days” (Isaiah 37:26), that is, I decreed them and gave My assent; and now, when the time called for it, I have brought what was foretold to its end, so as “to lay waste nations in strong cities” (Isaiah 37:26), that is, cities that were not weak or easily taken.

“I let go My hands, and they were dried up” (Isaiah 37:27). For I, who long held them together through My forbearance so that they might exist and stand, withdrew the hand that defended them; and they withered like grass, faded like hay, and, like dry couch grass, were given as food to the fire.

This is what He says to him in another place too. For when the ungodly man had carried out what God had decreed should happen and thought great things of himself, he heard God saying again: “Shall the axe be glorified without the one who cuts with it? Or shall the saw be exalted without the one who draws it?” (Isaiah 10:15). For just as such tools do not, of course, move themselves to their work, but rather wait for the hand that moves them, so you too, He says, have become an instrument of the divine wrath. You did not do these things by your own powers; rather, you were like an axe and a saw, appointed to serve the will of the one who moves you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that God foretold and permitted the conquests, and that Assyria was only His instrument.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God knows all the Assyrian's doings and will punish his raging blasphemy, putting a muzzle in his nose like a beast.
comments.comment:
So you boast, He says, though you were only the servant of the divine judgments, and perhaps you think that by yourself and alone you prevailed over so many nations and lands, so as to burn them and take them. But I know your rest, your going out and your coming in. By rest, as I think, He means death; and by going out and coming in, the path into anything whatever that is to be done. For nothing at all escapes the Mind that knows all things.

And when He adds, “Your wrath with which you raged, and your bitterness, has come up to Me,” He all but says: You will not have blasphemed without punishment. For I will by no means overlook the malice and bitterness of your unholy thoughts; but, as one provoked to grief, I will lay on your rages the penalty that befits them.

… Since the Assyrian, in a senselessness most like a beast's, mocked God, and, as though he had bolted into unbridled wildness, let loose words of blasphemy against the glory of God, for this reason He says, and very fittingly, as of a beast: “I will put a muzzle in your nose and a bridle in your lips,” all but saying that by the blows He would bring upon him …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the muzzle and bridle are said of the Assyrian.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Merodach's envoys came to Hezekiah because he marvelled at the angel's destruction of the besiegers of Jerusalem in one night.
comments.comment: … And we say that Merodach [king of Babylon] marvelled in another way too, at what had happened, beyond all expectation, to those who besieged Jerusalem with Rabshakeh: the hand of an angel fell upon them and destroyed them in one night, so that in the morning all the bodies were found dead (Isaiah 37:36). So the envoys came, Merodach having marvelled at Hezekiah's righteousness because of these very signs from God, which pass all telling.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hezekiah should have told the Babylonian envoys of the help and wonders God had given him, but in boastfulness he showed them only his wealth.
comments.comment:
Hezekiah ought to have given those who had come from Babylon a splendid account of the help that God, who can do all things, had given at each time of need, and of the greatness of His wonders, so that, marvelling even more at the divine pre-eminence and at the invincible authority of the Master of all through the words in which he had instructed them, they might return to their own land enriched with the knowledge of God. For in this way they could also have helped others by proclaiming what they had learned.

This he did not do. Instead he was carried away into human boastfulness. He did not order his own glory by the things for which God had honoured him, but by the wealth of his kingdom, and he made these the limit of all the glory he possessed. For he showed them, it says, the house of Nechotha (Nechotha means “of the spices”), and of the oil of myrrh, and of the perfume, and of the silver and of the gold, and all the houses of the vessels of his gaza, that is, of his wealth (Isaiah 39:2). For gaza is said to be a Persian word, and it means riches or wealth.
comments.selected_reason: Says why Hezekiah's showing of his treasures was a fault.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah asks what the men said as though he came on his own, a question framed with great art.
comments.comment: The prophet had been sent by God; yet at first, when he met Hezekiah, he made as if he were speaking on his own account, as though he had come of his own accord. That is why he says, “What do these men say?” And his words are framed with great art.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In Christ the steep and rough places of the way to the Father become smooth and level for us.
comments.comment: … ‘Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and all the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough places smooth roads’ (Isaiah 40:4; Luke 3:5). For in Christ even the steep places are smooth for us, and rough ground can be walked; the hard roads lie clear and level.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the levelled mountains and smooth roads mean for believers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Grass and flower stand for the glories, honors and prosperities of this life, which seem abundant but depart and wither as if they had never existed.
comments.comment: … Isaiah says: 'All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the grass; the sun rises and withers the grass, and its flower falls' (Isa 40:6-8). These things represent the glories, honors, and all the prosperities existing in this life which seem to those living in the flesh to be abundant, yet they depart like a flower and grass, and wither as if they had never even existed (Psalm 103:15-16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of grass and flower for a general reader.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who speak the mystery of Christ must not have a low, fearful mind but one set high like a mountain, so they may see the beauty of the doctrines and speak boldly.
comments.comment: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who announce good news to Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who announce good news to Jerusalem; raise it, do not fear.” (Isaiah 40:9) For I say that those appointed to the sacred service, and who speak the mystery of Christ the Savior of us all, must not have a cast-down and ground-level mind, conquered by hesitation and contracted by fear, but must have the mind set high as if well planted and somehow lying on a mountain, eager thus to survey the excellent beauty of the doctrines of the truth, and also to make their words with boldness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what going up a high mountain and raising the voice mean for teachers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The prophet recalls the Only-begotten's coming in the flesh, gathering us like lambs under a good Shepherd, and confesses the divine Mind to be beyond our reach.
comments.comment: The prophetic word has recalled for us the dispensation of the Only-begotten in the flesh, and has marvelled fittingly at the ineffable wisdom through which we have been saved and, having come to know Him who is Master by nature and in truth, have been counted worthy of His grace: gathered like lambs by His arm (Isaiah 40:11), and placed under Him as under a Shepherd exceedingly good, for He laid down His life for His own sheep (John 10:11). It has also shown that the Mind is beyond our reach, whether to see or even perhaps to measure (Isaiah 40:13), and has confessed Him to be the highest Wisdom, beyond all things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Beside God's power and glory all the nations are small and worth nothing, and Lebanon would not suffice to burn for Him.
comments.comment:
He therefore shows the measureless pre-eminence of God, who rules all things, and the surpassing dignity of the majesty that is in Him, and that all things are small to Him and would be reckoned as equal to nothing when set beside, I mean, the exceeding greatness of His power and glory. That is why he says: “All the nations are counted as a drop from a jar and as the tipping of a scale, and they will be counted as spittle.” These things are small and worth nothing at all. For what is one drop falling from a jar? And what would the tipping of a scale be, which brings the side that seems lighter up to an even balance? And what is spittle, that is, the spit of a man?

But Lebanon, he says, would not be enough for Him for burning, nor all the four-footed beasts for a whole burnt offering …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the images of the drop, the scale and Lebanon are meant to show.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If all the nations count for nothing, nothing can be likened to God in nature, weight or glory, not even an image made by craftsmen.
comments.comment: And if all the nations, he says, are as nothing and have been counted as nothing, “with what likeness have you likened Him?” (Isaiah 40:17-18). For what will be like Him and of equal weight with Him, whether in nature, or in weight, or even in the measure of glory? Is it by the arts of a carpenter and the skill of a woodworker? Is it by goldsmiths? Or has He been shaped, as in an image, to resemble any creature at all? That is, he says, has a statue in the form of a man been made? Not at all. For nothing could be equal to Him. Since He is God by nature, and there is no other beside Him, He will surely be above all things in every way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why nothing can be likened to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet mocks idols: the carpenter must choose wood that will not rot and set the image so it will not fall, so the gods depend on his skill.
comments.comment: Having shown, then, that He is beyond everything that has been made and called into being, he next laughs to scorn the making of idols, and says: “The carpenter chooses wood that does not rot, and wisely seeks how he will set up his image so that it may not totter” (Isaiah 40:20). So it would be the work of the carpenter's skill, by the measure of the intelligence he has, to construct a god for those in error as they see fit, and to secure it with the greatest care so that it may not totter and fall and be shattered. So the worshippers of idols would be short of gods if there were no carpenter's skill on earth! Nor would the handmade things, once made, have been kept safe, unless the craftsman had wisely sought the means by which they could stand and keep an unshaken seat.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mockery of idol-making in this verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By asking whether they have not known or heard, the prophet shows that idol-worshippers are without excuse, since the one true God was proclaimed from of old through the patriarchs, the Law and the Prophets.
comments.comment:
Having laughed to scorn, then, the fashioning of idols, he turns his discourse to shame and correct those who have gone astray, and shows that their offence in this is without excuse, saying: “Will you not know? Will you not hear?” (Isaiah 40:21), instead of “Did you not know? Did you not hear?” “Has it not been told to you from the beginning? Have you not known the foundations of the earth?” By the foundations of the earth he means its farthest parts and its ends. So you have known, he says, you who live from one end of it to the other. You have heard, and it has been told to you from the beginning.

And what has been told? That God, who is God by nature and in truth, is one and alone; but the things men craft into gods for us are wood and stones and nothing else. For the God-inspired Scripture has not kept silent; rather, the knowledge of the truth has been proclaimed from of old, through patriarchs, through the Law and the Prophets. For it was not when the only-begotten Word of God, having become like us, shone forth as man on those upon the earth, that they first fell under the gravest charge of going astray. No, as I said, the charge of idolatry was ancient.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the questions of the verse mean and why they are put.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The holy teachers will all say the same thing and proclaim the Gospel in harmony, and this proclamation is the true judgment set against the Law given through Moses.
comments.comment:
All will say the same thing to those being taught the mysteries. For since they speak from one Spirit, they will not fight against each other's words; rather, they will make their proclamation about the divine doctrines in harmony, and will announce, in a hidden way, the mystery of Christ. For this, I think, is the meaning of “Then let them declare judgment” (Isaiah 41:1). For since those of Israel called the Law given through Moses “judgment,” he very fittingly sets against it the saving proclamation of the Gospel, and by these words calls that “judgment.”

For true righteous judgment, and the force of a lawgiving that pleases God, does not shine out in the shadow of the Law, but rather in the proclamation of the holy teachers of the mysteries, the new rulers. They learned the judgment, that is, the will of God the Father, from Christ, and they have announced it to us as well, all saying the same thing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'declare judgment' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Righteousness raised from the east is Christ, the sun of righteousness, who followed the Father's footsteps and showed Him to us in His own works.
comments.comment:
God, who holds authority over all things, should not be marvelled at only for the bare greatness of His works in creation; for He also gives proof of the gentleness that is in Him through the benefits He confers. For He has saved those upon the earth, and has rescued the human race, which had wholly perished, from death and corruption, and from the greed of the devil. For He has brought the devil to nothing, together with the powers that are with him, and He has justified us through faith, driving away the sin that had tyrannised over us.

But all these things were accomplished through Christ; for “He has become for us, from God the Father, righteousness and redemption and sanctification” (1 Corinthians 1:30). And we have been enlightened through Him, and have shared in mercy and love, and, in a word, in everything that has power to save. And this He foretold to us through one of the holy prophets, saying: “And for you who fear My name the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2).

Who, then, he says, caused righteousness to rise like the sun from the east, that is, Christ? Who called it, that is, caused it to come, and to appear in such a way that it walked at the heels of the One who called it, which is as much as to say that it followed in the very footsteps of God the Father? For so the Lord lived on earth, fulfilling the works of the Father and showing Him to us in His own nature. For He was and is equal to Him in power, and through the deeds themselves He has fully assured those on earth that He is in every respect equal in measure to the One who begot Him. Indeed, He said plainly: “If I do not do the works of My Father, do not believe Me. But if I do them, even though you do not believe Me, believe My works” (John 10:37-38). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is raised from the east and what following at His heels means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'I am' show a single person speaking, since the pronoun and the verb together testify to the unity of the divinity.
comments.comment: If you wish to hear something else of the same prophecy confirming one God for us, he says, "I am God first, and I am the one who is to come" (Isaiah 41:4). For the "I" is indicative of a single person, for the two sayings signify one person to us. For having said "I," the "am" follows, so that through these two parts of the word, both the pronoun and the verb, the unity of the divinity is testified.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra

comments.capsule: God promises the calling of the nations and His own marvelled hand, and tells the idol-makers that their judgment, their shame and punishment, has come near, and their counsels have come to an end.
comments.comment:
He has declared very clearly how the calling of the nations will come about in its due time; He has promised to turn the desert into marshes and the thirsty land into watercourses, and to make it thick with cedars and box trees and other plants (Isaiah 41:18-19); and He has said that His own hand will be marvelled at as the Maker of such great things (Isaiah 41:20). Now He speaks again to the makers of idols and to the craftsmen of such things, and says that their judgment has come near. By judgment He means the punishment owed to them, that is, their shame and disgrace. For by the holy sentence of God and by a just judgment they would be punished, as men who have deceived the whole world under heaven and brought in counsels that are not true. For they taught those on earth to say to the wood, “You are my father,” and to the stone, “You begot me” (Jeremiah 2:27).

That is why He says that their counsels have drawn near, that is, have come to their end, since God is shaking down the error and scattering the mist of ignorance: not one of the gods they have, those falsely so called, we mean, but the Lord, God in truth, and the King of Jacob, that is, of those of the blood of Israel. By these words He brings to remembrance the signs that took place at the redemption of those of Israel, through which the power of the authority befitting God that is in Him, or of His incomparable pre-eminence, is very clearly recognised.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The trees set in the waterless land hint at the fragrance and the heights of virtue of those who blossom anew through faith in Christ.
comments.comment: … For God said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, hinting at the fragrance of those who through faith in Christ have blossomed anew into life (a spiritual fragrance, clearly), and at the heights they reach in virtue: ‘And I will make living water in the desert, and rivers in a waterless land’ (Isaiah 43:19–20), ‘and I will set in the waterless land the cedar and the box tree, the myrtle, the cypress and the white poplar.’ (Isaiah 41:19)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: To know all things, past, present and to come, is the mark of divine glory, and Christ who spoke through Moses of the beginning has told us the things at the end.
comments.comment:
It is the proper and singular mark of the divine and ineffable glory to know all things and to be wholly ignorant of nothing, whether of what has happened before, or of what is present, or of what will be. Indeed, through the all-wise Moses He makes plain to those on earth the things before the framing of this world and the things at the beginning, saying: “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth. And the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss” (Genesis 1:1-2); and He goes through the making of the whole world most exactly.

But our Lord Jesus Christ too, who spoke those things of old through Moses, has declared to us the things at the end; for, as His disciple says, “We look for new heavens and a new earth, and His promises” (2 Peter 3:13). And one may hear Him saying plainly: “Will anything be hidden from Me?” (Jeremiah 32:27); …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, who did not strive or cry out, broke no bruised reed and refused no one, showing the patience of God in his Son.
comments.comment: When he who is God becomes a teacher, teaching a human being to escape death—trained in patience, of course, for the sake of salvation and the pardon of offenses—he does not strive or cry out, nor does anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he does not break, and smoking flax he does not quench (Isaiah 42:2-3). For the prophet had not lied—indeed it was the testimony of God himself, placing his Spirit in his Son with all patience. He refused no one who wished to cling to him; he despised no one's table or roof. He did not spurn sinners or tax collectors; indeed, he himself ministered in washing the disciples' feet. He was not even angry at the city that had refused to receive him, though his disciples wanted heavenly fires brought down on so insolent a town. He healed the ungrateful and yielded to those who plotted against him.
comments.selected_reason: Shows in the life of Christ what it means that he does not cry out or break a bruised reed.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: God gives the breath of life to those who have risen above sensible things, His people.
comments.comment: God offers this breath [of life] to those who have ascended far above the sensible things and tread upon them, called His people, just as the prophet says concerning him: 'Thus says the Lord God who made the heavens and established the earth, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it' (Isaiah 42:5); it is evident what is the earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is appointed a covenant because Moses was only a minister of shadow, while Christ is the mediator of a new covenant that renews man for worship in spirit and truth.
comments.comment: For our Lord Jesus Christ has been appointed by God the Father as a covenant for the race according to the flesh, I mean those of Israel, to whom God promised long ago through one of the prophets, saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and for the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers” (Jeremiah 31:31-32). For the divine Moses was a minister of shadow and type, standing in the rank of a suppliant; but Christ, as Son and Lord, became the arbiter of a new covenant. I call it new because it reshapes man into the newness of a holy life, and through the Gospel way of life shows him to be an approved and true worshipper; for “God is Spirit,” it says, “and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'a covenant of the race' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is light of the nations because Satan had darkened their hearts, and as the true light He scattered that darkness and freed those held by the chains of their sins.
comments.comment:
So He has been appointed as a covenant of the race and as a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and to bring out of bonds those who are bound. For Satan, the author of evil, darkened the hearts of the nations; for “they became futile in their reasonings, and claiming to be wise they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things” (Romans 1:21-23).

But the true light (John 1:9), that is, Christ, rose for us as a spiritual morning star and as the sun of righteousness (Malachi 4:2); spreading the ray of the true knowledge of God, He scattered the darkness that the devil's deceit had brought down on those upon the earth, and He set free from their bonds those who were held fast, beyond escape, by the chains of their own sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the light of the nations and the opening of blind eyes.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father's glory, which He gives to no other, is given to the Son, who is another only as a distinct person.
comments.comment: Yet I plainly hear God the Father say, “My glory I will not give to another” (Isaiah 42:8); and see, He has given it to the Son. The Son, then, is not other than He, except in His own hypostasis [distinct person] and in His distinct existence; otherwise the Father would seem to have spoken falsely when He set His own glory in the face of the Son.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The new song suits the newness of what has happened, since in Christ we are a new creation.
comments.comment:
For he commands those who have received mercy from God to glorify him, and he speaks thus: 'Sing to the Lord a new song, you his dominion; glorify his name from the end of the earth, you who go down to the sea and sail on it, you islands and those who dwell in them' (Isaiah 42:10).

The song is new, and fitting for the newness of what has taken place. For 'if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,' as it is written, 'the old things have passed away, and all things have become new' (2 Corinthians 5:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the song is called new.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What Israel received at the exodus has its far better counterpart in us, rescued from spiritual slavery, crossing the sea of this life and entering the promised land.
comments.comment:
Those of the blood of Israel were indeed redeemed from the greed of the Egyptians, with the all-wise Moses acting as mediator at that time. They were rescued from brick-making, from the empty sweat spent on earthly tasks, from the savagery of the taskmasters, and from the inhumanity of the ruler. They were brought across through the midst of the sea, they ate the manna in the wilderness, they drank water from the rock, they crossed the Jordan with dry feet, and they were brought into the land of promise.

In our case all these things are new, and beyond comparison better than the old. For we have been rescued not from a slavery of the flesh but rather from a spiritual one, and in place of earthly tasks we have been set free from the defilements that come from love of the flesh. We did not flee Egyptian taskmasters, nor a tyrant who was godless and savage, yet a man like us, but rather the wicked and unclean demons who drive us into sin, and the one who stands over their herds, that is, Satan.

We crossed, as though it were a sea, the surge of this present life, with its turmoil and its truly pointless distractions. We ate the spiritual manna, the bread from heaven that gives life to the world (John 6:33). We drank water from the rock, delighting in the streams of Christ, spiritual streams, of course (compare 1 Corinthians 10:4). We crossed the Jordan when we were counted worthy of holy baptism, and we entered the land promised to the saints and fitting for them, which the Savior himself also mentions when he says: 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the land' (Matthew 5:5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The song had to come from those ruled by Him and to rise from one end of the earth to the other, since God was once known only in Judea.
comments.comment: So for new achievements the song had to be new, coming from 'his dominion,' that is, from those who have come to be under him and are ruled by him. And this song, that is, the praise fitting for him, had to arise not only in the land of the Jews but from one end of the earth to the other, that is, through all that is under heaven. For of old God was known in Judea, and his name was great in Israel alone (Psalm 76:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the song is sung from the end of the earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's long silence is His long-suffering, which will not last forever, and His threats come out of much goodness to turn sinners to repentance.
comments.comment: … 'I was silent from eternity, shall I also be silent forever?' (Isaiah 42:14). I was long-suffering, I did not go out against the evils being done. This shall not be forever. Goodness is again known by the one threatening the one already being punished, so that through the threat he may be stirred up and be brought to repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God's silence in the verse means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul is blind when it is ignorant of the things of God, for those with open ears did not hear.
comments.comment: That the soul is blind when it is ignorant of things concerning God, Isaiah testifies, saying: 'And the servants of God were blinded' (Isaiah 42:19). How were they blinded? For, he says, you have repeatedly failed to take heed, having open ears, and you did not hear. And who is blind, but my children? And who is deaf, but their rulers?
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: To give ear is not merely to hear but to lodge God's word in the mind, and the history of Israel is told so that later hearers avoid the same faults.
comments.comment:
It is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture to say 'give ear' when someone receives a word about necessary matters not carelessly or negligently, but soberly, so as to keep what has been told stored up in mind and heart. Such is what is said through the voice of the Psalmist: 'In my heart I have hidden your sayings, so that I may not sin against you' (Psalm 119:11). And in the forty-eighth psalm it is written: 'Hear these things, all you nations; give ear, all who dwell in the world' (Psalm 49:1).

To hear is common to all who have once taken a voice, or some other sound, into the ear; but to give ear is, as I said, to lodge in the mind something of what God has declared.

So the prophetic word here seems to be looking for those who listen more fairly, that is, more wisely, since it tells what befell the people of old for the safety of those to come. As Paul says: 'These things happened to them as types, and they were written for our warning, on whom the ends of the ages have come' (1 Corinthians 10:11). For we must not read the accounts about Israel to no purpose, but receive them for the good of the soul, and firmly refuse to be caught in the same faults, so that we may not fall into the same misfortunes as they did.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what giving ear means and why the prophet asks it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Fire is the burning trial of the soul and water the trial that drowns those who do not bear it bravely, and God brings us through both.
comments.comment: … To burn and to move the soul hotly, it is called fire; but by another thought, it is called water because of its drowning and suffocating those who do not bear these things bravely. This, having been passed through by the cooperation of God, comes forth for the refreshment of life, hoping for rewards upon them. And since the beginnings and the progress belong to our practical efforts, while the ends belong to the gift of God—giving to themselves the passing through fire and water, while writing the cause of the end to God—what are the circumstances of fire and water? It is shown by the prophet Isaiah saying from the face of God: 'Fear not, for I am with you; and if you pass through fire, flame shall not burn you; and if you pass through water, rivers shall not overwhelm you' (Isa 43:2). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not being overwhelmed by the rivers of the senses would be no great thing; the prize of the just is not to be carried off by the streams of the opposing powers.
comments.comment: … And again, 'If you pass through fire, flame shall not burn you, if through water, rivers shall not overwhelm you' (Isaiah 43:2), which is an athletic prize given to the just. And if someone took these things from the rivers of the sensible, it would not be a great thing not to be overwhelmed by the rivers of the sensible, with many and other evil things being expected of this; but it is a great thing not to be carried away by the streams of the opposing energies nor by the immeasurable wickedness of these, which is a reward becoming the just and a proper end. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God says that no one can take out of his hands those he has saved, as Christ also assures us of his sheep.
comments.comment:
… 'For there is no one,' he says, 'who can deliver out of my hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?' (Isaiah 43:13). For I have brought about the calling of the nations, he says, that is, I have saved those who were going astray. And who will change this, or rather alter it so that it is not so?

That no one will snatch from the hand of God those whom he has saved, the Savior himself assures us when he says: 'My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand' (John 10:27–29). This is plainly what is written: 'There is no one who can deliver out of my hands.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'no one can deliver out of my hands' means and ties it to Christ's own words.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God turns from the nations to Israel, who had slipped into idols, and foretells their captivity and the fall of Babylon to show his power and win them back.
comments.comment:
… In the words we have just read he has woven no mean exhortation for those called from the nations to the knowledge of him. He has shown that he alone has knowledge of the things at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, and indeed that apart from him there is no one at all who can save. Having set faith firmly in them by these words, he now turns his words to those of the blood of Israel, and tries to assure them that he is all-powerful and a worker of wonders, and that the natures of things yield to his nod. The very elements of the world serve him, and whatever he wills is brought to pass without fail, with nothing standing in its way.

For it was necessary, truly necessary, that those of Israel should have the fullest enlightenment, and the exhortations and reminders that would settle them in firmness of mind, since they had slipped into what is unlawful, and, inclining to other gods, had sacrificed to idols and to the host of heaven, as it is written (compare Acts 7:41–42; Jeremiah 19:13). So he foretells to them what will be, and very skillfully reveals beforehand the misfortunes of the Babylonians. He shows in advance that they themselves will be taken captive by the Babylonians, but he also proclaims in advance, as I said, that the Babylonians will suffer the most shameful things of all because of them. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God foretells Babylon's fate in this verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, the giver of their being, deserves their honor, and by promising help he gives sinners courage because a remnant of his gentleness remains for them.
comments.comment: … God says that He Himself is, and He leads them to consider that they ought to honor Him, as the one who has become the giver of their very being and the cause of existence to those who once were not. And by saying to those who have sinned, “You will still be helped” (Isaiah 44:2), He gives them courage: although they are caught in many charges they cannot escape, a remnant of gentleness and love for humankind has been kept for them. Nothing would keep them, too, from being saved, if they chose to pass over to what is better and more fitting and in keeping with the laws He gave. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God calls himself their maker and what 'You will yet be helped' offers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God offers Israel gentleness again, calling himself Former and Maker, since the Creator deserves more honor than our parents and is both Lord to be feared and Father to be honored.
comments.comment:
… He had charged those of Israel with their apostasy, with drifting away from their love for him and giving themselves over to gods that do not exist; for he had said: 'Your fathers and your rulers have acted lawlessly against me, and the rulers have defiled my holy things' (Isaiah 43:27–28). Now, with great wisdom in his dealings with them, he adds these words as well. For he does not let them be carried off into apostasy, or rather into despair, nor slip away altogether from their hope in him. He promises them gentleness again, wins them back by his usual love for humankind, and brings them round to repentance.

He gives them to understand that he has not wholly turned away from those who have sinned, and that Israel will not perish root and branch, since he has pity on them and makes the way of salvation quite smooth for those who believe in him. In calling himself Lord and God, who made and formed Israel from the womb, he seems to hint that Israel has also gone astray by putting the name of divinity on others and thoughtlessly attaching the glory of lordship to gods that do not exist.

He hints again that Israel did not know his Maker, the one who brought the human being on earth into existence when he once did not exist; for he firmly declares that he himself is Former and Maker, and as it were charges with ingratitude those who have leapt away from their love for him. For it is absurd that we should offer the highest honors to our parents according to the flesh, the divine law also awarding them this (Exodus 20:12), and yet that the Creator of the universe should not, far more than they, be extolled by us with the praises fitting for him and honored by our complete submission.

He says something of this kind through one of the holy prophets too: 'A son honors his father, and a servant his lord. If then I am a father, where is my glory? And if I am Lord, where is the fear of me? says the Lord Almighty' (Malachi 1:6).

For he is both at once. He is Lord, as holding the whole creation under the yoke and in service; for the divine Psalmist said to him somewhere, 'All things are yours' (Psalm 119:91). And again he is Father, as Former and Maker, who brought it into being. So, as though paying a debt, we must render to God both the submission fitting for sons and the fear proper to household servants. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse stresses that God formed Israel from the womb.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The beloved and chosen Israel is here the company of the apostles, called to preach the gospel and to shine like lights in the world.
comments.comment: … Here he seems to call the company of the holy apostles Israel and Jacob, understood as a single person; for all are one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). See how he says that this Israel is beloved and chosen; and surely it is plain to all that He would never have called those who had rejected faith in Him beloved and chosen. But since, being of the blood of Jacob, who is also Israel, they became precious and chosen vessels and were called to the sacred service of the gospel preaching, He thought it right to crown them with words so splendid, since they were to be like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life (Philippians 2:15-16), and guides into the mystery for all that lies under the sun. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the servant Jacob and beloved Israel are taken to be.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Fear not means be strong against persecutors, for God will refresh those who labor for godliness with the Holy Spirit, as water refreshes travelers in a thirsty land.
comments.comment:
… “Fear not,” then, he says; that is: be of good courage and be strong, keep a mind that endures hardship and is full of vigor, laugh at the assaults of those who persecute you, and hold your faith in God firm. For a great many fight against the sacred preaching, and an unholy multitude will rise up against you, working against the words you speak. But be stronger than fear, he says, than hesitation and faint-heartedness. For “I will give water to those who walk in a waterless land” (Isaiah 44:3).

For those who walk through a thirsty land it is sweet and life-saving to come upon springs of water. And for those who labor for the sake of godliness, we say, it is still more longed for to be watered by divine and spiritual streams, that is, by the comforts given through the Spirit, by which the human mind, when it has somehow grown faint, may soon be strengthened again for courage. The water here, which God promises to supply to those who walk in a waterless land, we say is the Holy Spirit. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the water promised to those in a waterless land.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those in ignorance receive baptism, and God's Spirit poured out on them makes it overflow like plants sprouting beside water.
comments.comment: … Isaiah says similarly: 'I will give water in thirst to those going in no-water; I will pour my spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children; and they shall rise up in the midst of water like grass, and like a willow tree beside running water' (Isaiah 44:3). And this contains an intellectual division through hidden things. For those in ignorance, he says, happen to receive the baptism, and because of this, 'those going in no-water,' 'I will pour my spirit' is able to make the baptismal pool overflow upon them like the sprouts of plants, and: 'like the tree planted by the outlets of the waters; which will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not wither' (Psalm 1:3). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heavens rejoice because God has mercy on Israel, and the foundations of the earth that sound the trumpet are the apostles and evangelists, who build up the faith upon Christ the foundation.
comments.comment:
… So while the heavens rejoiced because God had mercy on Israel (Isaiah 44:23), and not only on Israel according to the flesh but also on the Israel understood according to the spirit, the foundations of the earth sounded the trumpet, that is, those who perform the sacred service of the gospel oracles. Their piercing sound was carried everywhere, and like sacred trumpets they cried aloud, proclaiming the Savior’s glory to people everywhere and calling to the knowledge of Christ both those of the circumcision and those who once worshiped the creation rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25).

For what reason do we say they are called the foundations of the earth? Christ is indeed the foundation of all and the unshakable base, who upholds all things and holds firm in well-being whatever has been set upon Him. For on Him we are all built up, a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5), fitted together through the Spirit into a holy temple, into His dwelling place (Ephesians 2:20-22). For He dwells in our hearts through faith (Ephesians 3:17). But the apostles and evangelists may be understood as foundations nearer to Him and closer than we are, since they became eyewitnesses and ministers of the word (Luke 1:2), and became also a firm support for the faith. For when we recognize that we must follow their traditions, we shall keep our faith in Christ straight and undistorted. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'foundations of the earth' that sound the trumpet are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles are called foundations and mountains because their knowledge is laid beneath those who came after, and their sound, unlike the weak voice of Moses, goes out to all the earth.
comments.comment:
… For somewhere He said to the godly Peter, when Peter was wisely and blamelessly confessing his faith in Him and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16): “You are Peter, and on this rock I will found My Church” (Matthew 16:18). By the rock, I think, He means the disciple’s unshakable firmness in faith. It is also said somewhere through the voice of the Psalmist: “His foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 87:1). The holy apostles and evangelists may very fitly be compared to holy mountains; their knowledge has been laid like a foundation for those who came after them, and it does not let those whom they gathered in their net fall away into what is counterfeit in faith.

So the foundations of the earth sound the trumpet. But notice the exactness of the words. Moses was weak of voice and slow of tongue (Exodus 4:10), for the Law could be heard only by those in Judea. But sound the trumpet, you who are ambassadors for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:20)! “For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18). He has commanded the mountains to shout for joy (Isaiah 44:23), here again calling the foundations of the earth mountains. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God shows the diviners' prophecies to be false, while he stands every word of his child Christ and the counsel of those who proclaim the faith, proving them true by signs and wonders.
comments.comment: … ‘Who else will scatter signs of ventriloquists and the prophecies from a heart, turning wise ones backward, and making foolish their counsel, and standing words of his child and making true the counsel of his angels?’ (Isaiah 44:24–26) For the prophecies from a heart he shows stale and false-speaking; yet of his own child—that is Christ—he stands every word; and the counsel of his angels—that is, as many as the heralds of the faith upon him should wish to speak—these he shows all full of truth, witnessing with signs and wonders, and the other workings of the Spirit. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: Bodily and external things are loosely called goods or evils, and the sayings that God creates evils trouble readers who cannot tell what Scripture means by them.
comments.comment: But we may also find bodily and external things called goods and evils in a looser sense: those that contribute to life according to nature are regarded as goods, and those that work against it as evils.
