It is in this sense that Job says to his wife: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). Now in the divine Scriptures we find, in one place, God saying in his own person, “I am he who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7), and in another place, again about him, “that evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen” (Micah 1:12–13). These texts have troubled many who read Scripture, since they cannot discern what Scripture means by goods and evils. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God creates bodily or external evils to purify and train those unwilling to be trained by teaching.
comments.comment: … In this way we also explain “who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7): he creates bodily or external evils, purifying and training those who were unwilling to be trained by word and sound teaching. So much, then, for “How did God make evils?”
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense God 'creates evils'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The mercy and righteousness that spring from the earth are Christ himself, who became our righteousness and was born in the flesh of a woman who was of the earth.
comments.comment:
… One might also say that the mercy and righteousness that rises from the earth, or springs up from it (Isaiah 45:8), is our Lord Jesus Christ Himself. For He has become for us, from God the Father, mercy and righteousness (compare 1 Corinthians 1:30), since it is true that in Him we received mercy and were justified, receiving forgiveness of our old offenses; that is, from Him we have received the righteousness that can bring us to our share in every good, the righteousness by which we have also been saved.

If the earth is commanded to make righteousness spring up, let no one be annoyed, when he considers that the Psalmist too says somewhere, of God the Father and of Emmanuel Himself: “He worked righteousness in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74:12). For Christ did not bring His own flesh down to us from above, out of heaven; rather, He was born according to the flesh of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who was herself one of those on the earth. So when He is said to have become the fruit and shoot of the earth, you will understand, as I said, that He was born according to the flesh of a woman taken for this service, though she was one of those from the earth. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the righteousness springing up from the earth is taken to mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The clouds that rain down righteousness are not visible clouds but divine men who pour out the word of virtue, and the rejoicing heaven is the blessed natures above or the Savior.
comments.comment: … And in Isaiah, among the clouds, it is remembered thus: 'Let the heaven rejoice anew and let the clouds rain down righteousness' (Isaiah 45:8). But perceptible clouds do not rain down righteousness or truth, but rain down water. The clouds raining not righteousness are divine men, pouring forth the spiritual rain, that is, the word according to virtue. And above these, a heaven rejoicing, meaning the blessed natures inhabiting the heaven, or the Savior is allegorically so named; for the heaven above is, that is, above every generated nature, and it rejoices for the benefit of all. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If we are good earth, the clouds, whether angels or men, pour the spiritual rain, and men are commanded to sprinkle righteousness, not water.
comments.comment: … If, then, we are so as to be “approved earth” and “bringing forth useful vegetation,” the “clouds” pour the “rain” that increases the spiritual “vegetations.” Again: the ministering angels? — “Are they not all ministering spirits sent forth for service for those who are about to inherit salvation?” (Heb 1:14). And men too minister the divine “rain,” and to these it is commanded to “sprinkle righteousness” (Isa 45:8), not to “sprinkle” water, not to pour rain. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's words 'I am' give the reason the Son, true God, took the form of a servant and cared so much for those on the earth.
comments.comment:
“I am the Lord God, who created you. What better thing have I made, like a potter’s clay?” (Isaiah 45:8-9).

Here He gives, as it were, the reason why the Son, though He is God by nature, emptied Himself, chose even to suffer for us, and counted those on the earth worthy of so great a care that He gave up His own life in exchange for them; or rather, why He consented to take the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and to exchange the supreme glory for the lowliness of human nature. That is why He says, “I am”; this is to be taken here in place of “I subsist and live,” since He is true God and Lord of hosts, who brought all things into being, who did not make death but rather created all things for incorruption (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13-14; 2:23). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The earth opens to bring forth a shoot before receiving seed, which is fulfilled in the Virgin's childbirth, and the woe falls on those who deny God's promise that a virgin could conceive.
comments.comment: The earth opens to bring forth a shoot before it receives seed through the cultivator's work. This is fulfilled in the Virgin's childbirth: through the gift of motherhood she preceded and excluded the function of a wife. Almighty God promises to do what was not customary. Foreseeing the multitude of unbelievers, he adds: “Woe to one who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earth's earthenware!” (Isaiah 45:9). That is: “Woe to those who, despite God's promise, insist that a virgin could not become pregnant! Although every one of them is shaped in a mother's womb from seeds established by God, with God's power intervening, they obstinately insist that flesh could not have been fashioned from the Virgin's flesh without a man's service” (compare Luke 1:34–35). …
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The potter is only a comparison, and the newer translation shows that the passage, historically about Cyrus, foretells the Savior's birth from the Virgin.
comments.comment:
Both the prophet and the apostle therefore introduced the potter as an example to serve only as a comparison, not to indicate that human beings are as worthless in God's sight as clay is in potters' kiln and wheel. Having completed the explanation just given, we point out that according to the recent translation another meaning shines out in the same passage: “Drop dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one. Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together with him. I, the Lord, created him. Woe to one who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earth's earthenware! Does the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and ‘Your work has no hands’?” (Isaiah 45:8–9).

Although historically these words describe King Cyrus, prophetically they describe the Savior's incarnation. Since he was to be born of the Virgin, the stubbornness of Jews and all unbelievers is challenged, so that they may not be enemies of trustworthy signs. For after saying, “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together with him”, he said: “I, the Lord, created him.”
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: God does not forbid examining his judgment but explains his reasons so as not to seem to act by power alone, here announcing to captive Israel that redemption is near and why they suffered.
comments.comment: These arguments concern the apostle's testimony. In Isaiah, however, from whom Paul took the statement itself, God is so far from deterring rational creatures from examining his judgment that he deigns to explain the reasoning of his dealings, lest he seem to have acted by power alone rather than justice. Through the same prophet he had said: “Cease acting perversely, learn to do good, help the oppressed; and come, argue with me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:16–18) (Isaiah 45:9). Here likewise he announces to the Jewish people suffering in captivity that the time of redemption is approaching, when they will return to their own land. He discloses the reason both for their preceding distress and for their coming joy. …
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Human nature, formed like a potter's clay, is no contemptible creature, since we are made in God's image and enriched with the stamp of his glory.
comments.comment:
… Then, honoring human nature, and showing that of all living creatures on earth none at all could match it, He says, “What better thing have I made, like a potter’s clay?” For we were formed by Him when He took dust from the earth (Genesis 2:7) and shaped it very well, as a potter does. Yet the dignity of human nature does not stop there; there is in us something greater still, a guest-gift and a present from God’s fine craftsmanship. For we have been made according to His image and likeness (Genesis 1:26), and we have been enriched with the stamp of His glory, shining spiritually in our souls, even though according to the flesh we are earth and from the earth.

So man is no contemptible creature, but rather a living being on earth worthy of admiration; and God takes such pride in him. Indeed He said to Job, who endured so much, when He was setting out His mighty works plainly: “Did you take clay of the earth and form a living creature, and set it on the earth able to speak?” (Job 38:14) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the clay comparison says about the dignity of man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God counts all people as one, since each generation takes the place of the one before and we are all called Adam.
comments.comment: … In the present life these words could apply to one human being after another in succession, because as the earlier ones depart, there are others who take their place in their territory. For this reason we are all called by the name of Adam, as being those very ones, and God says, "I made the earth and humanity upon it," reckoning all as one (Isaiah 45:12). …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Working with hands is said of God figuratively, so it is not absurd that he works by hands or by commands, and what is done at his command is good.
comments.comment: … But let “working with the hands” be said loosely or figuratively, so that we may explain also: “The firmament proclaims the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1), and: “His hands set up the heaven” (compare Isaiah 45:12), and anything said like these, when we take the hands and limbs of God figuratively. What, then, is absurd in God’s working with His hands in this way? And as it is not absurd for God to work with His hands in this way, so neither is it absurd for Him to give commands, so that the things carried out by the one commanded may be good and praiseworthy because the one who gave the command about them is God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who oppose God are shamed, and no one can know him without confessing the crucified and risen Christ as Lord and God.
comments.comment: For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior (Isaiah 45:15). All who oppose him will be put to shame and disgraced. Those oppose him who do not confess that he and his Spirit are of the same being as the Father, and that besides him there is no God, and those who are ashamed of his suffering and his poverty. For no one can know God unless he confesses with the apostle Thomas the one who was crucified and risen from the dead as Lord and God …
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: Since he made heaven and earth, no one else can be thought God or equal to him in strength and glory.
comments.comment: … “I am, then, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:18). For if He it is who made the heaven, who showed forth the earth and did not make it for nothing but to be inhabited, who else could be thought to be God besides Him? Or who could equal Him in strength and glory? Or who could come near Him at all, even by a little? And how is the whole nature of created things not surpassed by a glory, strength and wisdom so great and so far above all things? There is no one. He alone, then, and no other at all besides Him, could be thought to be God by nature and in truth. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'there is no other' follows from God's making heaven and earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord who made heaven and set the earth firm is the one who is Lord by nature, as his works prove, and there is no other besides him.
comments.comment:
… Having proclaimed beforehand the coming of Christ, the Savior of us all, and having marked out the time of salvation, when all will leave the darkness of their old ignorance and pass over to the light of the true knowledge of God, he here gives a needful exhortation to Jews and Greeks alike. He adds clear proofs by which they will know very plainly that He is the God and Maker of all, and that there is no other besides Him.

That is why he says, “Thus says the Lord”; and not simply “Lord,” for there are very many in heaven and on earth who have received that name by a loose use of it (compare 1 Corinthians 8:5), but He Himself who by nature and in truth is what He is also called, and who, from the very things He has accomplished, has a glory that is not false. For this, he says, is the Lord who made the heaven. To have made the heaven, and to have shown forth the earth and set it firm, is a very great proof of supreme glory and almighty pre-eminence. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God marked the earth out by separating dry land from the waters, and made it to be inhabited so that those formed from it might worship him alone.
comments.comment:
… For He marked it out; that is, when of old it lay hidden in the deeps, invisible and unformed (Genesis 1:2), He made it visible and finished. He marked it out, for, as the books of Moses attest, He said: “Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9). So it appeared out of the waters; and though it was under water and wholly unworked, He set it apart by itself, placing bars and gates on the deeps (compare Job 38:10) and separating it thoroughly from the waters.

That He brought it forth usefully and of necessity to this end, not only so that it might be seen but so that it might have inhabitants, namely those formed from it, just as heaven has the holy angels, he made clear beforehand by saying, “He did not make it for nothing, but to be inhabited.” So it was shown to be a support and, as it were, a house for those who tread on it, that is, for us. And if we were brought into existence by Him, how is it not true to say that we were surely made for this very reason, that we might worship Him and Him alone, and acknowledge Him who is the Author of all things …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'marked it out' and 'to be inhabited' mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God says he has not spoken in secret, he means that he gave Israel his laws clearly and openly, not in a corner.
comments.comment: … Yes, but someone might perhaps say: “Who has known His purpose in this? Or who can tell whether He wishes some others also to be crowned with the glory and the name of God, or Himself alone?” So He answers this and says: “I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, ‘Seek vain things’” (Isaiah 45:19). I laid down laws for them about these things, He says, not speaking in a corner or trying to escape notice, but clearly and openly. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'I have not spoken in secret' answers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God spoke openly at Sinai and forbade idols; by righteousness he means the Law and by truth the teachings of Christ, whose outline is already in the Law.
comments.comment:
… For the Lord came down on Mount Sinai in the form of fire; there was darkness and storm and smoke, and the piercing sound of trumpets (Exodus 19:16-19; Hebrews 12:18-19). The whole people stood by, with Moses acting as mediator, and laws were proclaimed from God. He did not charge Israel to seek anything vain, that is, an idol or a falsely named object of worship; on the contrary, the commandments kept them from such things. For it was said to him: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve (Matthew 4:10; Deuteronomy 6:13); and you shall have no other gods besides Me. And you shall not make for yourself an idol, nor the likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth” (Exodus 20:3-4).

So it was said to him. And the words “I am the Lord” are as if He were saying, not once but many times over, “I alone am God and Lord of all, speaking righteousness and declaring truth” (Isaiah 45:19). By righteousness, I think, He means the Law, for the Law is the arbiter of righteousness; and by truth, the teachings of Christ. Yet the outline of the truth is present in the Law (Romans 2:20), and the mystery of Christ lies hidden in its shadows; for Moses wrote about Him (John 5:46). So in speaking righteousness, the power of the truth is also declared along with it, since it is true that the Law was a shadow (Hebrews 10:1), and that in it now lies the outline of the truth. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'righteousness' and 'truth' mean in the verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God points to his announcing the last things before they happen as the sign that no other is by nature and truly God.
comments.comment: … ‘Remember these things, and groan; repent, you who have wandered, turn in the heart, and remember former things from the age, that I am God, and there is not still besides me one announcing beforehand the last things before they come to be, and at once it was finished, and I said: All my counsel will stand, and all as many as I have counseled I will do.’ (Isaiah 46:8–10) For he was setting for the hearers as it were an indication of there not being any other by nature and truly God beside him—the being able to announce the last things before they come to be. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God cites his foretelling as proof that he alone is God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: No one can stand against God's counsel, and the bird called from the east is the Babylonian, who took Jerusalem and carried Israel off into captivity.
comments.comment:
But if the God of all wishes to do anything, what could there be to stand against it and oppose it? For “what the holy God wills, who will scatter? And His high hand, who will turn it back?” (Isaiah 14:27). So, as proof that He is God by nature and in truth, He may fittingly say: “All My counsel will stand, and all that I have planned I will do” (Isaiah 46:10). Then He adds to this: “calling a bird from the east, and from a land far off, for the things I have planned” (Isaiah 46:11); and to this also the words “I am” will be joined.

The bird called from the east and from a land far off we say is the Babylonian, who set fire to the whole country of the Jews, took Jerusalem and shook down the temple in it. Then, uprooting very many of both the common people and the notable, he carried them away from their native land and settled them in the country and land of the Persians, laying on them the hard and unbearable yoke of captivity. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the bird called from the east is taken to be and why God's counsel stands.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does not hand people over so that they may act without mercy, but they do so eagerly, as Pharaoh did toward the sons of Israel.
comments.comment: … To whom indeed is it said: 'I gave them into your hands, but you did not give them mercy' (Isaiah 47:6) and 'I was angry with them a little, but they persisted in evils' (Isaiah 47:6)? For God does not hand them over so that they may use mercy without restraint; but they, doing this with much eagerness, act without mercy; and Pharaoh toward the sons of Israel is such. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God shows star-sorcery to be laughable and useless by telling the astrologers to let their charms and counsels stand and save them.
comments.comment: … And he said somewhere again, reproaching some for the things adulterated by God’s law: ‘Stand then in your charms, and in your much pharmacy, which you were learning from your youth, if you will be able to be benefited; you have toiled in your counsels; let them stand and save you—the astrologers of the heaven, those seeing the stars; let them announce to you what is about to come upon you.’ (Isaiah 47:12–13) You see then how God convicts the cursed star-sorcery as worthy of laughter and altogether useless. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the challenge to the astrologers shows.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: God does not bring fire like a cook but as the benefactor of those who need pain, and the Word speaks grim things in a veiled way to frighten those who cannot otherwise turn from their sins.
comments.comment: … That we do not say God brings the fire like a cook, but as God, the benefactor of those who need pain and fire, the prophet Isaiah will also bear witness, in the place where it is written that it was said to a certain sinful nation: “Since you have coals of fire, sit upon them; these will be a help to you” (Isaiah 47:14–15). The Word, arranging what suits the multitudes who will read Scripture, speaks the grim things in a veiled way and with wisdom, to bring fear on those who cannot otherwise turn back from the flood of their sins. Even so, the attentive reader will find shown there the end that the grim and painful things bring about for those who suffer. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the coals of fire are for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jews swore by Jerusalem as the city of God and leaned on the Lord of hosts, yet they profaned the city with altars and sacrifices to demons and provoked the one they trusted.
comments.comment:
… “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God” (Psalm 87:3). The Lord Himself also recalls this, when He says that no one should swear by his own head, because he cannot make one hair white or black, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King (Matthew 5:35-36). For they used to swear by Jerusalem, calling it, as I said, the city of God. And they leaned on Him too, saying that the Lord of hosts was their strength (compare Isaiah 48:2).

But those who then held this belief ought not to have profaned the city of God with altars and sacrifices, entangled as they were in the deceits of demons, nor to have provoked against themselves the One in whom they trusted; rather they should have gladdened Him with good pursuits, bringing Him, like a sacrifice, a steadfast devotion. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses accuse Israel of: trusting God while profaning his city.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God says he himself declared the former things, which went out of his mouth and not another god's, and these are the misery of the war and exile, followed by what befell the Babylonians.
comments.comment:
… Yet “hear these things,” He says (Isaiah 48:1). And what are they? “The former things I declared long ago; they went out of my mouth and were made known. Suddenly I did them, and they came to pass” (Isaiah 48:3). For, as I said, in the beginning Manasseh, hateful to God, gathered from everywhere the so-called diviners and augurs (compare 2 Kings 21:6) and was always prying into the future; carried away by their charlatan tricks, he perhaps thought that he knew it clearly. That is why the God of all says: It was I who declared to you the first things too; these were not spoken to you by any other of the falsely named gods, but went out of My mouth; it was made known to you, and suddenly I did it, and it came. That is, even if you did not expect these things to come to fulfillment, still you learned through the events themselves and by actual experience that I both did it and it came.

He seems to call “former” the misery brought on them by the war, when they were carried off from their native land, took up the yoke of bitter slavery, and were taken away into the country of the Persians and Medes. For it was second, after those events, that the things brought on the Babylonians by divine wrath befell them, which we have already described at great length. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'former things' are and why God says he declared them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God shows incomparable gentleness and mercy even to those who are used to grieving him deeply.
comments.comment:
“I know that you are hard, and your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze. And I declared to you of old, before it came upon you; I made it known to you” (Isaiah 48:4-5).

Here he shows the incomparable gentleness of the supreme nature, and how great the mercy it shows to human beings, even to those who are used to grieving Him deeply. For its calm forbearance matches its own glory. And just as by boundless excellence it rises far above the measure of created things, so too it is beyond comparison in its love for humankind. …
comments.selected_reason: Says what the verse shows: God's gentleness toward a people he knows to be hard.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The phrase could mean that the Father and the Holy Spirit sent Jesus or that the Father sent both Christ and the Holy Spirit, and the second is true.
comments.comment: … But since it is a Jew who raises difficulties about the Holy Spirit, recorded to have come down upon Jesus in the form of a dove, we should say to him: Sir, who is it that says in Isaiah, “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16)? Since the phrase there is ambiguous, whether the Father and the Holy Spirit sent Jesus, or the Father sent both Christ and the Holy Spirit, the second is true. And since the Saviour was sent, and then the Holy Spirit, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, and the fulfilment of the prophecy had to be made known to those who came after as well, for this reason the disciples of Jesus recorded what took place.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to read 'the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The better reading names Father, Son and Spirit; the other has the Father and the Spirit sending the Son.
comments.comment: … Others, however, read it this way, and this reading is better: "and the Lord, the Lord, has sent me; and his Spirit also has sent" (Isaiah 48:16); the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The former version says this: that the Father and the Holy Spirit sent the Son. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The islands addressed are the Churches of the nations, surrounded by persecutions as by waves, and the speaker is the Savior, whose coming is promised after a long time.
comments.comment:
Having helped Israel by a great many exhortations and counsels, he moves his teaching of the mystery over to the flocks of the nations, and again makes the mystery of Christ clear to them. Through it they were to leave their brutish and accursed life, be brought back to the way of life dearest to Him, and receive the true light into their minds, so as to know clearly who is God by nature and in truth, the nature that rules over all things.

He addresses the islands, which we say are the Churches of Christ. They lie as if in a sea, that is, in the surge of the present life, and are surrounded by the unbearable onset of waves, that is, by persecutions and troubles, which the enemies of the truth, who fight against God’s calling, bring upon them. Of such islands the God-inspired Scripture speaks in very many places. Blessed David too sings somewhere and says: “The Lord has become King; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad” (Psalm 97:1). For when Christ became King over the whole world under heaven, taking it all into His hand and wrenching it from the tyranny of the demons, then the Churches throughout the whole earth rejoiced, that is, were filled with gladness.

That the prophet, in calling them islands here, means the Churches drawn from the nations will become clear from what follows. For right after “Listen to me, you islands,” he added, “Pay attention, you nations.” Then he says: “After a long time it will stand, says the Lord.” As I said, he promises the manifestation of Jesus Christ, the Savior of us all, and that the Word, though He is God, lives among those on earth in a form like ours (compare Baruch 3:38). Yet he shows that the time then was a time of prophecy, not yet of the events themselves coming to light, by saying that after a long time it will stand, namely what was promised, that is, what was being prophesied.

What, then, is this? The Savior Himself is brought in as the speaker, saying: “From my mother’s womb He called my name.”
comments.selected_reason: Says who the islands are and who speaks.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He is Emmanuel and Jesus, but the name Christ is given only when He came forth from His mother's womb, since one not yet anointed could not be called Christ.
comments.comment: So He is Emmanuel because, being God by nature, He came to be with us, that is, became man; and Jesus because, being God and having become man, He was to save the world under heaven. When, then, He came forth from His own mother’s womb (for He was born of her according to the flesh), then His name was also called (Isaiah 49:1). So I say that the name Christ does not suit God the Word before His birth according to the flesh. For if He had not yet been anointed, how could He be called Christ? When He came forth as man from His mother’s womb, then He receives the name, together with His birth according to the flesh. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of the name given at His birth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The same Savior is the bow, the archer and the chosen arrow hidden in the quiver, which He had from the flesh of Mary.
comments.comment: And behold the paradox: the same Savior is the bow, the archer, and the arrow. For in the present prophetic word spoken to Him by God, it is said: 'I have bent you, Judah, as my bow' (Zechariah 9:13); but in the Psalm, those praising Him say: 'Your arrows are sharp, mighty' (Psalm 45:5); and He Himself says about Himself in Isaiah: 'He has made me like a chosen arrow; He has hidden me in His quiver' (Isa 49:2). For how could the one fashioning those who are being pierced as chosen not be a chosen arrow, hidden in the quiver which He possessed from the flesh of Mary?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ was foreknown before the world's foundation but shone forth at the times the Sovereign willed, and the time of the incarnation is called a day of salvation.
comments.comment: He addresses the chosen and says: “In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). Christ and His mystery were foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), but they shone forth at the times the Sovereign willed, the times at which He has helped us; and the time of the incarnation he calls a day of salvation. So too, somewhere, the divine Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). And the prophet David sings and says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it” (Psalm 118:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some earlier interpreters took the words as the Father's answer to Christ's prayer about the cup, but the writer finds this implausible, since Christ knew He had to drink it and went through the prayer as a step in the divine plan.
comments.comment:
Some of the earlier interpreters decided to make the beginning of the present chapter the words: “Thus says the Lord: In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). And they say that these words were spoken by God the Father to Christ, the Savior of us all. They weave in besides a meaning of this kind. He prayed, they say, before the precious cross, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); and He was not heard, for He drank it. But since He trampled on death with the Father’s help, the words “In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” were of necessity said to Him.

But this account seems to me to be sorely lacking in plausibility. For He knew that He had to drink the cup, and that the world under heaven could not come to be saved except through the death of His flesh and the resurrection from the dead. Even so, He went through the form of the prayer as a carefully chosen step in the divine plan, so that His begging to be spared the Passion might accuse the bloodguilt of the Jews. For how would Israel have become liable to the charges of impiety against Him, if suffering had not been against His will because of its shame? Yet even so it became His will, both to take away sin from the world and to remake our state into the newness of a holy life (compare Romans 6:4).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The acceptable time is the one Paul says was fulfilled when the Savior came, when all had sinned and the earlier means of God's care, patriarchs, the Law and prophets, had not stopped wickedness.
comments.comment: This is the time about which he himself says through Isaiah, “At an acceptable time I heard you” (Isaiah 49:8). Paul also writes that this time was fulfilled when the Savior came, saying, “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (2 Corinthians 6:2). For properly the Savior’s descent also happened, he having shone forth at the consummation of the ages. For since the Savior came to take away the sin of the world, it was not fitting that so great a one should come and suffer for few sinners. When the time stood apart in which it is said, “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and there was no longer a righteous person on earth who understood and sought after God, he came who by the grace of God tastes death for everyone on behalf of all of them. And these things might also be said: when the human race had turned to wickedness, it was necessary for God, who provides for their salvation, to hinder the wickedness. And indeed this was done through many devices. Patriarchs were sent who were able by their own way of life to benefit human life, but when the law given through Moses also spoke against wickedness, they themselves despised the God who gave it. And when appearances of prophets and angels were sent to them, God did not cease providing for their salvation. And yet nothing more happened, but they were worn down into an increase of wickedness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The day of salvation is the day Christ came back to life from the dead, destroying death's power, and then appointed the apostles as builders of the Church from the Gentiles.
comments.comment: The prophet too mentioned this day, speaking as in the person of God: ‘In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you’ (Isaiah 49:8). And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation’ (2 Corinthians 6:2). On that day Christ came back to life from the dead, having destroyed the grim power of death; and then he also appointed the holy apostles as builders, so to speak, and spiritual craftsmen of the Church from the Gentiles, saying: ‘Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age’ (Matthew 28:19–20). Or would you not say that this is what forms the Church?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Those in bonds are bound by the cords of their own sins and those in ignorance are told to come into the light, and the promise of pasture in every path is seen fulfilled in simple believers all over the world.
comments.comment: [Of Christ:] He also said "Come out" "to those in bonds," since "each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins" (Proverbs 5:22), and he told those in ignorance to come into the light. These things too were foretold, in this way: "And I have given you as a covenant of the nations, to establish the earth and to inherit a desolate inheritance, saying to those in bonds, Come out, and to those in darkness, Show yourselves" (Isaiah 49:8-9). And at his coming one can see fulfilled, in the simpler believers all over the world, the words: "And in all the ways they shall feed, and in all the paths shall be their pasture" (Isaiah 49:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A virtuous soul is set free from the bonds of wickedness even in this life, thanks to Jesus, who spoke as Isaiah foretold: "To the prisoners, Come out."
comments.comment: … we must answer him that a virtuous soul is set free from the bonds of wickedness even while it is still in the life of those whom Jeremiah called “prisoners of the earth” (Lamentations 3:34). It is set free thanks to Jesus, who spoke as the prophet Isaiah foretold long before his coming. And what did Isaiah foretell him as saying, if not, “To the prisoners, Come out, and to those in darkness, Be brought to light” (Isaiah 49:9)?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sons Zion lost say "Make room for me," showing how great a multitude will be called, and the Church, the spiritual Zion, finds that faith in Christ has made her rich in children.
comments.comment:
… shows the multitude of those who will be called, how great and countless it will be. “For your sons,” he says, “whom you have lost, will say in your ears: Make room for me” (Isaiah 49:20). It is said somewhere to the spiritual Zion as well: “Enlarge the place of your tent and of your curtains; fix them firm. Do not hold back; spread out still further to the right and to the left” (Isaiah 54:2–3). We have read also in the books of Moses that around the tabernacle in the wilderness, the one made, I mean, of skins, wide and long courts were laid out, some facing the dawn and the sunrise, some to the west behind the tabernacle, and to the north and the south as well (compare Exodus 27:9–18). The figure hinted at the breadth and length that the sacred courts, that is, the churches, would have in time to come.

Yet even so, since the grace from Christ keeps on overflowing, the places everywhere are too narrow for those who have believed, so that the Church, which is the spiritual Zion, in her joy reflects and cries out within herself: “Who has begotten these for me?” (Isaiah 49:21). And I would say: faith in Christ. For through it you, who were childless and a widow, have become great in children. It has reared your peoples for you; and you who were once left alone have grown rich beyond all expectation, and have been seen with many children, you who were once bare and alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The multitude promised to Zion comes mainly from the nations, whom the apostolic preaching has brought to Christ, while the saved remnant of Israel is small, and the lifted hand means raised-up power.
comments.comment:
He has promised Zion that she will have many children, and fine ones, and that her children will come to such a multitude that she will need wider places than before and will be urged to enlarge her tent. Now he at once shows that the multitude of the children promised to her appears not so much from Israel as from the flock of the nations. And the thing is true, and one can see it from the events themselves. For the remnant of those from Israel has been saved, but it is small and easily counted (compare Romans 11:5); while the world under heaven has been caught in the net through faith in Christ, and the power of the apostolic and gospel preaching has brought to Him those throughout all the earth.

That this will happen, then, he makes plain by saying: “Behold, I lift up my hand to the nations” (Isaiah 49:22). “Lift up” means “raise high” and “exalt”; and the hand would suggest strength, that is, power. For when Christ was made known to the nations through the gospel preaching, He became exalted and renowned through the miracles He worked, and through the resurrection …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: After crying out against the Jews' disobedience and bringing in those who accepted the faith, the prophet has Christ Himself enter to set His obedience against their madness.
comments.comment: In the passages already read, or rather already examined, he has raised a very great outcry against the disobedience of the Jews. For he said: “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none to answer” (Isaiah 50:2). He then brought in between them the person of those who accepted the faith, saying: “The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word” (Isaiah 50:4), with what follows these words, and they raised their voices in thanksgiving. Now the person of Christ Himself enters again, as He is eager to set His own obedience against the madness of the Jews, so as to expose them completely as hateful to God, since they lift a proud and harsh neck against Him who calls them to salvation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who says "The instruction of the Lord opens my ears" speaks not of sensory hearing but of hearing God's intellectual words.
comments.comment: An addition of ears occurs at the common hearing, when someone is able to hear intellectual words. The physician hearing medical words has a medical ear, but another does not. The one powerful enough to say, 'The instruction of the Lord opens my ears' (Isaiah 50:5), does not speak about sensory hearing, but about that which is able to hear the intellectual words of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ sets His own obedience against their refusal, lowering Himself to human poverty and giving His back to scourges, His cheeks to blows and His face to spitting, in order to carry through the Father's will.
comments.comment:
“For I have called,” He says, “and there was none to answer.” They have grown sluggish toward obedience, slow and wholly without understanding when it came to grasping what would bring them profit, and the means by which they might well have escaped, and very easily, both the tyranny of sin and the plots of the devil’s malice. “But while they disobeyed, I do not disobey. For when God the Father willed to sum up all things in me, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:10), I lowered myself to self-emptying and came down into the limits of human poverty, appearing as a man, that I might become obedient even to death, and death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). So I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows; and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isaiah 50:6).

For these are the very things He came to suffer, when the boorishness of the Jews raged against Him like drunken men: Pilate tore Him with scourges (John 19:1), one of the unholy attendants insulted and struck Him (John 18:22), and others spat on Him (Matthew 26:67). But the One who suffered had a single aim: to carry the good will of the Father through to the end. Indeed, Christ said somewhere: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Speaking as a man, Christ says the Father became His helper and drew near to justify Him, and the punishment that fell on those who killed Him bore witness that He was blameless.
comments.comment:
So, to win life for those who believe in him, he did not refuse insults, or whips, or the trial of being spat upon, though he is God by nature and true Lord.

Then he says, as a man: “And the Lord became my helper; therefore I was not put to shame, but I set my face like a solid rock, and I knew that I would not be ashamed, because he who justifies me draws near” (Isaiah 50:7-8). So he speaks in a human way, as I said, and in no way out of keeping with the measures of his self-emptying.

Yet through these words he seems to hint at the judgment that came down on them for their impiety toward him. For he says, “The Lord became my helper.” It is as if he said: When I had given my back to whips and my cheeks to blows (Isaiah 50:6), and had suffered the sufferings on the cross as well, the Father became my helper. For he came to his defense, and did not allow his own Son to be utterly disgraced, nor indeed to be put to shame. For those who dared to fight against God have been punished, and have paid the penalty for their offenses against me.

By adding, “He who justifies me draws near,” he again deftly made plain that the judgment on those who had outraged him would not be far off or put off, but would come near, as it were, and follow close on the heels of their deeds.

We say that the Son was justified in this way. Since they dared to kill him, though he was righteous and in no way guilty of any fault, they have been punished, as I said; and the punishment of those who suffered it has borne witness that he whom they so impiously outraged was wholly blameless.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God is with a person nothing harmful can harm him, for the troubles of life such as poverty and sickness are painful but not strictly evil, and sin is far from all who are united with God.
comments.comment: When God is with one, nothing harmful can harm or injure, as the prophet says: 'Behold, the Lord will help me; who will harm me?' (Isaiah 50:9). If indeed one has walked in tribulations and pains, which is called the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4; LXX 22:4c), I will not fear the harmful things, having God with me. The evils here are not the strictly evil things, but the painful ones: poverty, sickness, distress, and the like, concerning which Job says: 'We shall not suffer evils' (Job 2:10). For no one having God with himself encounters evils that are the opposite of the strictly good; for sin is far from all that is in union with God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In "Who can harm me?", as in Paul's "Who is against us?", the word "who" stands in place of "no one."
comments.comment: In the Scriptures: 'What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?' (Romans 8:31) stands instead of 'no one.' 'Who shall bring a charge against the elect of God?' (Romans 8:33) stands instead of 'no one,' and furthermore: 'Behold, the Lord helps me; who can harm me?' (Isaiah 50:9) because of many things signified by the word, as it has been said elsewhere, now the 'who' lies instead of 'no one.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah's "Sarah who was in labor for you" cannot be said of the Sarah long dead, so it must mean the upper Jerusalem, the mother of those born according to the spirit.
comments.comment: But observe toward allegory how one becomes a child of Abraham and Sarah; according to the apostle, Abraham had two sons, one from the slave girl and one from the free woman; then, having led them into the two covenants, he says with something else that the latter became free according to the spirit, having spoken of the upper Jerusalem (Galatians 4:22-26). This agrees with: 'look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who was in labor for you' (Isaiah 51:2); for it is not possible to refer these things to them; for how could she, who owed death by nature many generations ago, still be in labor at the time of the prophet? Therefore, these things should be applied to the mother of those born according to the spirit, the upper Jerusalem, whom he prepared the women to have as Sarah for a mother through good works.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: "Hear me" calls the people to receive His words and not cling to the letter of the Law, "my people" offers them spiritual kinship, and the kings are the leaders of the peoples.
comments.comment:
So, “Hear me,” he says, that is, receive my words, and do not become unruly as Israel did, clinging to the oldness of the letter of the Law and seeing nothing beyond the types. The commandment given through Moses was laid down “until the time of reformation,” he says (Hebrews 9:10). But since the time of the incarnation is no longer awaited, but is already here, let the shadow give way to the truth.

“Hear me, then, my people” (Isaiah 51:4). In saying “my people,” he holds out to them the spiritual kinship granted to them in due time. By this too, I think, he puts them to shame, and makes them more eager to accept the word that comes from him.

He calls not only those who belong among the peoples, but kings along with them, so that you may understand the rulers, that is, the leaders of the peoples. For many were brought to this rank from the multitude of believers, and the divine disciples were their firstfruits. Then those who followed after them in their footsteps were given the name of kingship, since they were rich in the name of kingship and were also appointed to lead the peoples.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The "law" that goes out is the Gospel proclamation, a change of the old law for the better, in which the types pass into the truth.
comments.comment:
Here he calls the divine Gospel proclamation a law. For the new and saving decree is of another kind, as it were; yet it is, as it were, a change of the old law for the better, and a passing over of the types, which have run their course, into the truth. So Christ said, “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill. For I tell you, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things take place” (Matthew 5:17-18).

But the law in letters was given through Moses, while the saving proclamation, that is, the Gospel, went out through Christ (compare John 1:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah's "as smoke" gives heaven a fine nature, not a solid or thick one.
comments.comment: But concerning the substance of heaven, we are satisfied with what Isaiah said. In simple words he gave us an adequate understanding of its nature when he said, “He who made firm the heaven as smoke” (Isaiah 51:6)—that is, he gave the heaven a fine nature for its composition, not a solid nor thick one.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Things that began in time wear out like a garment, and the heavens' oldness means they are within time.
comments.comment: Furthermore, he says, 'And all shall be worn out like a garment' (Isa 51:6), referring to all things that are under necessity. For having taken a temporal beginning in their becoming, they grow old as much time passes by. … But the oldness of the heavens signifies not that they are before time, but that they are within time.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Where the Holy Spirit, adoption, unending good things and the hope of the kingdom are present, there is rejoicing, and pain, grief and groaning have fled away.
comments.comment: Where there is the supply and grace of the Holy Spirit, the honor of adoption, the enjoyment of unending good things, and the hope of the kingdom of heaven, there surely we must rejoice, and pain, grief, and groaning have fled away (Isaiah 51:11). For what place will pain have, and over what could there be groaning, where there is no cause at all for groaning and pain, but rather hope prevails, hope of exultation and gladness, of delight that cannot be lost, and of joy?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "I am" means "I live and exist," a title fitting for God alone, and "I am he who comforts you" means He gives every spiritual comfort and holds you up toward every virtue.
comments.comment:
Here “I am” means “I live and exist”; for he himself is He Who Is (Exodus 3:14). This is a title fitting for God and surpassing all others. For being and living belong only to the nature that is beyond all things, which did not receive them from another by participation, nor holds them as a gift, but rather is itself life.

So he says, “I am he who comforts you,” that is, he who gives every spiritual comfort, and holds you up with his help so that you stand firmly fixed, ready to go with courage straight toward every virtue. Or perhaps you will understand the comfort here in another way too. For through the Gospel proclamations the Savior was calling people to the washing away of sin through faith in him, I mean, to a share in the Holy Spirit, and to the boast and glory of adoption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God accuses Israel's leaders, who feared a perishable man, forgot their Maker, and said the Savior cast out demons by Beelzebul.
comments.comment:
But you, O Israel, he says, did not stand in awe of me, who am, but looked down on me and despised him who calls you to life; yet you were afraid of a perishable man and of a son of man, who have withered like grass. Then you forgot God who made you, who fashioned heaven and established the earth, and you feared the face of him who afflicts you.

Here God accuses the leaders of the Jews, who persisted to the end in opposing the Savior's glory, and, as far as it lay with them, declared it to be nothing at all. He worked wonders in many ways, but they poured out astonishingly bitter words on his divine signs; for they said that he cast out demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons (Matthew 12:24).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Zion and Jerusalem here mean the Church, drawn from Jews and nations, and the repeated "Awake" gives abundant comfort, since where judgment is bitter the comfort far outweighs the gloom.
comments.comment:
When you hear of Zion and Jerusalem here, do not think that only cities built of stone are meant. Rather, the word of the prophecy signifies the assembly of those called through faith, that is, the Church, drawn both from the ranks of the Jews and from the nations.

In saying “Awake,” and that quite often, he grants them the most abundant comfort. For just as, in the words of the all-wise Paul, “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20), so where the bitterness of judgment is great, there the comfort matches the calamities, or rather far outweighs the gloom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Strength is the strength that works in action and glory is Christ, whom we put on, so that He is the robe and the tunic of gladness for every saint.
comments.comment:
He has commanded her to put on her strength, and besides this her glory. Strength may fittingly be understood as the practical strength that works in action, by which each person's soul presses on with youthful spirit toward whatever must be done. And what else could glory be but the Lord of glory, who is Christ? To him the divine Psalmist speaks, at one time saying, “Awake, my glory” (Psalm 57:8), and at another, of everyone who believes in him, “You are the boast of their strength” (Psalm 89:17).

The all-wise Paul has made clear to us how we shall put on both the glory and the strength itself. For he said again, “Put on our Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires” (Romans 13:14); and besides this, “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

Indeed, the prophet Isaiah too brings in the person of the Church as a woman adorned in many ways, saying, “Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness” (Isaiah 61:10). So Christ is a robe most fitting for every saint, and a tunic of spiritual gladness, who gains for us strength and glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Church is made holy not by the Law but by being conformed to Christ and sharing in the Spirit.
comments.comment: He calls the Church a holy city. For she was made holy, not through worship under the Law (for the Law made no one perfect; Hebrews 7:19), but by being conformed to Christ and becoming a partaker of his divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), that is, by sharing in the Holy Spirit, in whom we were also sealed for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Historically the unclean are the nations that trampled Jerusalem, and spiritually they are the demonic powers that hold souls under their feet until those souls become God's own.
comments.comment:
He teaches this when he speaks to Zion, that is, to Jerusalem, which is “the Church of the living God” (1 Timothy 3:15): “The uncircumcised and unclean will no longer pass through you again” (Isaiah 52:1).

Taken historically, you will understand the saying in this way. The nations living around Jerusalem may be taken as the uncircumcised and unclean, since they neither knew the One who is God by nature and in truth nor had received the training that comes through the Law. They fought very often against those of Israel’s blood, so that in most places they were seen to be stronger than the strength Israel had, and they all but walked through Jerusalem, holding her thrown down under their feet.

Come, then, let us shape the spiritual meaning from what at times happened in history. The troops of demons, that is, “the world rulers of this darkness” (Ephesians 6:12), and with them the profane Satan, hold under their feet the souls that have not yet come under God. They pass through them, as it were, with no one to stop them, that is, no one to come to their defense. But when those souls have been made God’s own and have him as their glory and strength, then, yes then, the greed of those powers will come to an end. For it is written: “The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will rescue them” (Psalm 34:7).

So the uncircumcised and unclean may be understood as the loathsome and profane powers that produce every kind of filth, the wicked and opposing powers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dust to be shaken off is the earthly mind and the uncleanness of fleshly desires, which settle on those whose outlook is thrown to the ground.
comments.comment:
“Shake off the dust, and rise up, and sit down, Jerusalem. Loose the bond from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isaiah 52:2).

He now shows her to be skilled in boasts fit for saints, and he teaches plainly how she will put on the strength of her arm and her glory as well (compare Isaiah 51:9; 52:1). First he commands her to shake off the dust, and so to rise and sit, and to take off the bond from her neck. Here, I think, the dust should be understood as the earthly mind and the uncleanness of fleshly desires.

For just as those who lie on the ground cannot help being covered with dust and dirt, so in the same way, I think, the thoughts of fleshly uncleanness settle on those whose mind is thrown to the ground and whose outlook is earthly. So we who have been called into spiritual kinship with our Lord Jesus Christ, and who are about to put him on as strength and glory (compare Romans 13:14), must first shake off the dusty, earthly mind …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The name is blasphemed when the nations, who admire the oracles of God from our mouth, see that our deeds do not match our words.
comments.comment:
For the Lord says: "My name is blasphemed continually among all the nations" (Isaiah 52:5), and again: "Woe to the one through whom my name is blasphemed" (cf. Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24). In what way is it blasphemed? In your not doing what I want.

For when the nations hear from our mouth the oracles of God, they marvel at them as beautiful and great. Then, when they observe that our deeds are not worthy of the words we speak, they turn from this to blasphemy, saying that it is some myth and delusion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the name comes to be blasphemed among the nations.
comments.author: Anonymous (2 Clement)

comments.capsule: As spring crowns the mountains and woods with new growth, the coming of the Savior has done the same in us.
comments.comment: And I hear Christ saying through one of the holy prophets as well: ‘I who speak am here, like springtime upon the mountains’ (Isaiah 52:6–7). For what spring does on the mountains and in the woods, crowning the plants with new growth, the coming of our Savior has also brought to completion in us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The Word has no form or beauty for those still below and a more divine form for those able to follow him up the high mountain.
comments.comment:
… how did he not see that his body differed according to what the beholders were able to receive, and was useful for that very reason, appearing such as it had to be seen by each? And it is not surprising that matter, which by nature is mutable and alterable, can be changed into whatever the Creator wills, and can receive every quality the Craftsman wills, should at one time have the quality of which it is said, “He had no form nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2), and at another time one so glorious and awe-inspiring and wonderful that those who beheld such great beauty, the three apostles who had gone up with Jesus, fell “on their faces” (Matthew 17:6).

… But the account also holds something more mystical: it declares that the different forms of Jesus refer to the nature of the divine Word, who does not appear in the same way to the many and to those able to follow him “onto a high mountain,” as we have explained it.

For to those who are still below and not yet ready to go up, the Word “has no form nor beauty”; for to such people “his form” is “without honour, and falls short compared with” the words that men have brought forth, which are figuratively called “sons of men” in this passage (Isaiah 53:2–3). For we might say that the words of the philosophers, which are “sons of men,” appear far more comely than the Word of God preached to the many, which also shows a “foolishness of preaching” (1 Corinthians 1:21); and because of the “foolishness of the preaching” that shows in it, those who look at this alone say, “We saw him, and he had no form nor beauty.”

But to those who, by following him, have received the power to keep up with him even as he goes up “onto the high mountain,” he has a more divine form.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says he had no form or beauty.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah had before seen him in his divine and glorious form on the high throne, and afterwards sees him in the form of a servant, and so says he had no form or beauty.
comments.comment: And again elsewhere he [Isaiah] says: “And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty” (Isaiah 53:2). For before this he had seen him in his divine and glorious form, seated on a high and exalted throne, when the seraphim glorified him, saying, “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3). And after these things he sees him having taken the form of a servant and having come to be in the likeness of men. Therefore he says: “We saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was dishonored and failing beyond all the sons of men. A man in affliction, and knowing how to bear weakness. For his face was turned away; he was dishonored and not esteemed. He bears our weaknesses and suffers pain for us. And we considered him to be in toil and affliction and mistreatment. But he was wounded for our sins, and he was weakened for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:2-5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet who saw the Lord in glory says here that he had no form or beauty.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: The prophet speaks in the voice of those who did not yet know the mystery of Christ and supposed that he suffered for his own sins.
comments.comment:
Rightly, then, the prophet says: “This man, who was under the blow, who knew how to bear sickness, whose face was turned away, who was dishonored and not esteemed, bears our sins and suffers pain for us; and we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow, and in affliction” (Isaiah 53:3–4).

Look again, I ask you, with what skill the prophetic word moves forward here. It takes on the part of those who did not know the mystery of Christ, and who thought that he came to suffer as one paying for his own sins. “For we reckoned him to be in toil, under a blow, and in affliction,” he says; that is, we supposed that the suffering had come upon him from God, as if for some sins, and that he was in toil, under a blow, and in affliction because of that sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is speaking in the verse and why they judged him wrongly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ took up our weaknesses by displaying in himself the passions of our nature: the soul's distress and grief, and the flesh's weariness and wounding.
comments.comment: … Rather, the Word was displaying in himself the passions of our nature, taking up the part that was given over to suffering. As it is written, “He himself took up our weaknesses and bore our ailments” (Isaiah 53:4; Matthew 8:17). For distress, grief and fear are ailments of the soul; but weariness, sleep and the wounding of the body are weaknesses of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Says what bearing our weaknesses means in plain terms.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Isaiah's words point to the cross and Matthew's to healings, because the Savior's passion was itself a healing for men.
comments.comment:
How does the evangelist lift up the word brought to the cross according to Isaiah (Isaiah 53:4) into healings (Mt 8:17)?

… Isaiah brought the word to the cross, but Matthew to the healings of diseases; and he did this because even that passion of the Savior was a healing for men, and it is evident that his death also granted life to us.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ suffered not for himself but for the whole world, offering himself as the true Lamb to free everyone from death and sin.
comments.comment:
For he suffered not for himself (far from it) but for the whole world under heaven. …

The worship under the Law was of no use to those on earth for taking away sin, since the sacrifices of oxen and the slaughter of sheep were not what God wanted. So the true Lamb, “who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), offered himself for us “as a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2). Then, having endured death in the flesh, he set the whole world under heaven free from both death and sin. For One who outweighs all in worth suffered for all, so that he might rule and reign over all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The speakers who say 'by his bruise we were healed' are those who were in sins and were healed through the Saviour's suffering, whether Jew or Gentile.
comments.comment: Many arguments were put forward in that debate to prove that they have no good reason for referring to the whole people these prophecies, which concern one particular person. I asked whose character it could be that says, “This man bears our sins and suffers pain for us” (Isaiah 53:4), and, “But he was wounded because of our sins, and has been made weak because of our lawless deeds” (Isaiah 53:5); and whose character it was that declares, “By his bruise we were healed” (Isaiah 53:5). For plainly it is those who had been in sins and were healed through the Saviour’s suffering, whether they came from that people or from the nations, who say these words in the prophet, who foresaw this and, by the Holy Spirit, put these words in their mouths.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'we' of the verse is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since he was wounded because of our sins, the One who knew no sin suffered for our salvation, for we had long stood apart from God in enmity.
comments.comment:
… “he was wounded because of our sins, and made weak because of our lawless deeds” (Isaiah 53:5). Then he gives further reasons, through which one can see that he “who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21) came to suffer for the sake of our salvation and life.

For long ago we stood apart from God in enmity, fighting against his holy laws, not bearing the yoke of obedience, and refusing to serve him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the wounding is for our sins, not his.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God struck the human race in Adam, yet he also healed it, as Isaiah says: the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we are healed.
comments.comment: God struck us, then, when he condemned Adam to death, when he sentenced us to eat bread in the sweat of our face (Genesis 3:19), when he ordered the earth to spring up thorns and thistles for us (Genesis 3:18), when through the first-formed man he cast the whole race out of 'the paradise of delight' (Genesis 3:23). But having struck, he healed; having wounded, he bound up. How, and in what way? Hear Isaiah saying: 'The chastisement of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we have all been healed' (Isaiah 53:5).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the healing answers the striking in Adam.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The wound is the cross, which does not harm the one who bears it but benefits those for whom he bore it.
comments.comment: … 'By his wound we were all healed' (Isa 53:5). And his wound, they say, is the cross. Regarding the nature of the cross and the greatness of the injury, it is not a wound. But it is a wound in the sense that, as a wound to him, it is not harming the one possessing it, but benefiting those for whom he bore the wound.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He suffered not for himself but for us, so that his bruise is our healing and he is disciplined for the sake of our peace.
comments.comment: … For the immortal God did not come to save himself, but those who had been put to death; and he did not suffer for himself, but for us. For this reason he took on our lowliness and our poverty, so that he might grant us his riches. His suffering is our freedom from suffering; his death is our immortality; his tears are our joy; his burial is our resurrection; his baptism is our sanctification. … And his bruise is our healing: "By his bruise we have been healed" (Isaiah 53:5). And his discipline is our peace: "The discipline of our peace was upon him" (Isaiah 53:5)—that is, for the sake of our peace he is disciplined. And his dishonor is our glory. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the chastisement of our peace' and 'with his stripes we are healed'.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: He is called a sheep because of the slaughter, the partaking of his members, and the protection of the seal of his blood.
comments.comment: … He was called sheep: For he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before the one shearing it, voiceless (Isaiah 53:7). He was called sheep because of the slaughter, and because of the partaking of his holy members, and because of the immortal protection that comes from the seal of his holy blood. …
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms why the verse calls him a sheep.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Christ hides his divinity as a shepherd and puts forward his flesh as a sheep, so that the devil may seize it and be destroyed.
comments.comment: [Christ speaks:] … For as a sheep to slaughter I was led, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent (Isaiah 53:7). Since the devil lies in wait for me, wanting to seize my flesh as a sheep, but fearing the divinity as a shepherd he withdraws and flees, for this reason I hide my divinity as a shepherd and put forward my flesh as a sheep, so that he may take courage and approach, and approaching may seize it, and seizing my flesh as a sheep he may be destroyed by the two-edged sword of the Spirit. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why he was led as a sheep: the flesh is put forward so that the devil may seize it and be destroyed.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: If the prophecy were of the whole people, it could not say he was led to death for its lawless deeds, so the one who suffers is Jesus Christ.
comments.comment: But we seemed to press them hardest with the passage that says, “Because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death” (Isaiah 53:8). For if, on their view, it is the people who are the subject of the prophecy, how is this man said to have been led “to death” “because of the lawless deeds of the people” of God, unless he is someone other than the people of God? And who is he, if not Jesus Christ, by whose “bruise” we who believe in him “were healed” (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24), he who stripped off “the rulers and authorities” that were in us, and made a show of them “openly” on the tree (Colossians 2:15)?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As the times of the end are not ours to know, so how the Son of God became man is a great mystery that no one will declare.
comments.comment: … It is not for us to know the times or seasons which the Father has set in his own authority (Acts 1:7); but we must believe that there will be an end of this present time, and the manifestation of the age to come, the revelation of the judgment, the coming of the Son of God, the repayment of works, and the possession of the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. In the same way, it is not for us to know how the Son of God became man. For this mystery is great, as it is written: “Who will declare his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth” (Isaiah 53:8). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'who shall declare his generation' as the mystery of how the Son of God became man.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The wicked and the rich given in return for his burial and death are the leaders of the Jews, whose love of money carried them into their wickedness against him.
comments.comment:
[On the punishment of those who killed Christ:] … God the Father said something of this kind: “And I will give the wicked in return for his burial, and the rich in return for his death” (Isaiah 53:9).

By the rich and wicked he means the leaders of the Jews. For they were sick with an extreme love of money, and through it they were carried away into their wickedness against him. Indeed, although they had recognized him, they kept saying, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him and have his inheritance for ourselves” (Matthew 21:38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'the wicked' and 'the rich' of the verse are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ will come from heaven with the angels and distribute to each the fitting prizes, which is the dividing of the spoils that Isaiah speaks of.
comments.comment: … Christ is expected to come from heaven with the holy angels, and will sit upon his throne of glory, and will distribute to each the prizes fitting him, and the honors proportionally to the successes; therefore also wise Isaiah says to us concerning Christ: ‘Because of this he himself will lord over many, and of the strong he will divide spoils, instead of things for which his soul was handed over unto death, and was reckoned among the lawless.’ (Isaiah 53:12) In Christ therefore is the distribution of the goods …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what dividing the spoil means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The barren woman is the church, once without children.
comments.comment: When he said, "Rejoice, barren one who bears no children," he was speaking about us. For our church was barren before children were given to her.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who the barren woman is.
comments.author: Anonymous (2 Clement)

comments.capsule: The desolate one is the church, and the one who has a husband is the synagogue.
comments.comment: … And it is seen that the whole people is born by the word of God and the barren woman, who previously did not bear, is being born in entirety, to whom it is said: 'Rejoice, barren one who does not bear, break forth and cry, you who do not wail, for many are the children of the desolate rather than of the one who has a husband.' (Isaiah 54:1) The desolate is the church; the desolate is God's law. The one who has a husband is that synagogue which is called the congregation.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church from the Gentiles, once barren, is called to joy because she has far more children than she who has a husband.
