comments.comment: And the church from among the Gentiles, formerly barren, is called into joy, saying: 'Rejoice, barren one who does not bear children; break forth and cry out, you who do not labor in childbirth; for many more are the children of the desert than of her who has a man' (Isa 54:1). For truly, the church from among the Gentiles has become very much with children, more than she who has a man. The law of the man is the assembly of the Jews. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The call to enlarge the tent promises that the Church, confined at the beginning, would widen to east and west, north and south.
comments.comment: Is it not plainly what was promised long ago through the voice of Isaiah to the Church revealed in the last times: ‘Enlarge the place of your tent and the coverings of your curtains. Fix them; do not hold back; spread out still further to the right and to the left’ (Isaiah 54:2–3)? For the Church of Christ, confined at the beginning, afterward widens to east and west, to north and south, and reaches every place.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the enlarged tent stands for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The stones stand for the righteous, every kind of precious stone.
comments.comment: Some of the righteous, then, are carbuncle stone, others sapphire, others jasper, others crystal (Isaiah 54:11–12); and so the righteous are every kind of choice and precious stone.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cypress and myrtle that replace the stack and boxwood picture the repentant becoming useful and fragrant.
comments.comment: … 'Instead of a stack, a cypress shall rise up' (Isaiah 55:13), instead of being fruitless and thorny, useful and fragrant—for this is what the one repenting becomes—'and instead of boxwood, myrtle shall rise up' (Isaiah 55:13), changing from a foul odor to a fragrance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the plants of the verse mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scrub and fleabane stand for souls still untamed, which look like wild thorn to God.
comments.comment: … ‘And it shall be,’ he says, ‘that instead of the scrub a cypress shall come up, and instead of the fleabane a myrtle shall come up.’ (Isaiah 55:13) By scrub and fleabane, I think, he aptly names souls still untamed, which appear in the eyes of the Godhead like wild thorn.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Their readiness for idolatry and bloodshed was nothing new but long-standing, for they urged others to worship idols under leafy trees and some even slaughtered their own children.
comments.comment:
Having shown them to be killers of the Lord, he shows that their God-hating sickness and their readiness for bloodshed were nothing new in them, but had been in them for a long time, from of old. “For you are the ones,” he says, “who in the times of old urged others on to the idols under leafy trees.”

The Law given through Moses awarded them what was good for them and said plainly, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10; compare Deuteronomy 6:13). Yet they slid into such madness, or rather into a godlessness unrestrained and beyond all measure, that they became makers of idols, offered sacrifice to them, and urged others, that is, taught them, to worship under leafy trees and to crown the idols with honors fit only for God.

The God of all makes this plain through the voice of Jeremiah, saying: “Have you seen what the house of Israel has done to me? They went up on every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there they prostituted themselves” (Jeremiah 3:6). For they took over the mountain peaks and the most flowering parts of the groves, built altars and sacred precincts, and brought sacrifices and drink offerings there to the unclean demons. And there were some who did not spare even their own children. Jechonias, indeed, slaughtered his own son to gods that do not exist.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the idolatry under leafy trees refers to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The portion and lot of those who worshiped empty things will be like theirs, or else the slaughter they committed will become their own lot.
comments.comment:
“You, then,” he says, “are the ones who urge others on to the idols, slaughtering their children under leafy trees in the ravines among the rocks.” What then follows? “That is your portion, this is your lot.” “You have worshiped empty things,” he says, “and you will have a portion like them, and your lot will be empty.”

Or perhaps he means this: “You slaughtered their children in the ravines,” he says. “So that is your portion, this is your lot”; that is, you will be caught in the same evils, and slaughter will become your portion and lot. For what reason? First, because you became a killer of children; then, because you poured out drink offerings to unclean demons and lifeless idols, and offered up sacrifices to them.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A road is prepared when hindrances are taken away, and since stumbling-blocks differ for each person, God must prepare the way and cast them off.
comments.comment: For in this way a road is prepared when the hindrances are taken away, according to the words, Cast the stumbling-blocks out of the way of my people (Isaiah 57:14). For example, for the divine David a stumbling-block was the woman and the untimely encounter with the sight; for another it was food seen for pleasure, as for Esau; for another it was glory, as for Saul; for another it was a possession, as for Ahab (Psalm 119:6; LXX 118:6). Against all these things there is need of God, who prepares the way, so that he may cast these things off and preserve the love of what is good, drawing off the more violent impulses of the will and, as it were, drying them up because of the inclination of nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the stumbling-blocks of the verse are.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Men accuse God of not seeing their fast, and he replies that he did not choose it, but abstinence joined with good works.
comments.comment: But concerning the blameworthy, base and impious men accusing God say: 'Why did we fast and you did not see? We humbled our souls and you did not know?' (Isaiah 58:3). To whom, whom they impiously accuse, he says: 'I did not choose this fast' (Isaiah 58:5) — but rather the abstinence from poisonous foods done with good works …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sackcloth and fasting without repentance is a false repentance that the prophet rebukes in hypocrites, though harsh discipline does benefit when joined with repentance.
comments.comment: The false repentance of one wearing sackcloth is brought in the context of Isaiah against those fasting and praying, becoming a rebuke against the hypocrites: 'For if you bow your neck like a yoke and bend your neck and put on sackcloth and ashes, you will not even call it a pleasing fast' (Isa 58:5). I do not say this as if no one benefits from the painful discipline and harsh diet, which then becomes beneficial when it is accomplished along with repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is wrong with the fast of the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When a person fasts purely and shows mercy, God's light breaks forth like a flash of lightning, and rewards and healing come to the good man early.
comments.comment:
If you fast purely, he says, and show God hands washed clean and a mind set free from every stain; that is, when you scrub yourself clean of striking the lowly with your fists, of goading those under your hand into lawsuits and quarrels, and of following your own wishes and pleasures (Isaiah 58:3–4); when you break your bread for the hungry, clothe the naked, and bring the homeless poor into your house (Isaiah 58:7): then your light will break forth early.

The word carries very great force. For he did not simply say, “The light will be given to you by God,” but rather “it will break forth,” like a flash of lightning sent down from God with rush and speed. This clearly shows the eagerness of the Giver. And by saying “early” he teaches that it will come down even before its time.

For God, the steward of our affairs and the giver of spiritual gifts, knows, yes he knows, the time that suits his generous gifts to each person. But if someone proves good and upright, and compassionate and easy to guide besides, to him the rewards from God will be given early, so that they spring up in him like ears of grain. So too will his healing, that is, the casting off of every sickness and the entry of better things in its place.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'break forth early' and 'healing' mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the divine light dawns in us, healing rises with it, righteousness goes ahead to make the road to godliness easy, and the glory of God surrounds us.
comments.comment:
For when someone is freed from the sicknesses of the soul, he will surely bear the fruit of longing and eagerness for every good thing whatever. So when the divine and spiritual light has dawned in us, healing surely rises with it in every way, as God dresses our wounds, saps the strength of our passions, and puts in their place within us the will to do good and to excel in righteousness.

That is why he says, “Your righteousness will go before you.” It will go before us, plainly, by making the road to godliness easy in advance, turning what is rough into what is smooth and passable, bringing down what is steep, and, as it were, setting straight our course toward all that is best.

He adds something else as well: “For the glory of God,” he says, “will wrap around you,” that is, it will surround you, make you someone all eyes turn to, and make you a benefit shared by many.
comments.selected_reason: Explains each part of the promise: healing, righteousness going before, and glory around us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The brightness of the saints benefits those who look on them, so that we shall be radiant with the glory from God around us like clothing.
comments.comment: … [the saints'] brightness benefits in no small measure those who look on them. Indeed, Christ said to the holy apostles: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). So we shall be radiant, with the glory from God moving all around us and, as it were, clothing us, the glory he would grant to those who devote themselves to righteousness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God hears the righteous at once, saying 'Here I am' while they are still speaking, which shows his readiness to give without delay.
comments.comment:
When these things are yours, he says, then you will cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking he will say, “Here I am” (Isaiah 58:9). For “he listens to the prayers of the righteous” (Proverbs 15:29), as it is written. And as the Psalmist says: “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer” (Psalm 34:15).

Because he is good, he will grant the requests of those who ask, but not to all at once. To those who have excelled in righteousness, however, he holds out what they ask without any delay and lends them a most ready ear, so that over each of their requests they say with joy: “He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will come into his ears” (Psalm 18:6). So the cry “Here I am,” while the righteous man is still speaking and lifting up his prayers, shows plainly the generosity that will not delay and the great readiness of God who gives.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'Here I am' shows about God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By 'bond' he means wickedness of character, perversity and love of quarrels, and by 'the stretching out of the hand' perhaps taking bribes and reaching after shameful gain.
comments.comment:
So he says, “If you take away from yourself the bond, and the stretching out of the hand” (Isaiah 58:9). By “bond,” I think, he means wickedness of character, perversity and love of quarrels, and, as it were, tying knots of trouble against people and searching out crooked schemes, so as at times to bind people fast and throw them into snares of hardship from which there is no escape.

For a person must be straightforward and easy to approach, if he aims to be watched over by God and longs for the gifts that come from him. And by “the stretching out of the hand” he perhaps means taking bribes and reaching after shameful gain …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'bond' and the 'stretching out of the hand'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's 'Here I am' comes while a prayer for virtue is still being spoken, before the words of the prayer are finished.
comments.comment: The 'you have preceded in blessings' is equal to: 'While you are still speaking I will say: behold, I am here' (Isaiah 58:9). For example, suppose a certain prayer is being sent up concerning living well, concerning having virtue; it says: 'while you are still speaking,' not yet having fulfilled the word of the prayer, because of the giving, I say I am present.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Rejected Israel is to be saved in due time, after the nations are called.
comments.comment: “As it is written: ‘The Deliverer will come from Zion’” (Romans 11:26; Isaiah 59:20). He [Paul] confirms the hope that even rejected Israel is to be saved in due time, by setting out a sacred oracle. For Israel will be saved in due time, called last, after the calling of those from the nations.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the promised Deliverer means for Israel.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The glory of God that Isaiah says will be seen and will rise is Christ, who is the radiance of God's glory.
comments.comment: Proclaiming Christ the Savior, who is the salvation of God, they announce to all nations the glory of God, which is Christ, who happens to be the radiance of the glory of God; concerning this, it is written in Isaiah: 'The glory of God shall be seen' (Isa 60:1), and also, 'And the glory of God shall rise upon you' (Isa 60:1). For just as Christ is the wisdom and power and truth and righteousness of God, so also his glory is.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the glory of the Lord that rises is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah's call to shine is an exhortation to be enlightened by the true light, so that souls and the nations are led up by the brightness of the Church.
comments.comment: This divine exhortation is also brought forward in Isaiah, with the Holy Spirit crying out: 'Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of your God has risen upon you. Behold, darkness and gloom will cover the earth, but upon you the Lord will appear' (Isa 60:1-2). He emphasized as a sign that it is fitting to be enlightened by the existing true light: 'But upon you the Lord will appear, and the glory of your God will be seen,' signifying how the royal souls, held by the King of all, go forth by the light of the one receiving them, and the called nations into the gospel by the brightness of the glorious Church, as Jerusalem is being led upward, since one sees 'the peace of God surpassing all understanding' (Phil 4:7) through perfect height and royal eminence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The doves with their young are the saints with those they are teaching, such as Paul with Timothy and Peter with Mark.
comments.comment: These wings are thoughts having a heavenly dimension and magnitude, and from this they are called doves, just as the one who betrothed her calls the bride thus: 'My dove, my perfect one' (Song 5:2). And concerning the saints it is said: 'Who are these that fly like clouds and like doves with their younglings?' (Isaiah 60:8). The 'younglings of doves' are those being discipled by the perfect ones, such as Paul becoming a dove and having the young Timothy, and Peter having the evangelist Mark. And concerning the old times it was written that some were sons of prophets, whom if I call younglings of the prophets' doves, I would not be erring.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The day with the Lord as eternal light is uninterrupted, and the words are not about the visible sun and moon.
comments.comment: That long day, therefore, is uninterrupted; for it will be a long time before that time is fulfilled: 'The Lord will be to you an eternal light' (Isa 60:19), when the sun no longer fails, 'nor shall the rising of the moon light the night' (Isaiah 60:19). And these things are not said about the sensible luminaries; for 'immediately' 'after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light' (Matt 24:29). But these lights will no longer give light to those who are friends of this world; for the sun will be sevenfold and the moon like the sun.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sun and moon are not needed because the Savior is the unfailing spiritual light that the Holy Spirit puts in believers' minds.
comments.comment:
The Savior himself said something of the same kind: “In those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (Mark 13:24; compare Matthew 24:29). For the glory of the Savior itself will be enough to give the saints their light.

But so that the present words may seem in some way to follow the sense of the verses before them, we approve this interpretation and say that the present lines also signify something else. The light of the sun, and that of the moon as well, is useful and necessary to the eyes of the body. Yet at night the sun’s light is withdrawn, and by day the moon’s, for they take turns yielding the work of shining to each other.

But the divine and spiritual light, he says, which the Savior of all puts into the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit and through those who know well how to lead others into the mysteries, will be unquenchable, unceasing, and always shining. So the mind of each person stands in need neither of sun nor of moon to be enlightened or to see. For the mind is not lit by light that the senses perceive. It is content instead with the guiding light that comes through the Holy Spirit, and with a brightness that lets it behold the glory of Christ and how great a likeness he bears to the One who begot him, a likeness of essence, of course, and also lets it know without straying the way of the best life.

The Savior, then, has become everlasting light for us, and he makes this plain to us when he says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and again, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:5), and, “Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why sun and moon give way to the Lord as everlasting light.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: On the day the Lord comes there will be no perceptible light, since those who have become light no longer need something to shine on them.
comments.comment: On the day in which the Lord God shall come, there shall not be perceptible light, because of the true and eternal light making him bright, according to what was pre-proclaimed in Isaiah concerning the perfect illumination, having it here: 'The sun shall not be your light by day, nor the rising of the moon shall light your night, but the Lord shall be to you an eternal light, and your God shall be your glory' (Isa 60:19-20). It must also be said thus: those not possessing light need that which shines upon them, not needing this when they themselves have become light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some take the failing of sun and moon to mean the consummation, when those who mourn now will be comforted and their mourning ended.
comments.comment:
“And the days of your mourning will be fulfilled, and your people will all be righteous, and they will inherit the land forever, guarding the planting, the works of his hands, for glory. The fewest will become thousands, and the least a great nation. I, the Lord, will gather them in due season” (Isaiah 60:20–22).

Those who say that the time of the consummation is indicated by the light of the sun or the moon no longer working, but rather being withdrawn so that our Lord may become everlasting light, say that for those who mourn now, whom the Savior also says will be comforted (Matthew 5:4), there will be an end of mourning …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul that falls under the devil is freed from captivity by fleeing to Christ, who proclaimed release to captives.
comments.comment: If we see the soul becoming subject to the devil or also to his angels, and simply to the hostile powers—the soul that by nature is contemplative and able to see the things that are and to attend—we will somehow understand the captivity and the one who took captive. But fleeing for refuge to Christ, who according to the prophet Isaiah proclaimed “release to captives,” (Isaiah 61:1) we will be freed from the captivity, even if the one who took captive reaches as far as binding. For Jesus came “to lead out those bound from bonds and those sitting in darkness from a house of prison.” (Isaiah 42:7) (Luke 4:18)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'release to captives' means for the soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah calls 'priests, servants of God' the spiritual priests appointed under Jesus the great priest, a promise held especially by those who serve God in celibacy.
comments.comment: … To this great priest [Jesus] the angel of the Lord says: 'Hear then, O Jesus, the great priest, you and those near you' (Zech 3:8), the spiritual priests, those having been appointed under you being high priest, to whom also in Isaiah it is said they are righteous ones: 'But you shall be called priests, servants of God' (Isa 61:6). And they possess this promise especially, those who through all-pervading holiness in celibacy serve God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be clothed in a garment of salvation is to have a quality, like virtue, become a garment of the person.
comments.comment: Moreover: the 'to clothe oneself'? As we say to clothe oneself in a virtue, or to clothe oneself in a wickedness, or to clothe oneself in a 'garment of salvation': 'Let my soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a robe of gladness' (Isaiah 61:10). The quality becomes like a garment of the thing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The garment of salvation is the holy robe from heaven that Paul tells the justified to put on, which Isaiah foretold in the Church's voice.
comments.comment: Now the most wise Paul advises those who have been justified in faith that they must put on the robe that is truly holy and from heaven, writing: ‘Put on our Lord Jesus Christ’ (Romans 13:14). This is what the prophet Isaiah cried out beforehand, speaking as in the person of the Church: ‘Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness’ (Isaiah 61:10).
comments.selected_reason: Shows what the garment of salvation is and who is speaking.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: The angels who announced the savior's birth were proclaiming the one Isaiah foretold when he said a savior is coming to Zion.
comments.comment: Immediately after Mary gave birth in Bethlehem, a great angel appeared: 'A savior has been born to you today,' he said, 'who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David' (Luke 2:10-11). Those proclaiming his descent here were arranging themselves around the born Christ, according to Isaiah: 'Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, a savior is coming to you' (Isaiah 62:11); and this is no other than he who announced about himself, Jesus: 'The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10); and again: 'Just and saving, there is none beside me' (Isa 45:21).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the verse was read as fulfilled at Christ's birth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah sees Christ coming from the punishment of the unjust with his garment reddened from the slaughter of foreigners.
comments.comment: Isaiah also shows this in Christ, foreseeing him coming from the punishment of the unjust with his garment reddened from the slaughter of the foreigners: Who is this who has come from Edom, redness of garments from Bozrah, and the rest? (Isaiah 63:1). So the things that are referred to the Father in divine terms clearly belong to the Son and are fulfilled in the Son.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the one coming from Edom is and why his garments are red.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Isaiah says the Holy Spirit guided Israel in the wilderness, while Paul says it was Christ.
comments.comment: … Isaiah says that the Holy Spirit guided Israel in the wilderness. You can hear him say: “He led them through the deep as a horse through the wilderness, and they did not grow weary, and like cattle through the plain. And the Spirit came down from the Lord and guided them” (Isaiah 63:13-14). But to the Corinthians the apostle writes that Christ was the one guiding: “For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: The people say Abraham did not know them because those they boasted in had turned from them, so they plead for mercy.
comments.comment: The blessed Jeremiah says on behalf of the people: 'Lord, have mercy on us; the mountain and the city, which our fathers blessed, became consumed by fire; you, Lord, have mercy on us, because Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us; you, Lord, spare us' (Isaiah 63:16). Because, he says, those on whom we take pride were alienated from us, and they denied our race, you have mercy on us, conquering all through philanthropy. … For if our things were his own, he would not have interceded for his own children. He interceded for the Sodomites, and he was heard; and for his own interceding, was he not heard?
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Isaiah's words that no other God has been seen are read as pointing to the one born of the Virgin Mary and attested by the Father.
comments.comment: But Isaiah cries out to Him without comparison as the God the Father: 'From eternity we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides You' (Isa 64:4). … For we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary, nor did we hear of any except the one attested by God the Father: … 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even the righteous have a righteousness that is dim compared to God the Judge.
comments.comment: For he knew that 'stars are not pure before him' (Job 25:5), and what was said by those having been made righteous: 'All our righteousness is as a filthy rag before you' (Isa 64:6). For as toward you, the one being Judge, even if we have righteousness, we have it dim compared to you.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain sense of 'all our righteousness is as a filthy rag'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After lamenting over Zion, Isaiah at once announces that God is made known among the nations who did not seek him.
comments.comment: The restoration of Israel's affairs is laid up for them, as the prophecies say, but the church from all the nations enters in beforehand, leaving a second place for those from Jerusalem who will turn back. … Just as in the prophet Isaiah, while the word beforehand laments over Zion that she became desolate and the holy place became a curse, immediately the knowledge of God among the other nations is proclaimed, according to the words, "I became manifest to those not asking for me; I was found by those not seeking me" (Isaiah 65:1).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ foretold the Jews' unbelief and used it for the calling of the Gentiles, who were found by him though they did not seek him.
comments.comment: He did not come for this, to produce unbelief in the Jews; but knowing beforehand that it would come about, he foretold it, and he made use of the Jews’ unbelief for the calling of the Gentiles. For “through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Romans 11:11). Of these Gentiles the Christ who speaks in the prophets says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 18:43–44); and “I was found by those who did not seek me; I became manifest to those who did not ask for me” (Isaiah 65:1; compare Romans 10:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the verse about those who did not seek God applies to the Gentiles.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who serve the Master are called by a new name, Christian, and take their honor from it.
comments.comment: It was both necessary and wise to persuade them that they ought to take their honor from the Master’s name, as the Master himself says through one of the holy prophets: “But those who serve me shall be called by a new name, which shall be blessed upon the earth” (Isaiah 65:15–16). For we have been named Christians, and we are rich in the new name.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the new name in the verse is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The days of God's people being like the days of the tree of life means sharing its eternal life and bearing divine fruit.
comments.comment: And he who becomes like the tree of life is planted in paradise to be with it; thus it is heard of what is written in Isaiah from the face of God: 'The days of the people of my God shall be as the days of the wood of life' (Isaiah 65:22). This being true, since the wood of life is eternal, it joins and shares in the passion of Him; thus the likeness makes us grow together in the wood, so that we may be made branches and shoots to bring forth divine fruit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's promise to answer while they are still speaking means the perpetual hearing of prayers, enjoyed through Christ.
comments.comment: He brings forward the favor of God and the perpetual hearing of prayers, about which it is said in the prophecy of Isaiah: “While they are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isaiah 65:24) (Psalm 84:9). This will happen when we enjoy the honor that comes through Christ, with the Father looking on us as on the face of the Son, because Christ will be in us.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Heaven is God's throne because he rests on the powers above, and the earth is his footstool because he lived among humans in flesh.
comments.comment: That is why the scriptures name heaven “God’s throne” (Isaiah 66:1): God rests upon the powers above. For in heaven are the angels who do his will and always glorify him; that is rest for him. “But the earth is the footstool of his feet” (Isaiah 66:1): for in it he associated with humans through flesh. And God’s “foot” is his holy flesh, and it is named in various ways.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why heaven is called a throne and the earth a footstool.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does not delight in houses of stone, for he fills all things and is beyond place and quantity.
comments.comment: … God does not delight in the buildings from stones, he was teaching saying: ‘The heaven is a throne for me, and the earth a footstool of my feet. What sort of house will you build for me? Or what place of my rest? says the Lord.’ (Isaiah 66:1) For God fills all things, and rests upon heaven, yet also reaches upon the earth; for the divine is not in quantity, but just as it is farthest from bodily fantasy, so also from place and from seeming to have been quantified.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: God looks on the humble one who trembles at his words, and that person's cry reaches him.
comments.comment: For then we shall find God gracious, and, if we may put it so, looking on our affairs with his whole eye and showing the saints the sparing care that best befits them. ‘On whom shall I look,’ he says, ‘but on the humble and quiet one, who trembles at my words?’ (Isaiah 66:2) For the one who is in this state will truly lift up holy hands (1 Timothy 2:8), and his cry will reach the very ear of the Godhead …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Calling those who hate you brothers is done by disposition of brotherly love, not by voice alone.
comments.comment: 'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word; say, brothers, to those who hate you' (Isaiah 66:5). They hate and are enemies. And you, he says, call them 'brothers' not by voice, nor by utterance, but by disposition, or you demonstrate toward brothers by a disposition of brotherly love. And this is enmity: to have an opposing disposition.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'say, brothers' to those who hate you means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A nation of Christians was born all at once after Jesus suffered, and those once strangers to the covenants received the truth by divine power.
comments.comment: So something new has indeed happened since the time when Jesus suffered: I mean what befell the city and the whole nation, and the sudden birth of a nation of Christians, born, as it were, all at once (Isaiah 66:8). New too is this, that those who were strangers to “the covenants” of God and aliens from the promises (Ephesians 2:12), those far from the truth, have received it by a certain divine power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about a nation born at once.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
